So the Truth brings the conditions of ablution in preparation for prayer, after speaking of the rules on the lawfulness of foods and the prohibition of some of them, and some rules of marriage, so that we know that the responsibilities of faith are all interconnected, and it is not correct for us to isolate one deed and say: "This is a act of worship and that is not an act of worship."

When the authors of jurisprudence write books and devote sections in these books to acts of worship and sections to transactions, this division is a classificatory, compositional division. But everything that the universe requires in order to be set right is worship to the Creator of this universe, as evidenced by His saying: "hasten to the remembrance of God and leave off trade," which is a command, followed by another command: "Then when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land."

A person does not carry out one command and neglect another; rather, by the requirement of faith he must carry out both together. If a person is delayed in either of the two, he is sinful. Therefore, after speaking of the blessings He has bestowed upon us, including the lawful beast of cattle and what He has related to us about marriage with chaste women, He now brings us into His presence by preparing for prayer, because He is the giver of all blessings, and He commands us to prepare for prayer and that each one of us prepare himself for it.

This preparation qualifies the Muslim to meet the Truth. So He said:

{O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, and wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles. And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves. And if you are ill, or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then perform tayammum with clean earth and wipe your faces and your hands with it. God does not want to put any hardship upon you, but He wants to purify you and to complete His blessing upon you, that you may be grateful} [al-Ma'idah 5:6]:

He, glory be to Him, commands us with a specific clarity: if you wish to rise to prayer, you must carry out the process of ablution. The verse addresses the essential pillars of ablution, and some people may become confused and be unable to distinguish the sunan (recommended practices) of ablution from its arkan (pillars), because the sunan require that a person wash his hands, then rinse the mouth, then sniff water into the nose, and so on. These are the sunan that are intermingled with the essential pillars of ablution.

The Truth begins the essential pillars of ablution with His saying: "wash your faces." Washing (ghasl) requires the flowing of water over the limb, and that water should drip from it afterward, whereas wiping (mash) is touching with water so that it reaches the limb without water dripping from it; it is merely a moistening with water. When the Truth spoke in this verse about ablution, He spoke of things to be washed and of a thing to be wiped: the command to wash includes the face, the hands up to the elbows, and the feet up to the ankles, and the command to wipe includes part of the head. Washing may suffice once, twice or three times so that a person is fully certain of the washing, but if water is scarce, it is sufficient that he wash the required parts once and make sure that he has washed the required areas.

Exceeding one washing up to three times is a recommended practice (sunna), not an obligation. The washing of the face is perfectly well known to all. The face is that which is faced, and facing extends from the hairline to the chin and below the extremity of the two jaws, which are the two bones on which the lower teeth grow. This is its length; in breadth the face extends between the two earlobes, and no one differs over the definition of the face. Therefore the Truth stated "the face" without specifying a limit; He did not say "wash your face from such-and-such to such-and-such," but commanded the washing of the face, so there is no disagreement about the meaning of "face," and all agree upon it. This is when we begin with the essential obligations; but if we begin with the sunan, we wash the two palms up to the wrists first, then rinse the mouth and sniff water into the nose.

Some of those who know God say about these preliminaries, which are among the sunan, that they were not prescribed arbitrarily, because the definition of water is: the liquid that has no color, no taste, and no smell; if any of these attributes changes, the liquid has left the state of being water. When you take water in your hands you will be assured of the water's color and know that it has no color; when you rinse your mouth you are assured that it has no taste; and when you sniff water you are assured that the water has no smell. In this way you are assured that the water you use for ablution has met these attributes before you begin to perform the required pillars of ablution that God demands. The sunna has been put forward before the pillars for a wisdom: to provide the person with confidence in the water with which he performs ablution. After that, the person washes the face from the hairline and below the extremity of the jaws, its length, and between the two earlobes, its breadth.

After washing the face, the Truth said: "and your hands up to the elbows." Here the Truth distinguished the hands by specifying the area required to be washed, namely up to the elbows, so He added a limit that did not occur for the face. But the command to wash the hands up to the elbows came because "yad" (hand) is used in the language to mean the palm, as in His ruling on the male and female thief: {And cut off the hands of both} [al-Ma'idah 5:38].

The word "yad" is also used to mean the palm and forearm up to the elbow, and it is also used to mean up to the shoulder. So "yad" has three usages. Had the Truth commanded the washing of the hand without specifying "up to the elbows," some would have washed only the palms, some would have washed the hands up to the elbows, and some up to the shoulders. Because the Truth wants the washing of the hand in one specific definite manner, He said: "and your hands up to the elbows."

Thus, when the Truth wants something specific, He uses a wording that defines it with a clarity that cuts off ijtihad regarding it. The word "ila" (up to/to) defines the limit, just as "min" (from) defines the beginning. But does the limit enter the washing here or not? Does the elbow enter the washing or not? "Ila" sometimes includes the limit and sometimes does not.

An example of its including the limit is His saying: {Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed} [al-Isra' 17:1].

Did the Truth carry His messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, to the Farthest Mosque without entering it? No one could think so. Indeed, "ila"...

Almighty Allah says next: 

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey." And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ (5:7)

And a person may ask: "What is dhikr (remembrance)?" Dhikr is the preservation of a thing or its being present in the mind. If it is the preservation of the thing, then it is the preservation of its essence; but presence in the mind is of the meaning of the thing. So there is a difference between preserving a thing and bringing a thing to mind. This is the sense of dhikr. Dhikr may also mean speech, because you do not say a thing except after bringing it to mind. For this reason we find in the makeup of the higher nervous system a memory (dhakira), a retentive faculty (hafiza), and an imagination (mukhayyila).

Among the wonders of human creation is that events pass over a person in a past time, and he does not recall them for a long period that may reach years; then a circumstance of the association of ideas comes to him, and he remembers that thing which happened twenty years ago.

So the thing that a person perceived twenty years ago, for example, has not gone; and if it had gone, the person would not have remembered it. Rather, it was absent from the mind for twenty years or more; then, when ideas became associated, the person remembered it, and this means that this thing was being preserved in the person even though it lay hidden from him for a long time.

So memory means that a person summons what is preserved so that it comes into the focus of his consciousness. An example of this: an incident occurred between one person and another more than twenty years ago, and the person forgot this incident. Then, when he met his friend and they sat recalling the past, the friend remembered the incident that had happened to him more than twenty years ago.

So the incident has not gone from memory; rather, it is preserved and present in the distant margins of consciousness. And the more time passes, the more it seems that the person has forgotten the incident; but when the association of ideas comes, the incident comes into the focus of consciousness. When it comes into the focus of consciousness from the margins of consciousness, where the store of retention is, the person remembers it. This is the power of the Creator, exalted is He.

One of us may record some speech on a cassette tape, and afterwards he wishes to record other speech on the same tape, so he erases what he recorded first. But the human memory is different: when matters come into the focus of a person's consciousness, he remembers them. If another matter comes after them, the first matter must shift from the focus of consciousness to the margin of consciousness, because the focus of consciousness receives only one thought at a time. If the focus of consciousness is occupied with another thought, it preserves the first thought in the margins of retention, and one thought does not erase another. If the person wishes to summon the old thought, that is within his capacity. This is the difference between the recording of the Creator and the recording of the created.

Furthermore, we find that remembrance concerns meanings. What is stored in the human memory is not bodies; for if they were bodies, the brain could not contain them. Therefore meanings do not crowd one another in it, but rather accumulate, so that when the association of ideas comes, a person remembers what he wishes to recall. This could not happen unless the brain were made by the Supreme Creator; and since meanings have no space, a person is able to preserve them in memory.

A person may sit to recall the names of the mountains of the world and say: "Among the mountains of the world are the peak of Everest, the Himalayas, Mount Uhud, and Mount Thawr." When he recalls these names, he conceives their meanings; what exists in the mind is the meanings of these words, not the physical bodies of these entities. Therefore there is never any crowding among meanings; rather, they remain present and stored in memory and the margin of consciousness.

Beware of supposing that a person possesses such intelligence that he retains a thing after one reading, while another less intelligent person retains it after two readings, and a third after three. No, because a person has a mind like a camera that captures in one exposure. But if someone takes a photograph of a place and something blurs the lens of the picture, he takes the photograph again. Likewise, the mind: if a person wants to capture a snapshot of something so that it settles in the focus of consciousness, while there is something else in the focus of consciousness, the thing does not settle in the mind; rather, the content of the snapshot must be read a second time so that the person confirms the information and it imprints on the focus of consciousness.

An example of this is the student who enters the school courtyard where the examination is held. Five minutes before the examination bell, a colleague comes to him and says: "Did you study such-and-such a topic?" The student says: "No, I did not review it." His friend says: "This topic will come up in the examination question." The student snatches a book and reads this topic once. At this moment the student is not thinking about what he will eat for lunch today, or whom he will meet; rather, he knows that he is facing a matter whose opportunity is narrow, and he concentrates his whole mind to receive what he reads. In a single moment he memorizes this topic, and when the examination comes and he finds the question, he answers it with the finest details. And we may find another student who sat for days trying to review this lesson to no avail.

So the mind captures in one go, on condition that the person does not receive what he reads or hears of information while his mind is occupied with other things. The evidence for this is that a person may hear a poem once, or hear a sermon once, and memorize more than one verse of the poem or more than one section of the sermon, because his mind in that moment was empty and so it captured the verses he memorized, and likewise the sermon. As for the remaining parts of the poem or sermon, the mind may have wandered to other things. For this reason a person tries to repeat the listening, hearing and reading more than once, to prepare and ready the focus of consciousness so that he memorizes what he wishes.

So the mind captures in one go, but memory recalls, that is, summons the meanings that may be hidden in the store of retention. Nothing is ever lost in the store of retention, so that when summoning comes, meanings rise to the surface. It is as if the impressions of a person regarding the blessings of Allah are never forgotten; they are present in him, but they want the person to summon them from the store of retention and seek them.

Observe the precision of the Qur'anic expression: "And remember the favour of Allah upon you." Here He, glorified is He, says "favour" (ni'mah) in the singular, although the favours of Allah are many. Yet Allah preferred to use the singular and not the plural, to show the human being that any favour in any corner of human life deserves to be remembered by him. The favours of Allah are many, but so that a person may remember even one favour—the favour of bringing him into existence from nothing, or the favour of sight or hearing—and each of these favours deserves to be remembered by him always, and one favour does not expel another. How much more so when the favours are many?

And if a person were to reflect deeply on each favour, he would need to remember them always. Or the word "favour" (ni'mah) is a name of the whole genus, because the singular is applied to every genus, like "the human being," which is applied to each of its individuals, such as Muhammad, 'Ali and Khalid.

The word "favour" may be attributed to its cause, as a favour whose cause is the nobility of one of mankind, and it is limited by the measure of the effect it produced. But here we are before the favour of the Causer, who is Allah, and the favour of Allah must match the majesty, beauty and greatness of His bounty and giving.

"And remember the favour of Allah upon you and His covenant with which He bound you." The verb "wathaqa" (to bind by covenant) requires two things: the human being is the party of need, poverty and receiving, and the Lord is the possessor of grace, giving and wealth. He is the Lordship and you are the servanthood, and He is the Truth who says: ﴿And fulfil My covenant; I will fulfil your covenant﴾ (2:40).

So "wathaqakum" means confirmation from two parties, because the pattern "fa'ala" (as in "wathaqa") requires two parties. An example is "shaarak" (to partner with), which you say of two or more, as we say: "Zayd partnered 'Amr," and likewise "qaatala Zayd 'Amran" (Zayd fought 'Amr). When the Truth says that He "wathaqa His servants," it means He partnered them in this covenant and accepted it from them. But what covenant is this?

We know the first covenant, which is the covenant of the seeds: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾ (7:172).

It is the covenant of innate nature (fitrah) before the self and its desires came into existence. After that there is the covenant of reason, by which a person looks at existence and comes to see from that vision that existence is firm, ordered and vast, and that this existence must have a Finder, who is Allah. Then there is the covenant of faith in Allah. When the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, presented the method of Islam, some people believed in it; that is, he took from them a pledge that they would carry out what Allah requires. Did the Messenger not take a pledge at 'Aqabah when they said to him:

"Take for yourself and for your Lord whatever you wish." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then spoke, recited the Qur'an, called to Allah, encouraged Islam, and then said: "I pledge to you that you will protect me as you protect your women and your children." Al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur took his hand and said: "Yes, by the One who sent you with the truth, we will protect you as we protect our waists. So pledge to us, O Messenger of Allah, for we are the sons of war and the people of the arms (al-halqah, weapons), which we inherited generation after generation."(1)

This also happened at the Pledge of Ridwan under the tree. So the meaning of "wathaqakum bihi" is either the general faith-covenant in the realm of the seeds, or the faith-covenant that came through the messengers.

"And His covenant with which He bound you when you said, 'We hear and we obey.'" When a person believes, he says: "I have heard and I have obeyed." Thus the matter of the contract ends. Then the Truth follows it with His saying: "And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts." "Fear Allah" means: place between yourselves and the attributes of majesty of Allah a shield. What is required of us is that we adhere to the method of Allah with complete adherence. We must also place between ourselves and the attributes of the wrath of Allah a shield. We have known that His saying, "Fear Allah," is equivalent to His saying, "Fear the Fire." Someone may say: "Does the Fire have commands and prohibitions?"

We say: understand well about your Lord, and place between yourself and the wrath of Allah a shield. The Fire is one of the soldiers of Allah. Glorified is He, He clarifies: place between yourselves and the attributes of majesty a shield, because the Truth has attributes of majesty, which are dominance, vengeance and subjugation; and the Truth has attributes of beauty, for He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, the Enricher, the Wise, and other attributes of beauty. So let us place between ourselves and the attributes of majesty a shield that protects us from the soldiers of the attributes of majesty, among them the Fire.

We said before that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed us that on the last night of Ramadan the Almighty (al-Jabbar) manifests Himself with forgiveness. The superficial view asks: "Why did he not say that the Forgiver (al-Ghaffar) manifests Himself with forgiveness?" That is because (al-Jabbar) is an attribute of majesty which requires the punishment of the wrongdoer, and wrongdoing relates to the attributes of majesty and not the attributes of beauty. So logic requires that the wrongdoer stand before the One of severe vengeance, because the context suits the attributes of majesty. But we must well remember that Allah gives the wrongdoer rein, perhaps he will repent, that Allah rejoices at the repentance of His servant, and that His mercy overcomes His anger.

The verse concludes: "Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts." Piety, as we know, does not arise only from perceptible, apparent deeds; it also arises from hidden inner states. An example is an evil intention and a good intention. Spite, envy, plotting and deceit are all evil qualities. So beware of saying that piety concerns only what is perceived, but also what is sensed; and the work of the hearts has a role in the piety of Allah.

(1) Narrated by Ahmad and mentioned in Ibn Hisham's *al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah*.

Afterwards, the Truth says:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses to justice, and do not let the enmity of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness. And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ (5:8)

As we know, when the Truth addresses the believers with His words, "O you who have believed," He, glorified is He, does not impose on people's voluntary conduct regarding His method. Rather, He obligates and commands the one who has believed in Him and makes it binding upon him. It is as if He clarifies: "O you who have believed in Me as God, Wise and Powerful, take My method." But the Truth says, "O mankind," when He wants to draw all creation to belief in His existence. As for the one who believes in Him, he enters within the scope of His words, "O you who have believed." This address requires that the believer hear the obligation from the One in whose existence he believes.

We know that we are all servants (ʿabīd) of Allah, but we are not all worshippers (ʿibād) of Allah, and there is a difference between ʿabīd and ʿibād. The ʿabīd are those compelled to submission in every aspect of their lives, who cannot bring their choice into it. You may find a rebel who says, "I do not believe in a god," but can he rebel against what Allah decrees and what Allah compels upon him? If he becomes ill and claims he is not ill, what happens to him? Can any one of these rebels avoid death? No one can do that.

Thus every ʿabīd is subdued to Allah, and all of us are servants of Allah who summons us whenever He wills and carries out upon us what He wills beyond our choices. As for the ʿibād, they are those who come to what involves choice for them and say to Allah: "We have removed from ourselves this quality of choice and we are content with what You tell us, 'Do such-and-such' and 'Do not do such-and-such.'" So the ʿabīd are subdued by what the Truth carries out upon them as He wills, while the ʿibād are those who are content, and their choice conforms to what Allah loves and is pleased with. They have submitted their faces to Allah; they are subdued by choice, whereas the ʿabīd are subdued by compulsion.

"O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah." The word qawwām (persistently standing firm) is an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālaghah), and its root is qāʾim (standing). Whoever excessively performs standing is described by the word qawwām. An example: a man who is not a professional carpenter brings a piece of wood and wants to plug a hole in his door. This man is called nājir (one who does carpentry as a sideline), not najjār (professional carpenter), because his specialization in life is not carpentry. Likewise, the amateur who goes out to the sea with a fishing rod and catches two fish is called ṣāʾid (one who catches), but he is not ṣayyād (professional hunter/fisherman), because fishing is not his trade.

The Truth requires of every believer that he not merely be standing for Allah, but that he be qawwām, that is, one who excels in standing by the command of Allah. Standing (qiyām) is opposed by sitting (quʿūd), and after sitting comes reclining (iḍṭijāʿ), which is lying on the side on the ground, then lying on the back (istilqāʾ), and after that a person sleeps. We are faced with more than one stage: standing, sitting, reclining, and sleeping. The sleeper bears no obligation, and the one lying on his back is one resting on his back. The Truth says: ﴿So remember Allah, standing and sitting and [lying] on your sides﴾ (4:103).

That is, make Allah constantly on your mind. A human being in his natural state possesses energy by which he can stand and sit. If it is said, "So-and-so took charge of the people's affairs," it means he exerted every effort to manage people's affairs. Standing amid people's activities is the most difficult thing. He, glorified is He, does not want us merely to be standing; He wants us to be qawwām. As long as we are qawwām, not a moment of our standing will be void of being for Allah—for Allah, a direction, not a benefit—because no movement by any servant benefits Allah in anything. Allah created His creation with the totality of perfect attributes in Him, and He did not bring creation into being to gain any new attribute of beauty or perfection. When a person performs any act for Allah, he performs it in obedience and drawing near to Allah. If Allah wills of the believers that they be qawwām for Allah, then all the movements of the community of faith become divine movements, mutually supportive and ascending. If the movements of the community of faith are mutually supportive, the result of this movement will be the happiness of humanity. When a person is qawwām, he is qawwām for himself and for others.

What is meant is that we should be persistent in our standing in every matter for Allah. Do not think, O believer, that you are dealing with the creatures of Allah; rather you are dealing with Allah, who legislated for you so as to guarantee for you and guarantee from you. If you are required to be trustworthy, then all people are required to be trustworthy in what concerns you specifically, not others. When He forbids you from betrayal, the Truth has commanded all people to refrain from betraying you.

Thus, if you look at Allah's obligations, you will find them for your own benefit. Let no one assume that religion came merely to stand before himself. Religion stood before the self of all people. When He commands you not to stretch your hand to the property of others, you are one of the people, and this statement is a command directed to all people: do not stretch your hands to the wealth of so-and-so to steal it. Observe that when the Truth legislates upon you, He legislates for you. Therefore all your standing must be for Allah, glorified and exalted is He. That is why the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, manifests in some of His creation matters and events that make people understand that one who works for the creatures of Allah is deprived of bliss, while one who works for Allah is connected to bliss. We find someone saying, "I did such-and-such for so-and-so, and he denied me." We say to him: you deserve this because you did it for him; but if you had done it for Allah, Allah would have sufficed you in every matter. That is why the Truth says of those who acted for Allah: ﴿The Day every soul will find what it has done of good present﴾ (3:30).

So the believer must clarify the movement of his standing and develop it, meaning he should make his entire movement for Allah. If all his movement is for Allah, then Allah, glorified is He, does not waste the reward of one who does good deeds. The losers are those who work for people, because people possess no benefit for them; they may abandon them, may harbor resentment and hatred in their hearts toward one who did good to them, and may turn into enemies. The one to whom a favor was done may be given some status by Allah, and when the benefactor later meets him, his soul may become weak and humiliated. Sometimes we see someone sitting among people, overtaken by pride, and then a person who once did him a favor enters upon him, and when he sees him he dislikes his presence in his gathering and wishes this meeting had not occurred; if he meets him later on the road, he turns his face away, because the one who did the favor causes him embarrassment and makes his self weaken, while he wants to be arrogant toward people. So Allah clarifies: work for Allah, for nothing is lost with Him, and know that Allah is watching over you, and no work is lost with Him.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about ihsān (excellence), he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you."¹

Can you, O human, do before another person what would offend him in front of him? You offend the other person behind his back. So why does one of you offend Allah by disobedience, while He is watching you all?

Thus, when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wants you to treat yourself and others well, you must count every act of yours with Allah. The Truth has subjected all existence to us and given us all the necessities of life. He clarifies to each of us: O My servant, make all your standing for Allah. Do not merely stand, but be qawwām, meaning: as long as there remains in you some remnant of health for work, work. Do not work only to the extent of your need, but work to the extent of your capacity, because if you work only to the extent of your need, the one who cannot work will find nothing to live on.

Therefore, work to the extent of your capacity so that your movement may extend to all people, and the surplus of your work may go to others. When He, glorified is He, says, "Be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses to justice," He teaches us not to waste our effort in vain, but to direct effort to work and to perform it for the sake of Allah's countenance, because He, glorified is He, never forgets the reward of His servant, and He is the One who returns every kindness. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ (55:60)

And He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good﴾ (9:120).

When one of us is qawwām for Allah, he has used the movement of his existence for the good of Allah's creation. This work is required of you, and it is not sufficient for your movement to be confined to that; rather, the movement of your life must also extend to being a witness to justice. Likewise, direct toward justice whoever is inclined in his soul to deviate. When you are qawwām for Allah, this is a good matter, and you should try to persuade others to make their standing for Allah by being witnesses to justice and equity. Wherever you are a witness to justice and equity, no oppressor will persist in his oppression. What makes the oppressor grow bold and his injustice spread and his evil multiply is that he finds people who obscure justice, cover up and conceal defects, and deceive people.

But if a person finds someone who illuminates the path before justice, he will find no injustice. The oppressor, however, loves one who obscures for him, so he says to himself: "So-and-so committed a crime like mine and attained acquittal." Corrupting testimony leads to the ruin of societies. If society sees that the testimony of its members is testimony of justice and equity, then every individual in society, when he intends an injustice, will restrain himself before committing it, and the oppressor would receive his punishment and become an example for others' restraint. The believer is first required to stand for Allah by reforming himself, and second required to bear witness to justice and equity to reform others.

The word "qist" (justice) gives rise to many derivatives, and it is one of the words that may denote justice or denote injustice; it is one of the words used both for a command and for its opposite, and this is one of the beauties of the language. This requires the listener to scrutinize the word and to know its meaning by what the context requires.

"Qisṭ" means "ʿadl" (justice). Its imperfect verb is yaqsiṭu, and its verbal noun is qisṭan; sometimes the verbal noun is qusūṭan, and it is the verbal noun that may shift the meaning from justice to injustice. Qisṭ means justice, while qasaṭa yaqsiṭu qusūṭan means he acted unjustly and oppressed. Here we find the verb coming with its meaning and its opposite, so that the listener possesses the alertness and perceptiveness that enables him to distinguish between the meaning of justice and the meaning of injustice.

When we say "aqsaṭa," it means ʿadala (he acted justly). Here we note the following: there is a difference between justice that comes from the outset, which is qisṭ, and an unjust ruling that needs another ruling to remove the injustice, which is what we use aqsaṭa for, meaning he removed the injustice, as if an injustice existed and the ruling removed it. So qisṭ is initial justice. This is why we hear the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, say: ﴿As for the qāsiṭūn (deviators), they will be fuel for Hell﴾ (72:15).

The qāsiṭūn here are the unjust, so qisṭ here is from qasaṭa yaqsiṭu qusūṭan.

In the verse about which we are reflecting, the Truth says: "witnesses to justice" (shuhadāʾa bil-qisṭ), meaning witnesses to justice. The eloquence of the listener is what directs the word to its intended meaning through the context. The listener to the Qur'an is presumed to possess linguistic ease, so that he can distinguish between a thing and something similar to it. Thus there is qisṭ and aqsaṭa, qisṭ meaning justice, and aqsaṭa meaning establishing justice by removing injustice, while qusūṭ means injustice.

The Truth says: "Indeed, Allah loves the muqsiṭīn (the just)." The muqsiṭīn is the plural of muqsiṭ, from aqsaṭa, meaning he removed injustice and oppression. So what determines the meaning here is the context of the word and its source. The word may be intended in its verbal-noun sense, and the verbal-noun sense does not vary with the variation of its form. One says "rajul ʿadl" (a just man), "imraʾah ʿadl" (a just woman), "rajulān ʿadl" (two just men), "imraʾatān ʿadl" (two just women), "rijāl ʿadl" (just men), and "nisāʾ ʿadl" (just women). So if we intend the word as a verbal noun, it does not change in singular, dual, masculine plural, or feminine plural. The Qur'an says: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice﴾ (21:47).

There is another statement: ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾ (26:182).

In the Egyptian countryside, the merchant makes his own weights from stones: he calibrates a piece of stone against the kilogram weight, and calibrates other pieces for fractions of a kilogram. Because of frequent use and contact with the stone, the merchant knows that the stone wears away, so he re-weighs the stones he uses on the scale at short intervals of time. Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 9:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ (9)

When we reflect on the word "wa'ada" (promised), we find that it comes, and also "awa'ada" (threatened) comes. "Wa'ada" and "awa'ada" are used in such a way that when they are not followed by the object of the promise or threat, "wa'ada" is for good and "awa'ada" is for evil. But if something other than that occurs and you bring in the thing promised, the two are equal: it is correct to say "wa'adtuhu bil-khayr" (I promised him good), and it is also correct to say "wa'adtuhu bil-sharr" (I promised him evil). But if you do not mention the object, "wa'ada" is used for good and "awa'ada" is used for evil. The poet says:

"And indeed, if I threaten him or promise him, I will not break my threat, and I will fulfill my promise."

When He says "Allah has promised" (wa'ada Allah), this is an absolute promise that cannot be breached, because the one who breaks a promise is the human being, who is subject to changing circumstances. The time for fulfilling the promise may come and the person finds himself in a position of helplessness, or in a position where his heart has changed. But when it is Allah who has promised, He is glorified, the One whom changing circumstances do not affect. Rather, He is the One who brings about changing circumstances. Therefore His promise is the pure promise, and there is no other power that can prevent Allah from fulfilling His promise. As for the promise of human beings, another power may come and render that promise ineffective.

"Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness": Glorified and exalted is He, He makes clear that His forgiveness is for all His servants, and it is not restricted only to the righteous and the pious. Rather, He addresses those who committed sins: if they repent, then for them is forgiveness, because the averting of harm takes precedence over the attainment of benefit. You may be sitting, and someone comes from the right to offer you an apple, and in the very moment your hand extends to take the apple, you turn to find another person who wants to slap you. Which direction does your behavior take? You will certainly respond first to the one who is striking you. The Truth removes sins first by forgiveness. And we find that He, glorified and exalted, brings things that capture the heart. He says: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed succeeded﴾ (Qur'an 3:185).

The first step to success is being drawn away from the Fire, and the next step after that is entry into Paradise. So He, glorified, prevents harm and gives precedence to repelling and averting it over securing benefit. Therefore the Truth says at the outset: "for them is forgiveness." When a person's thoughts come to him, he thinks about things he aspires to, and there are things he fears, and the mind is first occupied with what it fears: he fears harm, he fears the non-realization of hopes. Thus the averting of harm takes precedence over the attainment of benefit.

"For them is forgiveness and a great reward": Every reward for a deed takes its life in proportion to its span of time. The reward of a person for his deed in this world goes away and vanishes, because the person himself goes to death. But the reward of the Hereafter is what remains forever, and it is a reward that does not escape the person nor does the person escape it. That is the great reward.

When the Truth speaks of a meaning related to faith and righteous deeds, the soul becomes prepared, because there is encouragement toward good and warning against evil. Therefore the Truth follows this verse with another verse, saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of Hellfire.﴾ (10)

When we hear His words, "the companions of the Blazing Fire," souls tremble in awe of that companionship from which we disown ourselves. Companionship indicates mutual adherence and means being bound together, and that neither one leaves the other, as if the Fire will not leave them and they will not leave the Fire; rather, the Fire itself yearns for them. On the Day of Resurrection, the Fire has two functions. The first function: the companionship from which the disbeliever cannot escape. The second: the Fire does not give the disbeliever any opportunity to free himself from it. And the Truth says concerning the Fire: ﴿On the Day when We will say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it will say, "Are there any more?"﴾ [Qaf 50:30]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 5, verse 11:

Then Allah says:

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you. And fear Allah; and upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ (5:11)

Remembrance (dhikr), as we have known, means bringing a thing to mind, because heedlessness (ghafla) overtakes a person, and he should not remain in it. Some of the people of illumination (ishraq) and ecstatic utterance (shath) play with their inner spiritual states (mawajid). One of them says: "Allah knows that I am not remembering Him." When a person hears such a saying, he may rebuke its speaker and criticise him harshly. But the speaker analyses the matter in the manner of the gnostics (irfan) and completes the line of poetry with its second half:

{ How could I remember Him, when I never forget Him?

Here the soul finds ease. And Allah says here also: "the favour of Allah" and does not say "favours," because every single favour deserves that we thank Allah for it, since each individual favour is great and immense and deserves gratitude. Or the favour of Allah is all of His overflowing bounty upon His creation, and the best of the favours is that He is our Lord. He, glory be to Him, says: "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you." Since He has come with "when" (idh), the meaning is a particular favour, because "idh" means "at the time when." Allah makes clear: remember the favour of Allah upon you at that time in which this matter occurred, for He has mentioned a time and asks that we remember His favour in this situation. He reminds us of the favour that occurred when a people determined to extend their hands against you.

There is the "restraining" (qabd) of the hand and the "extending" (bast) of the hand. The extending that is seen is that you see the favour. In the verse, the favour is the withholding of the hands of the disbelievers, since their hands had been extended with evil and harm. If we stopped at the extending of the hand, we would think that He, glory be to Him, had made among the causes of His creation a conduit for blessings upon us, that is, that the blessings of Allah reach us through them and by their hands. But this is not the intention of the noble text, because when we continue reading the verse we know that the withholding of their hands is the favour. These people wanted to extend their hands with harm, and they use the expression about the offensiveness of the tongue: "he extended his tongue" (basata lisanahu). They also say: "he extended his hand with harm" (basata yadahu bil-idha').

We know that Allah used "to you" (ilaykum) or "from you" (ankum), and both contain a pronoun referring to the believers together with the Prophet (ﷺ). The believers are bound to the method of the Prophet (ﷺ). So when they determined to extend their hands toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), this was an offence against the believers through the Messenger of Allah, because everything that reaches the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reaches the believers as well. There was an actual incident in a past and bygone time. Does Allah, glory and exaltation be to Him, mean by it the incident of the Banu al-Nadir? Between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Banu al-Nadir there was a treaty that they would not assist the enemies of Islam against him, and that if a killing took place at the hands of the Muslims, the Banu al-Nadir would share in paying the blood-money (diya). The Prophet (ﷺ) had sent a Muslim in a military detachment (sariya), and he killed two of the treaty-bound people by mistake. They demanded blood-money for the two slain men, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had no wealth, so he went to the Banu al-Nadir so that they would help him with the blood-money for the two slain men. They said to him: "Welcome! We will feed you and give you drink, and after that we will give you what you want." Then they set a man to throw a stone at the Messenger (ﷺ). The man climbed up to hurl a rock down on the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was sitting beside a wall of their houses. Allah informed His Messenger, so he rose and went out, and did not wait for anything.

﴿...when a people determined to extend their hands against you, but He withheld their hands from you.﴾ Allah informed His Prophet of what they were plotting before they could carry out the act. "Hamm" (determination) is the speech of the soul within itself. When it moves out toward the first step of inclination, that is intention (qasd). "Hamm" is the thing that dominates a person's thought within himself and is accompanied by grief.

In colloquial language we hear someone say: "I am in hamm and ghamm" (distress and grief), because "hamm" is a matter that does not leave the soul in speech and causes grief. So hamm is the enemy that no one can overcome, because it slips into the heart. As for any other enemy, a person may repel it. We know about our master the Imam Ali, may Allah be pleased with him and ennoble his face, that he was famous as the mufti: he would be asked about a matter and would answer it, to the extent that our master Umar himself said: "A problem with no Abu Hasan to solve it!" That is, it is a difficult problem for which there is no Abu Hasan to resolve it. Umar used to seek refuge from being in a place where Sayyidina Ali was not present. When people learned of this, they asked: "From where does he derive this speech?" So they devised a riddle and waited to see how he would get out of it. They said: "The universe is vast, and in it there are things stronger than all other things, and powers that dominate powerful ones." They tried to agree on something stronger than all things. One said: "The mountain is the strongest of things." Another said: "But we cut stones out of it with iron." While they were stringing this chain together, Sayyidina Ali came, and they said to him: "O Abu al-Hasan, what are the strongest of Allah's hosts?"

Sayyidina Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, answered as if he were reading from a book. This is evident from the fact that he knew the hosts of Allah, knew which was the strongest, and specified their number. Sayyidina Ali said: "The strongest of Allah's hosts are ten." As though he had been occupied with this question before, and had studied it.

He said: "The firm mountains; iron cuts the mountains; fire melts iron; water extinguishes fire; the clouds subjected between heaven and earth carry the water; the wind moves the clouds; the son of Adam overcomes the wind by shielding himself with a garment or some object and proceeds to his need; intoxication (sukr) overcomes the son of Adam; sleep overcomes intoxication; and hamm overcomes sleep. So the strongest of Allah's hosts is hamm."

We cannot pass over the word "hamm" in the Qur'an without reviewing its occurrences in the Book of Allah. The most important of its occurrences, about which many people have asked in their letters and in our meetings with them, is the matter of Yusuf, peace be upon him, when Allah, glory and exaltation be to Him, said regarding the seduction of the wife of al-Aziz toward him:

﴿And she certainly desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord.﴾ (12:24)

To investigate this matter: those who consider this thing unlikely for Yusuf, peace be upon him, hold that the man of infallibility (ʿisma) should not think within himself about such a thing. Yet if thinking within oneself has not reached the stage of inclination to action, it is possible. Indeed, thinking about a thing and then the soul turning away from it is stronger than not thinking about it at all, because occupying the soul with this matter and then restraining it means a severe resistance by the soul. But they also magnify and exalt Yusuf, peace be upon him, so much that it would not have passed through his mind, let alone that he would have considered it, especially since Yusuf, peace be upon him, had not yet been sent as a messenger. That is, he was not then a messenger.

The verse says: ﴿And she certainly desired him, and he desired her﴾ (12:24).

That is, the wife of al-Aziz was the one who initiated the seduction of Yusuf, peace be upon him. Was there then any movement toward the act? No, because movement toward the act requires that Yusuf take part in it. So "she desired him" means she came to wish to bring about the act of inclination, and the obstacle came from Yusuf. As for the one being sought, Yusuf, Allah says: ﴿and he desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ (12:24).

We give an example to make this understood. If someone says to you: "I would visit you if it were not for the presence of so-and-so with you," this means that the speaker did not visit you. By analogy, Yusuf, peace be upon him, saw the proof and did not desire. As for one who wishes to declare Yusuf free even from the speech of his own soul, we say: as regards her, she desired him. For the act to be realised it was necessary that this matter be accepted, and then refusal came. Yet the refusal did not come from her side; it came from his side, and he had desired her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord.

Why did Allah say that he desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord? Allah related that story to show us the wisdom in Yusuf's refusal to consent to the seduction. It was not because of any natural physical deficiency in him. Had it not been for the proof of his Lord, everything might have happened between them. Allah wished to tell us that his manhood was complete, his virility not deficient, and his sexual capacity fully present. What prevented him from going to her was the proof of his Lord. It was a religious restraint, not a natural one. Thus the difficulty in understanding the matter of hamm with respect to the wife of al-Aziz and Yusuf has been fully clarified.

Let us return to the verse we are discussing: ﴿when a people determined to extend their hands against you﴾. The word "qawm" (people), when you hear it, carries the meaning of standing (qiyam). Standing is the most energetic state of a human being. As we explained before, a person is either standing, or sitting, or reclining, or lying on his back, or sleeping, and rest is in proportion to these conditions. The one standing is the one who tires more than the others, because the weight of his whole body is on his two small feet. When he sits, the weight is distributed onto the buttocks; when he reclines, the area of bearing widens. Therefore the word is applied only to men, because it is the nature of a man to be upright and steadfast, and the nature of a woman to be gentle, calm, quiet, and modest. So "qawm" means men, and the opposite of "qawm" here is "women" (nisa'). Thus women by nature do not stand.

The poet says:

{ And I do not know, nor do I think I know, whether the people of Hisn are men or women.

When Allah says: ﴿when a people determined to extend their hands against you﴾, this means there were no women who had thought of harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). We also find here that extending (bast) is open to question: does extending mean harm or generosity?

Allah says: ﴿And if Allah had extended provision for His servants, they would have transgressed in the earth﴾ (42:27). This refers to the domain of giving. As for the domain of harm, Allah says, on the tongue of the son of Adam to his brother: ﴿If you extend your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not extend my hand toward you to kill you﴾ (5:28).

The hands are not mentioned except when we intend a movement of inclination that expresses a meaning in the soul which has already passed through the mind. So extending the hands requires plotting by thought. Thus we know that these people had extended their hands toward the Messenger of Allah and the believers.

When we look into the Muhammadan history with his enemies, we find Allah, glory and exaltation be to Him, saying: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to restrain you or kill you or expel you. They plotted, and Allah plotted; and Allah is the best of planners﴾ (8:30). That is, they sat down to plan by night. We do not know that plotting except when hands are extended to act. They devised and plotted evil, and they wanted to restrain the Messenger, that is, to fix his residence by imprisoning him, binding him, or wounding him severely so as to weaken and incapacitate him so that he could not rise or stand. Or they would kill him, or expel him from his land by confining him so that he would not leave, or expel him from the whole place, or kill him. What, then, was their position? They had determined to extend their hands toward him, and extending the hand against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) harms all the believers, because the affairs of the believers are not upright except through the Messenger of Allah. If the disbelievers extended their hands toward the Prophet (ﷺ), that would mean extending their hands against everyone. The Muhammadan history records matters in which the disbelievers extended their hands with harm toward the Messenger of Allah and the believers, and Allah withheld their hands and plotted against them, that is, He requited them with punishment for that.

Plotting (makr), as we know, is a tree whose branches are intertwined with one another, so that we do not know which leaf grows from which trunk or branch. In meanings, plotting is secret scheming, and it is a sign of weakness, not of strength. The strong confront and do not scheme. That is why it is said that the one who schemes against another is only the weak, because the open, frank person who is able to confront is the strong. Some people make the weakness of women a motive for the strength of their plotting, relying on the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, the plotting of Satan is ever weak﴾ (4:76), and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your plotting is great﴾ (12:28).

So only the weak one schemes, the one who cannot face others. If he were able to confront, he would have no need for that. People may plot and scheme in secret from others, but they cannot scheme in secret from Allah, because He knows the secrets of the breasts. The command of Allah in plotting is stronger than the command of creation. That is why we find His saying, glory be to Him: {And they plot, and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 5, verse 12:

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, places among the stories of the messengers for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a means of strengthening faith, of training and nurturing the model (al-uswa), and of developing it, so that the Messenger's chest is not constricted by what the Jews or the polytheists do. If there has befallen you, O Muhammad, some of this denial and pain, then many such events have befallen the messengers before you. So He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And Allah had taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains (nuqaba'). And Allah said, "I am with you. If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever disbelieves after that among you has certainly strayed from the sound way."﴾

Here the Truth reminds His Messenger of the covenant He took from the Children of Israel. It may be that what is intended is the covenant of the primordial state (mithaq al-dharr), or the covenant may refer to what is mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran).

Or the covenant meant may be what He explained in His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾ (part of verse 63, Surah al-Baqarah).

He says, "And We raised among them twelve chieftains." Let us look at the religious "tactic" that the Truth intended. He does not gather the different kinds of creation under one single type, because that might expose the call to tribalism (asabiyya). So He chose twelve chieftains according to the number of the tribes (asbat), so that no tribe would say, "How is it that I have no chieftain?" Allah settled the matter and did not make it an object of dispute: He appointed for each tribe a chieftain from among them. The naqib (chieftain) is the one who directs their doctrinal and religious movement. When we hear the word naqib, we know that its root is the letters nun, qaf, ba', and that *naqb* is making a hole with depth in any solid body.

The Truth's choice of the word naqib shows that a true naqib must be someone with two extremely alert eyes, so that he chooses for each individual the task that suits him, and focuses on each person in a way that makes him perform his work to benefit the complete movement. Thus each individual in the tribe has his work and his suitable place. This is achieved only through *tanqib*, that is, knowing the condition and inclinations of each person, so that he is placed in the appropriate position.

Therefore the naqib is the one who probes (al-munaqqib), who is not content with surface appearances but digs into them to know the circumstances and causes of each person. Allah chose from each tribe a naqib, and did not make a naqib of one tribe over another, so that domination of one tribe over another would be prevented, and so that the naqib would not be ignorant of those whose movement he directs from the other tribes.

In our daily life we hear the description of a person: "So-and-so has many *manaqib*," meaning he has virtues that people mention. It is as if the owner of virtues should not boast of them himself, but should leave people to probe for his virtues. This is why the treasures of the earth and the treasures of civilizations are buried, and we dig for them, whereas what appears on the surface of the earth is scattered by the winds and the forces of erosion, and nothing of it remains.

Thus the word *naqib* in all its derivation revolves around entering into depth. That is why one describes a virtuous man: "So-and-so has *manaqib*," meaning if you probe, you will find virtues to be mentioned for him. Allah has given him the gift of goodness, and he does not show off with it, but leaves people to judge and mention these qualities. From the same root comes *niqab*, that is, a woman covering her face.

His saying, the Truth: "I am with you" gives them a quality of faith. No one should think that he confronts the enemies of Allah's way by his own particular self, but by the help of Allah. So no one should weaken or falter as long as he is a believer. As the Truth said: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ (part of verse 60, Surah al-Anfal).

After the believers prepare what they are able to, they should leave the rest to Allah. There also came His saying: "And Allah said, 'I am with you.'" That is, each naqib over a tribe does not have absolute authority, but Allah makes clear: "I am with you, and I will see how each naqib manages these matters." That is, He, glorified and exalted, is aware of your reality. Being in authority does not mean that the one in authority has absolute control over his community, no, because Allah is the Watcher. The saying of the Truth, "I am with you," indicates that whoever takes charge of a matter must, after that, follow it up and oversee it. Then He said: "If you establish prayer, give zakah, believe in My messengers, support them, and loan Allah a goodly loan, I will surely remove from you your misdeeds." The *la-* ("if" with emphasis) combines a conditional and an oath. It is as if the Truth says: "By My might, if you establish prayer and do such and such, the reward will certainly be that I remove your misdeeds." The *lam* indicates the oath, and *in* indicates the condition, so it is the conditional *in*.

As we know, an oath requires an answer, and a condition requires an answer too. When one of us says to a student, "If you study, you will pass," and one of us says, "By God, I will do such-and-such," the "God" is the oath and "I will do" is the answer of the oath confirmed by the lam. When an oath comes alone in a sentence, its answer comes; when a condition comes alone in a sentence, its answer also comes. But what happens when an oath comes together with a condition? Do two answers come, one for the condition and one for the oath? When you find this case, look at which of the two comes first: is it the oath or the condition? For the one that comes first is the more important, so its answer comes and suffices for the answer of the second, and the one that comes first here is the oath, just as we say:

"If Zayd comes, I will certainly honor him" — here the answer is the answer of the oath. But if we say, "If Zayd comes, by God I will honor him," then the answer is the answer of the condition. This is if the condition precedes the oath, and nothing has preceded that requires a predicate, like the subject (mubtada') or what is in its ruling. If what precedes is one needing a predicate, then the condition is the preferred one, meaning the preferred view is to bring the answer of the condition and omit the answer of the oath, because the condition is an establishing (ta'sis) and the oath is an emphasis (tawkid). Ibn Malik in his Alfiyya explains this rule:

"Omit, when condition and oath gather, the answer of whichever is delayed; it is obligatory.
If the two follow each other and before them is one needing a predicate, the condition is preferred, absolutely, without caution."

The oath has come earlier in this verse, so the answer here is the answer of the oath, which is: "I will surely remove from you your misdeeds."

The Truth's saying, "If you establish prayer," shows that establishing requires two things: obligations that are performed, and that each obligation takes its right in being carried out. After that, "and give zakah." In books of jurisprudence (fiqh), prayer and zakah are placed in the section on acts of worship. The juristic classification came to facilitate clarifying the obligations, but every command from Allah is an act of worship, because worship is that you obey the one you worship in everything He commands and avoid what He forbids, so every divine command is worship.

We said before that the Truth, glorified is He, said: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten to the remembrance of Allah and leave off trade﴾ (part of verse 9, Surah al-Jumu'ah), and His saying: ﴿And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah﴾ (part of verse 10, Surah al-Jumu'ah).

Here we find one act of worship: to leave trade for prayer, and a second act of worship: to disperse in the land seeking Allah's bounty after the prayer ends. Any violation of either of the two is a violation of an act of worship. You are commanded to move about the earth according to your strength, in a movement that suffices you and overflows beyond your need, so that this surplus benefits others.

The Truth's saying: ﴿And believed in My messengers and supported them﴾ means that faith is established in the heart so that the matter does not surface afterward for discussion, and that you support the messengers, that is, you revere them and aid them. The word *'azr* in the language means prevention, but the prevention here is meant to keep people away from the Messenger of Allah anyone who wishes him harm. If any of the enemies intends evil to a messenger of Allah, then the believers should prevent this enemy from the Messenger (ﷺ).

In your life, if you have a beloved whom a person wishes harm, and you cannot reach him because he is far from you, you wish to take hold of your friend and protect him from the enemy. But if the enemy is in front of you, you repel him from your beloved. So *'azr* is prevention: you prevent him from his enemy and stand between him and it, or you prevent his enemy from reaching him with harm. For believers, the Messenger's life is dearer than their own lives, so in the course of preventing, one of the believers may be struck, and in that there is glorifying of the Messenger, supporting him, and revering him.

We say this so as to answer those who seek faults and say, "The scholars of Muslims do not agree on anything: sometimes they say that 'support them' ('azzartumuhum) means 'help them,' and sometimes they say it means 'prevent them.'" We say: all the meanings here converge, since *'azr* is repelling and preventing, either by preventing the enemy from the Messenger, or by people preventing the Messenger from being reached by the enemy, or both together. It is also permissible that the meaning of 'azzartumuhum' be 'helped them,' and likewise it is permissible that it means 'revered them,' because glorifying and revering are the cause of a person's support for the Messenger.

After that the Truth says: ﴿And loaned Allah a goodly loan﴾. The Truth lays down for us a policy of wealth, whether for the one who has means or for the one who is unable. To the one who has means, the Truth explains: do not make the movement of your life according to the measure of your need, but make the movement of your life according to the measure of your capacity, and take from it what suffices you and suffices those you support, and return the remainder to the one who cannot earn. If every person made the movement of his life according to his need, then whoever could not move would find nothing to live on. Let us remember well that the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, has said: ﴿Certainly will the believers succeed. They who are during their prayer humbly submissive. And they who turn away from ill speech. And they who are payers of zakah﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun).

When He, glorified is He, says, "And they who are payers of zakah," it does not merely mean paying zakah, but means that they move about in life with the aim that a surplus is achieved from which they give zakah. Otherwise, what is the difference between the believer and the disbeliever? The disbeliever works to sustain himself and those he supports, and Allah is not in his mind; but the believer's distinction is that he works to sustain himself and those he supports, and leaves over a surplus that he gives to the weak, as if giving to the weak was in his mind at the time of the action. This is what is meant by the Truth's saying: ﴿And they who are payers of zakah﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun).

That is, every act of the believer is intended to suffice him and to suffice for what he gives in zakah. There is another right in wealth beyond zakah: that the ruler, with it, meets what the community of faith needs, on condition that the ruler establishes the whole Law of Allah.

Zakah is the giving of wealth in a specific manner. Charity (sadaqa) is not counted as zakah, but it is above zakah. And there is the loan (qard), which is wealth to which the soul is attached, because a person gives it to another on condition that he return it. That is why it is said that the loan is better than charity: the borrower borrows only out of need, whereas the one you give charity to may not be in need and may ask without need. Also, because the soul of the one giving charity departs from the thing given and is not attached to it, whereas the one who gives a loan has his soul attached to the loan, and whenever he is patient with it he attains good deeds, and whenever he grants a postponement to one in difficulty, he has a great reward. Thus the loan is better than charity.

The Truth wants the movement of life to overflow with abundance. And how does He, glorified is He, say, "And loaned Allah a goodly loan," when He is the Giver of all blessings and the Owner of all blessings? How does the Truth grant humans blessings and then say to them: lend Me?

He, glorified and exalted, respects a person's movement and sweat, as long as he has journeyed in the land and striven in it. The wealth is the person's wealth, but his brother may need it, so let him lend it. He, glorified is He, counts this as a loan from the person to Allah. We see the head of a family say to one of his children: "Since you save from your pocket money, give your brother what he needs and consider it a loan from me." It is true that the head of the household is the one who gave the wealth to everyone he supports, so what of the One who brought us all into existence, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He? He has granted each of us the fruit of his labor and considered that fruit the property of its owner, and beyond that considers lending to the needy as a loan to Him.

The Truth describes the loan as goodly so that there is no reproach (min) or benefit returning to the lender, for otherwise the loan would become usury (riba). We have a good model in Abu Hanifa, when he used to sit in the shade of the house of a friend. The owner of that house borrowed some money from Abu Hanifa, and on the day after the loan Abu Hanifa sat...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 5, verse 13:

Then the Truth says: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places, and they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of. And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾

When the Truth says "mithaqan" (a covenant), a covenant demands fulfilment. Did they fulfil this covenant? No. They broke their covenants, so Allah cursed them. Cursing (la'n) means expulsion and removal from mercy. The Truth says in this regard: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them.﴾ That is, because of their breaking of the covenant, Allah cursed them.

The presence of "ma" here has raised some interpretations. Some scholars said it is extra (za'ida), and others said it is a connective particle (silah). But extra elements occur in human speech, not in the speech of Allah, and nothing in the Qur'an can be superfluous, because every word in the Qur'an comes to meet a situation that requires it to be in this place. Here the Truth tells us what Luqman advised his son: ﴿And be patient over what has afflicted you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ (Qur'an 31:17)

In another verse He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ (Qur'an 42:43)

In the first verse, the "lam" does not precede "man" [i.e., the lam of emphasis is not placed before the relative pronoun], while in the second verse the "lam" precedes "man." This is not a matter of stylistic variation. His saying, "And be patient over what has afflicted you, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination," is a call to patience over a calamity in which the person has no adversary, such as illness or the death of a relative. This call to patience comes here as consolation and solace. But His saying, "And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination," calls for patience together with forgiveness, which presupposes an adversary who has caused the person a disaster.

Here Allah asks the believer to forgive those who afflicted him and to be patient. As long as there is an adversary, the soul is attached to revenge, and this situation needs a stronger emphasis than the first one, since in the first situation there is no clear adversary from whom revenge is sought. The presence of an adversary stirs in the soul the desire for revenge, and therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, emphasises: "Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination." He, glorified is He, says in another place: ﴿There has not come to us any bringer of good tidings.﴾ (Qur'an 5:19)

When the grammarians parse (i'rab, grammatical analysis) "bashir" [bringer], they say: it is a subject in the nominative, marked by an assumed damma on its end, prevented from appearing by the vowel of the extra preposition. This is a long detour. There is no extra particle here. A person says, "ma 'indi mal" [I have no wealth], and this speaker may mean that he owns only a little wealth that is not counted. But when a person says, "ma 'indi min mal" [I have no wealth at all], then "min" here means that he owns no wealth whatsoever, from the very beginning of what is called wealth. Therefore "min" here is not extra, but has come to convey a meaning. So "ma ja'anا min bashir" means: there has not come to us, from the very beginning, anyone who is called a bringer of good tidings.

And here is the saying of the Truth: ﴿So by mercy from Allah, you were lenient with them.﴾ (Qur'an 3:159)

Some may suppose that "ma" here is an extra particle, but we say: what is the origin in derivation? The origin from which derivation is made is the verbal noun (masdar), and sometimes the verbal noun comes and is intended to mean the verb. As one says, "darban Zaydan" [striking Zayd], meaning "idrib Zaydan" [strike Zayd]. The coming of the verbal noun here is a statement intended to mean the verb, and likewise the saying of the Truth: "So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them."

Since "naqd" (breaking) is a verbal noun, it can take the place of the verb, and since the verbal noun has taken the place of the verb, it is permissible that the other verb should come, so the meaning becomes: "So because they broke their covenant, We cursed them." Thus "ma" here indicates that the verbal noun has come in place of a verb, and "ma" remains to indicate that the verbal noun is from a deleted verb. Or "ma" is interrogative, expressing amazement: "By what kind and form of breaking did they break the covenant, so We cursed them?" This is because of the abundance of what they broke of covenants, in many different forms and kinds of breaking.

His saying, "So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them," and "naqd" (breaking) is the opposite of "ibram" (confirmation), because ibram is the firm establishment of a ruling by evidence, while naqd is the dissolving of the elements of a matter. It is as if the sealed covenant that Allah took from them was broken, and we call the faith-creed "'aqidah" [creed], why? Because it is taken from "'aqd" [binding] of a thing so that it does not float away to be discussed again in the mind. Likewise the covenant is a firm and confirmed pact, and when they break it, they dissolve it, meaning they removed themselves from the requirements of that binding, and the curse came because they broke the covenant.

"And We made their hearts hard." When they broke the covenants, Allah sealed their hearts, because He did not seal their hearts at the beginning. They first disbelieved, and after that Allah left them in their error and misguidance and sealed the hearts, so that the disbelief in them does not come out, and what is outside does not enter them. "Hard" (qasiyah) means solid and having severity. Hardness is blameworthy in hearts, and not blameworthy in defending the truth, because we measure every existing thing by its function. When every existing thing is performing its function, the whole universe becomes beautiful. An example: we do not blame the swallow [kha!tif] for being crooked, since the swallow must have crookedness, because that crookedness suits its function. So the crookedness of the swallow is its straightness. Likewise hardness is not blameworthy provided it is in its proper place, but if it comes in the wrong place, it is blameworthy. Hard hearts are blameworthy, because the Truth wants hearts to be soft: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts become soft to the remembrance of Allah.﴾ (Qur'an 39:23)

"Qaswa" [hardness] is derived from "qasi," which is the solid and severe. We know that dinars were minted from gold and dirhams were minted from silver. When the money-changer examines them, he may take one out and say, "This is counterfeit (zayf or za'if)," because he has heard its ring. Is it solid in reality or not? When it is solid, it is called "hard dirhams" (dirham qasiya).

Gold is soft and silver is soft. When we say that gold is of twenty-four carat, meaning gold with no admixture of other materials that make it workable, because when it is pure gold absolutely, the goldsmith will not be able to fashion jewellery from it. Therefore the goldsmith mixes it with a hard metal so that the metal gives it the degree of hardness that enables him to shape jewellery from it. The proportion of hardness varies from carat to carat in gold, and likewise in silver. Wrought items made from high-carat gold are not liable to circulation like gold bars.

When hard metal enters gold or silver, it makes it hard, that is, solid. Hardness, then, is praiseworthy in what suits it and blameworthy in what does not suit it, like the hardness of hearts and their severity.

The Truth says: ﴿They distort words from their places.﴾ Like this is their transmission of Allah's command, which asked them to say "hittah" [remission], and they said "hintah" [wheat]. ﴿And they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of.﴾ The means of alteration (naskh) in the books that preceded the Qur'an were forgetting a portion of what they were reminded of. Forgetting may be an inability to retain, but it is also evidence that the method was not on their minds. If the books of the method had been on their minds, they would have kept remembering it. They also concealed what they had not forgotten, and what they had neither forgotten nor concealed they distorted, twisting their tongues with it. Would that the matter had been limited to this! But they brought things and sayings and claimed they were from Allah, and they were not from Allah.

﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands and then say, "This is from Allah," to exchange it for a small price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ (Qur'an 2:79)

There are four kinds of change: forgetting, concealing, distortion, and inserting things and claiming they are from Allah when they are not from Allah.

We may reflect on the beauty of the wise saying: "and they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of." They were of such great evil that they forgot the thing that would have brought them a great portion. Like their forgetting and concealing the good tidings of Muhammad (peace be upon him). Had they believed in them, their portion would have been great, because they forgot a matter that would have given them a good reward. So they have wronged themselves, because Islam would not have benefited if they had been guided or believing, and the loss falls on them. Allah did not leave them and let them remain in their forgetting so that they would have an argument by it. Rather He wanted to remind them of what they had forgotten, and that required them to do justice to themselves by returning to faith, because the Truth reminded them of what they had forgotten so that they would achieve for themselves the beautiful portion. It may also be meant that they left this deliberately, turning away from it and wilfully neglecting it.

The Truth says afterwards: ﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them, except a few of them. So pardon them and overlook. Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ (Qur'an 5:13)

That is, their treachery toward you, O Messenger of Allah, and toward your followers and toward the true method of Allah on earth, will continue. There is no better proof of this than what they did against their own messengers, although they were of their own flesh and blood and their own tribe. They are of the Children of Israel like them. So what about a prophet who came from another kind to break into their temporal authority?

Thus their treachery against Allah is conceivable, and "khaida'a" [treachery, in the form of a feminine active participle] means "khiyanah" [betrayal], like "qa'ilah," which is "qaylulah," meaning the period of time after noon. Its verb is "qala yaqilu," meaning he slept at midday.
