These are questions whose answers do not concern us, although some scholars have occupied themselves with them. Those are matters that neither benefit nor harm. What matters is that the Children of Israel did not enter Jericho except at the hand of Joshua son of Nun, after the forty years: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I possess none but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiant people." He said, "Indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land. So do not grieve over the defiant people."﴾ (Qur'an 5:25–26).

We may read this wise statement as follows: "He said, 'My Lord, I possess none but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiant people.' He said, 'Indeed it is forbidden to them.'" This pause gives us the understanding that the holy land became forbidden to them forever, and after that comes God's command to punish them in the wandering for forty years: "For forty years they will wander in the land; so do not grieve over the defiant people." But if we read this wise statement as follows: "He said, 'My Lord, I possess none but myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiant people. He said, "Indeed it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land; so do not grieve over the defiant people."'" then this reading allows us to understand that the period of punishment for these defiant people is forty years in the wandering, and after that they entered the city of Jericho.

The Truth commands Moses not to grieve over these defiant people. When Moses, peace be upon him, called upon God, saying, "so separate us," he felt some distress at this supplication and said to himself, "Why did I not pray for their guidance instead of praying for separation?" For this reason the Truth said to him, "So do not grieve over the defiant people," meaning: do not grieve over them, for they are more deserving of punishment because of their defiance and their opposition.

And after that, the Truth says:

﴿And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them and not accepted from the other. He said: "I will surely kill you." He said: "Allah accepts only from the righteous."﴾ (5:27)

When a person recites (*yatlu*), meaning reads, he speaks in an order that follows the images he has seen. When a person sees a matter or an event, he sees the whole at once, or he sees each image that makes up the event separately from the others. When a person speaks, he arranges the words one after another, and one letter after another. Therefore, following and reciting (*al-talawah*) belong to speech. "And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam." *Naba'* (news) is important information. We do not apply *naba'* to any information, but *naba'* is news that draws attention. An example is the words of the Truth: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ (78:1–2).

So the word *naba'* means important, weighty information that has a strong impact and great effect.

"And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam, in truth." When we hear the words of the Truth, "in truth" (*bi-l-haqq*), we know that this is a matter that came down from the Truth, so there is no alteration or change in it. For this reason He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended﴾ (17:105).

That is, what was sent down from Allah was not mixed with other speech. And with the truth that gathers all commands of good and prohibitions against evil, it descended. When He, glorified be He, says, "And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam, in truth," He narrates a Qur'anic story that relates a cosmic event. Since it is Allah who relates it, He brings it from the perfect model of truthfulness and benefit. For this reason He calls it "the true narrative": ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ (3:62).

He also calls it: ﴿We relate to you the best of narratives﴾ (12:3).

He, glorified be He, says: "And recite to them the news of the two sons of Adam, in truth, when they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them and not accepted from the other." We know that Adam is the first of the human creation, and that the two sons of Adam are Habil and Qabil, as the commentators said. Each of them offered a sacrifice. *Qurban* (sacrifice, offering) is what the servant draws near to Allah with. *Qurban* is on the pattern *fu'lan*, as in *kafara kafaranan* and *ghafara ghufranan*, and it is an intensive form of the verbal noun. Did the two of them offer one sacrifice, or did each of them offer a sacrifice specific to himself? Since the Truth accepted it from one of them and did not accept it from the other, this means that each of them offered a sacrifice separate from the other, because Allah accepted the sacrifice of one of them and did not accept the sacrifice of the other.

*Al-qurban* is a verbal noun (*masdar*), and verbal nouns do not change in pronunciation or writing for dual, plural, masculine, or feminine. We describe a man by saying: *rajul 'adl* (a just man). Likewise: *imra'ah 'adl* (a just woman), *rajulan 'adl* (two just men), *imra'atan 'adl* (two just women), *rijal 'adl* (just men), *nisa' 'adl* (just women). So the verbal noun is the same for singular, dual, plural, masculine, and feminine. We know that Adam is the first of the human species, and Hawwa' (Eve) came to him, so that the pairing for reproduction would be complete, because reproduction only comes from a male and a female.

﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ (51:49).

So every existing thing that the Truth willed to reproduce, He creates from it a pair.

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know﴾ (36:36).

We see this when we pollinate the date palm with pollen from the male palm. There are some creatures whose male and female we do not know, either because the male is not visible to our eyes, but it exists at a distance, and the wind is what carries the pollen grains. ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing, then We sent down water from the sky﴾ (15:22).

So the wind brings the pollen grains from any place to fertilize the plant. Or male and female exist together in one thing or in one space. An example is the maize stalk, where we find its male and female in one thing. The top of the stalk is the male, and from each cob there emerges a number of fine threads that we call the *shawsha* (silk). These are the threads of the female, and the air carries the male pollen from the maize tassel to the silk. Each strand takes from the pollen grains what it needs for the grains to ripen. When the leaves of the cob cling together and do not allow the fine threads of the female to emerge, the pollen does not reach them, and the cob comes out unripe and without maize grains. When we hold the cob and open it, we may find some of its grains dead, those that the pollen did not reach, because they did not have a fine thread to catch the pollen. A maize grain from which no fine thread emerged to catch the pollen does not ripen. So everything has male and female.

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾ (36:36). Likewise His words: ﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾ (53:45).

Everything that is called a thing must have a male and a female. Even rain must be fertilized; if the rain were not fertilized by charged particles, it would not fall. Even pebbles contain positive and negative particles, and when we invented electricity and discovered the positive and the negative, we were relieved. So when the Truth says: ﴿And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember﴾ (51:49).

And His words, glorified be He: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know﴾ (36:36).

This is the first knowledge of the Arabs, for they were not a people of knowledge before the Qur'an.

The Qur'an conveyed all knowledge to the Arabs, until they surpassed others when they took up the means (*asbab*) of Allah. But when they grew lax and others continued to take up the means, discoveries advanced, and we find these discoveries hidden in the Qur'an:

{Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know} (36:36).

So everything that is found, happens, or is discovered that has a positive and a negative, that is, male and female, falls within the scope of:

﴿and from what they do not know﴾ (36:36).

Man is the master of existence and must have a pair, male and female, for reproduction, not for origination. As for origination, it belongs to Allah, glorified and exalted, who originated everything from nothing. When Adam and Eve came and fertilization and reproduction began, the number of the earth's inhabitants began to grow. If we went back through the lineages of the whole world, we would find the number decreasing until we reached Adam and Eve. For example, if we went back a hundred years, we would find the population of Egypt not exceeding five million at most. If we went back further, centuries, the population would decrease, until we reached the first creation that Allah made, Adam, and made Eve for him. So a human alone does not produce offspring.

So when we carry out a census of descendants in the world and trace it back, we return to the first creation. Likewise every thing that reproduces, whether animal or plant. When we move the count forward, we find the numbers increasing, and the leap is large. When the Truth informs us that He created us from one soul and created from it its spouse and spread from both of them men and women, the science of statistics confirms this. Reproduction comes through pairing, and pairing came from Adam and Eve. The Truth willed that Adam have twins, so that each twin would marry the twin of the opposite sex from a different birth, that is, the male would marry a female who was not born with him in the same womb.

Our Lord brought us this story to clarify the origin of reproduction in a symbolic way. He, glorified be He, made clear that a pairing distance existed, but it was an additional distance. Indeed, this boy would be the brother of this girl, and this girl his sister. But when she is born with him and another birth comes with a male and a female in it, there will be an additional distance. So the girl from this birth marries the male from the other birth, and the male from the second birth marries the girl from the other birth. This is the additional distance that was available at that time, because the world was still in the beginning of its fragile childhood.

We notice a similar matter in the countryside, when one peasant says to another: "Your maize is bad." The second peasant says: "I take from the same land where I took the maize and give them seeds from it. I have planted a feddan of maize, and I keep two or three *kayla* (measures) to use as seed to plant, and the maize comes out weak." The experienced peasant says: "Oh, sheikh, bring maize from your neighbor's field, so that the maize becomes like my maize, with some distance in it. After that the quality becomes one." He says: "Bring it from another town," and after that from a third town. This is why crossbreeding (*tahjin*) and reproduction: how did it arise? Where do we get the seeds? Whenever we bring them from outside, the yield comes out strong.

Likewise pairing, so that in this pairing there are talents. For this reason the ancient Arab noticed this. It is remarkable that this Bedouin Arab, who had no culture and whom we know to have had no schooling or learning, was guided to such a truth, guided in a way that makes it a general natural principle. He wanted to praise a man for his vigor, so he said of him:

"A youth whom a paternal cousin's daughter did not bear, for the offspring of close relatives is often weak,
How did this poet come to this? And after that he says:
She exceeded the cousin's daughter, though she was beloved to me, for fear that her offspring would be weakened."

That is, he loves her, but he passed her by, so that her offspring would not be weak.

For this reason the poet says on this matter:

"I advise whoever has a far-reaching concern:
marry the children of paternal cousins,
for whoever is of weak offspring and sickness does not escape."

The Arab poet, who was not in a cultured nation and did not know crossbreeding or these things, noticed this matter. How? Either he was guided to it by observing the reality of the universe, finding that marriage between close relatives produces weak offspring; or it came from the remnants of earlier religions and the ancient admonitions that humankind kept. If Allah wanted reproduction to begin, a brother would have to marry his sister. But He, glorified be He, wants us to be distant: yes, brother and sister, but we keep distance and take the differing birth. For this reason, when they came to attribute the story of the two sons of Adam, Qabil and Habil, they differed. For instance, the *Sifr al-Takwin* (Book of Genesis) speaks. We take from the Book of Genesis, because changes in it do not concern them, since changes were in matters that concern them, such as the prophethood of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ)). Other matters do not concern them, yet there is also much in them.

They say that Habil was the first person killed in humanity, and that Qabil killed him. Some stories say he did not know how to make him die or kill him. So Satan showed him that he brought a bird and placed its head on a stone, then took and struck its head until it died, and thus taught him how to kill. Just as a crow will come and teach him how to bury. As for the matter of how to kill, it does not come in our sources; but how to bury does come in our sources.

﴿Then Allah sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal his brother's corpse﴾ (5:31).

So this was the first person to die and be killed. But how do you say that he did not know killing until Satan came and taught him how to kill his brother? We say: you have not paid attention, for the Truth said:

﴿If you stretch your hand toward me to kill me, I shall not stretch my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (5:28).

So Qabil understood killing, and do not say that he learned killing. The matter of burial is indeed new, and the story came to establish for us how reproduction began, so that Allah would bring together the two spouses in the additional distance, because non-additional distance was not possible at that time. So this one is a stranger to that one, and that one is a stranger to this one, until the matter expands. After that the legislation was reenacted, that a sister of any birth is forbidden to her brother forever. After that we expand the matter and extend it to other prohibitions by lineage and fosterage. So this story must have a basis. They said: "Let us offer a sacrifice." Why? "When they each offered a sacrifice, and it was accepted from one of them and not accepted from the other."

Why did the two of them want to offer a sacrifice? They said: the sister of Qabil, who was born in the same womb with him, was sweet and beautiful, and the sister of Habil was not beautiful. According to the rules of distance in pairing, it was incumbent upon Habil

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 5, verse 28:

﴿If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you. Indeed I fear Allah, the Lord of the worlds.(28)﴾ (Surat al-Ma'idah)

The word "al-bast" (extending, spreading) is the opposite of "al-qabd" (grasping, withholding). There are two usages: "basata lahu" (he extended to him/for him) and "basata ilayhi" (he extended toward him). You find "basata lahu" as though the extending is for the benefit of the one to whom it is extended. ﴿And if Allah extended provision to His servants...﴾ (part of verse 27, Surat al-Shura).

He did not say "ila 'ibadihi" (toward His servants) but said "li'ibadihi" (for His servants). So extending is for the benefit of the one to whom it is extended, and therefore it is not used with "ila" except in evil. We explained this matter before in His words, the Truth: ﴿When a people determined to stretch out their hands against you...﴾ (part of verse 11, Surat al-Ma'idah).

So the one who extends (his hand) to you gives you benefit, and the one who extends (his hand) toward you, the benefit is for himself.

"If you stretch out your hand against me to kill me, I shall not stretch out my hand against you to kill you." He clarified "to kill me" as the meaning of "ilayya" (toward me). The reason is not an inability to match your strength with strength, no; rather, it is because I fear Allah. There is no shortcoming in this in defending myself, because I want to subdue you in a way that brings you back to your right senses. When someone comes who wants to kill another, let him say to him: "By Allah, I will not fight you, because I fear our Lord."

So he made clear to him that his fear of Allah is a settled matter in the mind, even if it is contrary to preserving life. He may know it within himself, because his brother could have offered a strong defence. He referred the matter to the Highest Truth, so do not say Habil was passive; no, he raised the matter to the Most Powerful. The Truth says:

﴿Indeed, I want you to bear my sin and your sin, so you will be among the companions of the Fire. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.(29)﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 29:

And "tabu'" (تبوء) means: you will return from the transaction of my killing, by bearing the sin of that deed and receiving its punishment; and "your sin" (إثمك) refers also to the sin for which you wanted to kill me, because you rebelled against the method (manhaj), when your offering was not accepted by our Lord. You sinned in not accepting the required distance in the marital relationship. So you have two sins: "The first sin: it is your rejection and your non-acceptance of God's ruling and His method, and it is because of this that God did not accept your offering. The second sin: it is my killing, and I have no part in this matter, because the wrongdoer must receive his recompense."

Habil says: "I want you to bear my sin and your sin." He did not wish that his brother would be disobedient; rather he said: if he is going to disobey in this way, he will bear my sin and receive his recompense. So he has wished and desired for him to return to punishment and to receive it if he does it, while he does not want him to do it.

"I want you to bear my sin and your sin, so that you will be among the companions of the Fire; and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers." The recompense of the wrongdoers is a swift education to stand before the rages of injustice from wrongdoers, because if the truth left it to the Hereafter, injustice would spread, and whoever does not believe in the Hereafter becomes a professional in wrongdoing. That is why we said earlier: God, glorified and exalted be He, gave us that example in surah "al-Kahf" when He mentioned to us the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, to whom God gave of everything a means, so he followed a means. Then after that He showed us the task of those given the means and who follow the means, and made his mission on earth the building and betterment of the universe and securing of society. What did He say:

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring﴾ (part of verse 86, surah al-Kahf).

This is according to the eye's appearance: when you are riding the sea, you see the sun setting in the water; it does not set in the water, because the water is the limit of the extent of your horizon.

﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring, and he found near it a people. We said: O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or take towards them a good course﴾ (verse 86, surah al-Kahf).

So he gave him the choice: either you do this or you do that.

﴿He said: As for one who wrongs, we will punish him﴾ (part of verse 87, surah al-Kahf).

That is the law that must prevail in society, so that I do not leave to one who does not believe in a god and does not believe in an afterlife to spread injustice; let him receive his punishment in this world.

﴿And indeed for those who wronged is a punishment short of that﴾ (part of verse 47, surah al-Tur).

That is, before the Hereafter they have a punishment. That is why when people see the downfall of a wrongdoer, or see the defeat that befell him, they take a lesson from it. Our generation has witnessed many wrongdoers who inflicted torment on one another, and if the wronged had been empowered against them, they would not have done to them what some did to others. The Truth wanted their punishment to take place so that the matter would become clear.

﴿He said: As for one who wrongs, we will punish him﴾ (part of verse 87, surah al-Kahf).

His affair does not end with that; after that he is returned to whom? He is returned to God: ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment﴾ (part of verse 87, surah al-Kahf).

That is, the punishment of this world, its punishment will be bearable, because it is a punishment bound to the power of the weak; but the punishment in the Hereafter is by the strength of the Supreme Powerful:

﴿And as for one who believes and does righteous deeds, he will have a reward of the best, and we will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾ (verse 88, surah al-Kahf).

That is the mission of the Strong, the Firm God: the one who wrongs, He strikes his hand; and the one who does good deeds, He gives him incentives.

Al-Sha'rawi, commentary on Surah 5, verse 30:

The Almighty says here, in the verse we are reflecting upon: ﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him, and he killed him, and became among the losers.﴾ It is not said "taw'a'tu al-shay'" (I made the thing compliant) except when the thing resists the action. So do not say "I made the water compliant"; rather you say "I made the iron compliant." And His saying "so his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him" – is it his soul that will be killed, while it is his soul that was made compliant?

Let us take note here that a human being has two faculties. One is a natural faculty (malakah fitriyyah) that loves truth and loves good, and the other is a desire-driven faculty (malakah ahwa'iyyah) subject to whim. The two faculties struggle with each other.

"So his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him": it is as if the evil, desire-driven soul overcame the good one, so there is a pulling, a struggle, and a pushing. A human being does not love injustice if it falls upon him, but at the moment he imagines that he is the one who wrongs another, he may incline to it.

"So his soul made it seem good to him": there still remains in him a remnant of the traces of prophethood, because he is close to Adam, and the matter still sways with him. Evil in the good people descends, and evil in the wicked ascends. A good man may come across something that irritates his nerves, and he says: "If I meet him, I will surely strike him with a bullet, or slap him twice, or rebuke him." But the wicked man says: "By God, if I meet him I will spit in his face, or strike him twice, or strike him with a bullet." So the evil in the wicked one escalates; he finds the act insufficient to relieve his anger, so he escalates it. But the soul of the good one vents its anger, and afterwards it lets go with a word. This is noticeable in the Surah of our master Yusuf:

﴿When they said: Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we, though we are a band (of strength)﴾ (Yusuf 12:8).

What is remarkable is that they brought a justification that works against them, so that you know that desire, anger, envy and rancour overturn the scales. "Though we are a band" indicates that they are strong, and it is this that made their father Ya'qub incline toward the young one. You say: "Yusuf and his brother are dearer to our father than we"? Yes, because he is young. And if one asks the Arab: "Why do you love the young child?" he says: "Because his days with me are the shortest days; the firstborn stayed with me a long time, so I compensate the young one for the days he missed with some love and give him some tenderness." Their saying "though we are a band" is against them, which shows that when a man's scale of values is confused, he brings the argument that is against him and thinks it is in his favour. After that they said:

﴿Indeed, our father is in clear error﴾ (Yusuf 12:8).

They agreed, and began with their saying: ﴿Kill Yusuf﴾ (Yusuf 12:9).

And they said: ﴿Or cast him out to some land﴾ (Yusuf 12:9).

And because they were the tribes (asbat), the sons of Ya'qub, they gave up killing and casting him out on land, and a speaker among them said:

﴿Kill not Yusuf, but throw him down into the dark depth of the well; some of the travellers will pick him up﴾ (Yusuf 12:10).

And does anyone arrange salvation for someone he hates? It is as if the soul still had good in it: first they said "Kill Yusuf"; this is the extremity of anger. Or "cast him out on land," so that he might be eaten by a predatory animal. Then one of them said: "Let us throw him into the dark depth of the well, and some travellers will pick him up." Thus the good ones make concessions.

"So his soul made the killing of his brother seem good to him, and he killed him, and became among the losers." We know loss in matters of trade, because there is gain and there is loss: "gain" means the capital came back with an increase, and "loss" means the capital has diminished. So why did he kill his brother, who was his only brother, and with whom he found companionship in this world? This matter arose from the story of the girl: he wanted to take the beautiful sister and leave the other. When they offered the sacrifice and it was not accepted from him, the dispute escalated and he killed his brother. Thus he lost his capital, while he had wanted to gain: "and became among the losers."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 5, verse 31:

And the Truth (al-Haqq) says after that:

﴿Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth to show him how to conceal the nakedness of his brother. He said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow and conceal the nakedness of my brother?" And he became one of the regretful.﴾ (5:31)

We know that al-sau'ah (the nakedness, shame) is that which the soul dislikes. It derives from "sa'a, yasu'u, su'an", meaning it harms or distresses him. We call the private parts "sau'ah" because they are disliked.

"Then God sent a crow scratching in the earth": Did God send it so that Qabil would see how to conceal the nakedness of Habil, or was it the crow that told him? Both matters are equal, because our Lord is the One who sent it. If you look at the near means, it is the crow; if you look at the One who sends, it is God. The whole matter ultimately belongs to God, and when you trace causes, you find them all from God.

"He said: Woe is me": Whenever you hear the phrase "ya wailata" (woe is me), it has two meanings in usage. The first meaning of "wayl" is destruction (halak). If we want to intensify the destruction, we add the feminine ta' and say "waylah", just as when we want to intensify the description of a scholar we say: "fulan 'alim, fulan 'allam, fulan 'allamah", and the ta' here serves to emphasize the meaning. So "wayl" is destruction, and "waylah" also means destruction. What then does "ya wailati" mean?

We know that the vocative is made with "ya". How, then, does one call out to woe and destruction? Does one call out to what is not rational? Yes, it is called out to, because since "wayl" and "waylah" mean destruction, it is as if you were saying: "I can no longer bear what I am in of anxiety and grief, and nothing will free me from it except destruction. O my destruction, come, for this is your time." So his saying "ya wailati" means "O destruction, come!" Al-Mutanabbi was aware of this matter and said:

"It is a sufficient affliction for you that you see death as a cure, and it suffices for death's wishes that it be a hope."

What affliction is this in which you say: "O Lord, relieve me by death"? So what the one who calls out to destruction sees is more than death. The first meaning is that you call on destruction to come, and therefore the Truth says:

﴿And the Book will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it, and they will say: "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out nothing small or great but has counted it?"﴾ (18:49)

They wish for death, and likewise Qabil said "ya wailati".

Did woe come to him when he asked for it? No, the matter had ended, and he had become the slayer of his brother.

The second meaning: "ya wailatana" may be used to express wonder at a matter that the causes do not yield. There is a difference between the giving of causes and the giving of the Causer. If the giving of causes were to remain the controller of the laws of the universe, it would mean that the Almighty, glorified be He, had exercised His dominion in His kingdom only once, as if He had created the causes and laws and left them to govern. We say: No. By the freedom of power He created causes, and they come to establish the self-subsistence and sovereignty of power. So the Truth, when He wills, says: "Stop, O causes!"

Thus there are causes and there is the Causer. The wondrous matter is what the causes do not yield, and when the cause does not yield, a person wonders, and therefore he returns the matter to the origin, which is not a matter for wonder. Behold our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when the guests came to him and he offered them food and saw that their hands did not reach it. He disliked them, did not feel at ease with them, and sensed fear of them. The Truth speaks of this situation:

﴿So he sensed fear of them. They said: "Do not fear," and gave him good news of a knowing boy. Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, struck her face and said: "An old barren woman!"﴾ (51:28-29)

The Truth also said in this situation:

{And his wife was standing, and she laughed, so We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.} (11:71)

And here the wife of our master Ibrahim said:

﴿"Woe is me! Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man? This is indeed a wondrous thing!"﴾ (11:72)

That is, the causes do not yield, so the matter is returned to the Causer ("Do you wonder at the command of God?"). You had reason to wonder at the causes because they had ceased to function; but when the causes are traced to God, there is no wonder.

Our master Zakariya, peace be upon him, said the like of her words, when he saw Lady Maryam, and he was the one who had taken charge of her, bringing her what she needed for her life's sustenance, and he was surprised to find that she had provision of food and fruit, and asked her:

﴿"O Maryam, from where is this for you?"﴾ (3:37)

How does he say this to her? He must have seen something with her that he had not brought. Here she answered his wonder to alert him to the eternal truth:

﴿"It is from God. Indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning."﴾ (3:37)

The Truth willed that our lady Maryam say it while she was young in years, as if she were saying it as a preparation, because, as we said earlier, she would encounter a matter that only the Causer could resolve: she would give birth without a man, and this is a wondrous matter. Therefore it was necessary that she understand and utter:

﴿"It is from God. Indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning."﴾ (3:37)

It is as if the Truth were implicitly informing us that she must remember that she was the one who said this word, because the future will bring events that need the remembrance of this saying. It was she who reminded Zakariya, peace be upon him, of this truth. Let us see the precision of the Qur'an's indication of the moment when Maryam mentioned that truth to him:

﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾ (3:38)

As if, when he heard this matter, he resolved to supplicate God for his wish in that very sanctuary. Was Zakariya unaware of that truth? He knew it, but there is a difference between a judgment that lies at the margin of consciousness and a judgment that lies at the focus of consciousness.

Maryam's saying to Zakariya, "It is from God. Indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning," moved the matter from the margin of consciousness to its focus. ﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾ (3:38)

Why had he not called upon his Lord from the beginning? Zakariya was proceeding with the causes, and the routine of causes can distract and occupy one from the Causer. When he heard from Maryam, "He provides for whom He wills without reckoning," he wished to enter through this door. So he called upon his Lord, and the Truth gave him good news that he would have offspring. Zakariya wondered again at this matter, describing his state:

﴿"And old age has overtaken me, and my wife is barren"﴾ (3:40)

Since you, O Zakariya, have asked God to grant you offspring, and the matter of God's providing to whom He wills has leapt from the margin of your consciousness to its focus, the command of God came:

﴿"Thus says your Lord"﴾ (19:9)

So there is no investigation of causes and effects; they are the will of God. The Truth clarifies the grounds: "Indeed God provides for whom He wills without reckoning," and brings you the child, and He, glorified be He, says:

﴿"It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing"﴾ (19:9)

All these are preliminaries from Maryam and from our master Zakariya, her guardian, for Zakariya would be a witness when the child came to her without a father and she gave birth; he was her guardian, and he would be exposed to this matter.

And why all this preparation? Because breaking the causes, breaking the laws, and breaking the patterns occurred in other matters, but with Maryam it would be in her honour, which is the most sacred thing for a woman. Therefore all these preparations were necessary. It is thus a wondrous matter, yet it is not wondrous to God.

And here is Qabil saying: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow?" It is as if the operation of the crow showed Qabil that he did not know anything the bird before him did. Here is a matter that a crow does and you, O Qabil, do not do. You acquired the power to kill your brother, but you are unable to do what this crow does. Qabil would not say this except after passing through a severe inner state that weighed heavily on his conscience.

He had power over his brother and killed him, and he did not know how to conceal him, while the crow knew how to conceal the corpse of another crow. And so Qabil became one of the regretful: "So he became one of the regretful."

We must note the difference between "nadam" (regret) and "nadam" (regret). For example: a man dared to transgress God's limits and drank wine with the money he was to use to buy food for his family. When he returned home and found his family waiting for food, he regretted that he had drunk wine. Was the man's regret that he disobeyed God, or that he did not buy food for his family? He regretted not buying the food, and that is a rejected regret, not repentance.

And perhaps this wine-drinker put on his finest clothes and went out, drank wine, and fell to the ground, and here he regretted because wine had brought him to this state. Did he regret that he disobeyed his Lord, or that he had become a laughingstock among people? So too was Qabil's regret: he regretted his failure, because he did not know what the crow knew.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 32:

Allah (the Truth) says, after that:

﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had slain all mankind; and whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind. And certainly Our messengers came to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them after that were transgressors in the earth.﴾ (32)

We find that the Truth said: He has prescribed for the Children of Israel what came in this verse as a clear law, because the meaning of the word "min ajl" (because of) is "bi-sabab" (on account of), and "ajl" comes from "ajal", meaning that he committed a crime (jinayah), that is, from the offence of that.

Or, from this crime We legislated this legislation: "whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had slain all mankind." So when you hear "min ajl", know that it means "on account of that", or "by the occurrence of that", or "by the offence of that", or "by this crime that was the cause of that."

But is this prescription specific to the Children of Israel? Some scholars said: the two sons of Adam were not directly the sons of Adam, but were from the descendants of Adam, and they were of the Children of Israel. We reply: who is Israel first, the one to whom the sons of Israel are attributed? He is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and Ibrahim reaches Nuh through eleven fathers, and Nuh reaches Shith, and after that to Adam. Was this entire chain then unable to know how to bury the dead until the Children of Israel came?

Of course not. Since the Truth has made clear that He sent a crow searching the earth to show him how to conceal the nakedness of his brother, this is evidence that Habil was the first human to be buried. It is therefore unacceptable to say that mankind did not know how to cover the corpse until humanity reached the time of the Children of Israel, and that it was they who taught humanity that.

And why did the Truth bring up the Children of Israel here? The reason is that the Children of Israel dared not only to kill a soul, but dared to kill the guiding soul, which is the soul that carries the message of prophethood. For this reason the specification was made: they killed their prophets who brought them the practical method, because prophets come as practical models of the methods, so that they draw people's attention to the reality of applying the method of God. The prophets, therefore, do not bring a new law, but they follow the law of those before them. So why did the Children of Israel kill some of the prophets? Resentment against these prophets was generated among the Children of Israel.

We know that when a good person does good and a wicked person, who cannot do good, sees it, resentment, rancour and anger arise in the soul of the wicked against the doer of good. The doer of good, whenever he does good, indeed stings the wicked, and therefore the wicked tries to remove the doer of good from before him. The prophets were the behavioural exemplars, and the Truth said about the Children of Israel: ﴿Why did you kill the prophets of Allah before?﴾ (part of verse 91, Surat al-Baqarah).

The Truth brought "before" (min qabl) here for this wisdom, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in enmity with the Jews, and evil impulses may blow upon them so they try to kill the Prophet. They did try that, just as they wanted to throw a stone at him and put poison for him. Therefore Allah said: "before", meaning that your power to kill prophets was in the past, but with Muhammad the Chosen you will not be able to reach him.

He, glory be to Him, says: "Because of that We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had slain all mankind." This is an explanation of the Truth's will to establish the unity of faith, to make the believing society a bond, which the saying of the Messenger of Allah clarifies, in what Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated from him: (The believer to the believer is like a building, one part of it strengthening the other.)

And beware of looking at one who transgresses against others, wrongfully, and standing with folded hands, because the unity of faith makes the believers all like one body: if one organ complains, all the other organs respond to it with sleeplessness and fever. If someone kills a person and the believing society stands in the position of the helpless, this is corruption in the earth. Therefore society must confront such an act not on the basis that it killed one soul, but as if it had killed all people, unless the killing of the soul is for retaliation (qisas) or corruption in the earth.

The Truth, glory be to Him, completes the second part of that matter of faith: "and whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind." This is the unity of faith. Whoever attacks one innocent soul is like one who attacks all people, and whoever rescues a person from destruction is as if he had saved all people.

In the legal ruling (al-tawqi‘ al-taklifi), the practical application of that rule occurs. Whoever kills an innocent person, upon him is the curse of Allah and His wrath, and Allah will punish him, as if he had killed all people. If we look at it from the aspect of recompense, the recompense is one.

"Whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind." And Glory be to Him and Exalted wants the believing society not to receive one who dares with falsehood against truth, except that the whole society stands before him, so the one attacked is not left alone, because what emboldens the people of evil is that some people say the word "wa ana mali" ("and what is it to me?").

The "I-don't-care attitude" (al-anaiyya al-maliyya) is what emboldens the people of evil. Therefore, read the story of the three bulls: the black bull, the red bull, and the white bull. A lion schemed against the red and black bulls, and they allowed him to eat the white bull. The lion then schemed against the black bull, and the black bull allowed the lion to eat the red bull. Then the turn came to the black bull, and he said to the lion: "You ate on the day the white bull was eaten." It was as if the bull, by turning to "I am not his concern", brought about his own downfall. But had the three bulls united against the lion, they would have killed him.

And here is the noble Prophetic hadith that represents the one who stands upon the limits of Allah and the one who falls into them:

From al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The likeness of the one who stands within the limits of Allah and the one who falls into them is like a people who drew lots over a ship; some of them were at its top and some at its bottom. Those at the bottom, when they needed water, would pass by those above them, and they said: 'If only we made a hole in our share and did not harm those above us.' If they leave them and what they want, they all perish; and if they take hold of their hands, they are saved and all are saved."(1)

Likewise is the likeness of the one who stands upon the limits of Allah and the likeness of the one who falls into them. It is as if the Truth, glory be to Him and Exalted, is saying to us: do not look at a soul killing a soul without right, but look at it as if the killer killed all people, because all people are equal in the right to life, and since the killer has dared against one, it is possible that he will dare against the rest.

Or his act becomes a precedent for others. Since he has established such a custom, you will find everyone who is angry at another killing him, and the chain of killers and the killed continues.

The Prophetic hadith says: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it after him, without their rewards being diminished in any way; and whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it after him, without their burdens being diminished in any way."

It is precaution, precision and restriction: "whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth." Had the legislation been human legislation, and this matter had come up, it could later correct it with an explanation or amendment, but the Supreme Legislator does not need to correct.

"Whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth": it is as if whoever kills a soul for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is not said of him that he killed all people, but rather that he gave life to all people, because criminalizing any act means the arrival of a text clarifying that this act is a crime, and after that we set a penalty for this crime. One cannot come to someone who committed an act and say to him: "I will hold you accountable for it and punish you for it" without there being a text criminalizing this act.

There exists a legal principle that says: "No criminalization except by text, and no penalty except by criminalization." That is, we attach the penalty to the crime, or when an act is declared criminal, the penalty is mentioned alongside the criminalization. Is the aim then to punish the perpetrator of the offence? No, the aim is to make the punishment dreadful so that every person sees it before committing the crime, and the goal is to prevent the crime. For this reason you find the human saying: "Killing is the surest way to prevent killing." Naturally, that human saying cannot rise to the level of the Truth's saying: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life, O people of understanding﴾ (part of verse 179, Surat al-Baqarah).

Because we may ask: which killing is the surest way to prevent killing? We will find that the intended wisdom is not initial killing but the killing of retaliation. Thus we find that human reasoning missed the effective insight in preventing killing that is in the Truth's saying: "whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had slain all mankind, and whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind." The word "ahyaha" (gives life to it) has more than one meaning; specifically it has two meanings. The first meaning: that he preserved in it the spirit that moves matter. The second meaning: the reviving of the faith-spirit, in confirmation of the Truth's saying: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ (part of verse 24, Surat al-Anfal).

We should note that the Truth made corruption in the earth deserving of the penalty of killing.

Corruption (fasad) is taking the righteous out of its righteousness, and what is required of us in faith is that a thing that is righteous in itself we keep righteous. If we can make it more righteous, let us do so, and if we cannot, let us leave it in its righteousness.

Why did the Truth bring a punishment for corruption in the earth? The meaning of "the earth" is the realm in which the Truth made mankind His successors, and when the Truth says: "or corruption in the earth," this means that every corruption returns to every thing enclosed in the earth, and the first thing enclosed in the earth, or its master, is man. When we corrupt man, this means killing man.

Therefore, corruption must be in other things: in the cosmos or other kinds, animals, plants and inanimate objects. Corruption in these beings occurs by taking them out of their possessor's ownership, such as a group seizing the merchandise of another person, or someone taking the produce of another's crop, or taking some of the output of a manganese, iron or similar mine.

Corruption is of two kinds: corruption in the earth, which relates to what is enclosed in the earth, and the enclosed thing in the earth is a master, which is man, and corrupting him is killing him, or causing him an imbalance in his psychological security such as anxiety, agitation and fear. We note that the Truth, glory be to Him, bestowed favour upon Quraysh, that He fed them from hunger and secured them from fear.

Thus among corruption is terrorizing and frightening people, and it has two parts: a part in which you frighten someone who has a vengeance against you, or between you and whom there is enmity or hatred; or you frighten a people with whom you have no relationship and who have done nothing to you. Whoever attacks a person with whom he has a problem, enmity or hatred, we do not call him one who goes outside the Shari'ah by taking his right, but he does not exact his right with his own hand; rather, there must be a ruler who carries that out so that the matter is regulated and set right. He goes outside the Shari'ah only in the case of aggression.

As for the one who goes to attack people with whom he has no enmity, this is hirabah (armed brigandage), such as one who goes out to cut the road on people and frightens everyone he meets and causes him anxiety, terror and fear for his self and his property. Property may be of the kind of animals, plants or inanimate objects, and this is what the Shari'ah calls hirabah, and a specific verse on it will come.

Thus corruption in the earth means taking a righteous thing out of its righteousness, enclosed in the earth; the enclosed thing in the earth has the human as its master, and corruption against him is either by killing him or agitating him and spreading terror in him; or by something owned among the things below him in kind, such as crops, plants or animals. So corruption in the earth also qualifies for killing the soul: "whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the earth, it is as if he had slain all mankind." That is, killing without corruption in the earth is the killing that deserves punishment, whereas killing with corruption in the earth is another matter, because there is a difference between killing by retaliation (qisas) and killing as a hadd prescribed by the legislator. Even if the blood-owner pardons the killer in hirabah and highway robbery, this does not intercede in that or cancel the hadd upon the one who did it, because it is a crime against the community.

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapters on partnership and testimonies; narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the chapter on trials; and narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad.

The Almighty says next:

﴿Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption is only that they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides, or that they be exiled from the land. That is for them a disgrace in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ [5:33]

The first thing in war is seizure. The meaning of one people waging war against another is that they desire to seize the good things or property of the other party. So how can people wage war against Allah, Who is unseen? The first war against Allah is the attempt to seize His authority, which is His legislation. If you, O human being, attempt to legislate on other than the method of Allah, then you are seeking to seize the right of Allah to legislate, and this is the first war against Allah.

Do those who wage war against Allah wish to seize the dominion of Allah? No, because the hand of Allah in His dominion is eternal from the beginning and will remain forever, and He, glorified is He, will never hand it over to any of His servants. So what, then, do they wish to seize? They wish to falsify the legislations of Allah, whereas He, glorified is He, is the sole Legislator. Legislation, as we said, is the law that preserves the creation. So why do we not leave the Creator of man to set the rules that protect mankind? Therefore, the first usurpation that people commit is that they legislate for themselves, because the law that preserves man is set by the Creator of man. If someone comes and wants to set for man, who is of his creation, a law of preservation, we say to him: you are seizing the right of Allah.

And how do they wage war against the Messenger?

We know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had two states: Allah is unseen, but the Messenger was a visible person among us on certain days, and he was fought with the sword. When the Messenger passed on to the Highest Companion, his war became like the war against Allah, by taking his authority in legislation, which is the second authority. We say to it: we will legislate for ourselves and there is no need for this Messenger; or a certain system says: we will take only from the words of Allah, and that is what spreads in some countries. We say to each of these: Do you perform the prayer? He says: Yes. We ask him: How many rak'ahs did you pray for Maghrib? He answers: three rak'ahs. We ask him: From where did you get that? And from where did you know that the Maghrib prayer is three rak'ahs when it is not mentioned in the Noble Qur'an? Here he will fall silent.

We ask him: How do you pay zakat, and by what calculation do you reckon it? He says: I pay zakat at two and a half percent on gold and silver and on trade goods, for example.

We say to him: Then how did you come to know that? And likewise how did you know the Hajj? So the Messenger ﷺ has a function, and the war against the Prophet occurs in rejecting a saying, an act, or an approval of his, upon him be prayers and peace.

An example of this are those who say: the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah are many. We say to them: the period of the Messenger of Allah's mission was twenty-three years, and all of his speech is hadith. Every word that came out of his mouth is a noble hadith, and if we were to count speech alone it would fill volumes that cannot be enumerated. Every statement he heard and approved from others is a hadith, and every action that another performed in his presence and he approved, without objecting, is a hadith. So how many would the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ be? And how do some people consider a quantity of hadiths that have reached us, after a tremendous degree of most thorough purification, to be excessive? They say: "Keeping away from the Messenger what he said is better than entering upon the Messenger ﷺ what he did not do." They claim that this is preservation of Islam, but they overlook that Allah is the Guardian of His religion, and that the Messenger ﷺ had laid down the rules for sifting the hadiths when he said: "Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire." (1)

Behold, al-Bukhari transmits from the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who met him, and our master Muslim considers contemporaneity sufficient because it is the presumption of meeting, and each of them exercised the utmost precision. Any person who had a flaw in conduct is not taken for his word. Therefore, when some attempted to undermine the hadiths and one of them said: "It is enough for me to say, there is no god but Allah," I asked: How can he not mention that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah? How can he perform the call to prayer? How does he perform the prayer? And how can he understand the word of the Truth: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾ (part of 59:7).

This is an authorization from Allah that Muhammad ﷺ should have legislative authority.

Likewise, the audacity against the imams: they first dare against the Prophet, then they creep over the whole religion. And among them came the word of the Truth: "Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive upon the earth in corruption," meaning they take what is righteous in itself out of its righteousness so that it becomes corrupt. The penalty is that they be killed or crucified. This activation in His words, "that they be killed or crucified," came for severity and reinforcement, so that the general believing society stands against them as one standing upon this matter, and the legitimate authority stands on behalf of all in this matter, just as it is said: the public prosecutor is the representative of the people, in raising the case so that killing does not spread among people, without their understanding the wisdom of every matter.

"That they be killed or crucified or that their hands and feet be cut off from opposite sides or that they be exiled from the land." Is "or" here for choice, or is it, as is said, "lafa wa nashr" (folding and unfolding)? Al-laff is folding, and al-nashr is spreading out and separating a thing.

So what, then, are lafa and nashr? Like what the poet says:

My heart, my eyelid, the tongue, and my Creator

Several items have been mentioned, but the judgments are not mentioned; this is lafa, gathering the subjects without mentioning the predicate for each. Then he brought the judgments in the order of the things judged upon, and completed the verse of poetry with his words:

Content, weeping, grateful, and forgiving.

Let us read the whole verse: "My heart, my eyelid, the tongue, and my Creator / Content, weeping, grateful, and forgiving."
And the Truth says:

﴿And of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty﴾ (part of 28:73).

So His saying "that you may rest therein" refers to the night, and His saying "and that you may seek of His bounty" refers to the day. Here He came with lafa and then came with nashr.

Corruption, as we know, has many forms. Corruption against a person may mean killing him, or killing him and taking his property, or seizing his property without killing him, or instilling terror in a person without taking his property or killing him. So the word corruption encompasses the varieties of corruption: a soul killed, or a soul killed along with property plundered and taken, or property taken without a soul killed, or intimidation and terrorizing.

The Truth says: "or that they be exiled from the land." Exile means expulsion and banishment, and expulsion is only possible for something established and settled, and banishment is only possible for one who is firmly rooted. So before he is exiled there must be a settlement and rootedness for him in some place, which we term technically the dwelling, or the homeland, or the place where a person resides because he is established in it. Being established in it means that he moves within its sphere, yet he returns to a stable, settled place; therefore it is called a dwelling, that is, one dwells in it after his movement in its various domains. The meaning of exile on this basis is removing him from his dwelling and from his homeland, which he has taken as his home and which was the arena of his corruption. But to what place do we take out the one whom we sentence to exile? Someone may say: if you remove him from a place where he corrupted and take him to another place, his corruption may spread.

No, because exile does not give him that opportunity for corruption, since the first settlement gives him familiarity with the geography of the place, and familiarity with those he intimidates. He knows the behavior of his neighbors, knows how to frighten so-and-so and how to seize another's goods, and so on. But if he goes to a place where he is not settled, he will need a long time until he becomes acquainted with the geography of the place, the locations of the people, and their points of weakness. Thus exile is a prevention of the corrupter's corruption.

When He, glorified is He, says "or that they be exiled from the land," we know that the word "land" has a meaning. We now call the land the terrestrial globe, while they formerly understood it to be dry land and what is in it of waters. After we came to know that the atmosphere of the earth is part of the earth, we said regarding spatial sanctities that every atmosphere takes its sanctity from its place: the atmosphere of the Ka'bah is Ka'bah. Evidence of this is that one who prays on the third floor of the Haram and faces the Ka'bah prays facing the atmosphere of the Ka'bah, and one who boards an aircraft and wishes to pray faces the atmosphere of the Ka'bah. When the pilgrims crowded and the sa'i area could not accommodate all the pilgrims, they built a second floor so that people could perform sa'i on it. So the place of sa'i is not only the specified ground, but its atmosphere also has sanctity; if we build such and such a storey, it is also suitable as a place of sa'i.

Thus what applies to the land applies to the atmosphere of the earth. This is why, before there were Muslim pilots, they forbade a non-Muslim pilot to fly over the airspace of the Haram, because a non-Muslim is forbidden to enter the Ka'bah and the Haram, and as long as a person is forbidden to enter the Ka'bah, he is likewise forbidden to fly in the airspace of the Ka'bah.

For the atmosphere of a place takes the sanctity or ruling of the place. The atmosphere is part of the earth, and we know that the atmospheric envelope revolves with the earth. From this we know the Qur'anic gifts of the Speaker of His words, and He, glorified is He, is the Creator of His universe. Since the Speaker of the Qur'an is the Creator of the universe, there is no contradiction between a cosmic truth and a Qur'anic truth. The contradiction arises only from one of two matters: either we treat as a fact a matter that is still at the stage of theory, when it has not yet become fact; or we understand as a Qur'anic truth something that is not so. If the matter is truly a cosmic truth and truly a Qur'anic truth, there is no contradiction at all. Evidence for this, for example, is the saying of the Truth, glorified is He:

﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾ (part of 31:34).

Modern science comes with research and analysis, and some superficial people say: No, science knows what is in the womb, male or female. We say: we do not dispute that, because it is a cosmic truth and it does not clash with the correct understanding of the Qur'anic truth. But we ask: when do scientists know that? They do not know this matter until a period of time has passed. But the Truth knows it before any period of time passes. Then who said that the Truth means by "and He knows what is in the wombs" only male or female? Does its meaning have only one aspect? No, it has many aspects. No one knows whether what is in the womb will later be a tall or short person, intelligent or dull, wretched or happy, long-lived or short-lived, forbearing or ill-tempered. So why do we confine "what" to the matter of male and female only?

He, glorified is He, knows the future from eternity, before any scientist knows anything and before the world obtains any sample. Then does every pregnant woman go to a doctor to have laboratory tests on what she carries in her belly? Of course not, and we do not know what is in her belly, but the Supreme Creator knows. Then do all pregnant women in the world go to one doctor? Certainly not, but the Supreme Creator knows what is in all wombs.

Thus the Qur'anic truth has never clashed with any cosmic truth; the clash occurs only when we misunderstand that the Qur'anic truth in His saying "and He knows what is in the wombs" is meant to be knowledge of male and female only.

Another example: the Truth says: ﴿And the earth We have spread out﴾ (part of 15:19).

Some misunderstand about God and think that what is meant is that the earth is a carpet before man. It has been established for humanity as a cosmic truth that the earth is spherical, by the evidence of Magellan's voyage, then by the rules relating to the placement of masts and the appearance of the tops of things before their bottoms, and other things. Then in our age it has become something observed by artificial satellites. So this cosmic truth is not disputed, and the error was in understanding the meaning of the Qur'anic truth. The correct understanding of the meaning of the Qur'anic truth in His saying, exalted is He, "And the earth We have spread out," is that whenever we stand in a place we find earth, meaning the earth has no end and no edge.

So He, glorified is He, has spread the earth before man, such that whichever direction man travels, he finds earth, and this is not possible unless the earth is spherical. Therefore the error lay in understanding the spreading

1 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face.

Since the person has repented and handed himself over before society was able to seize him, accepting the repentance is a right owed to him. We must understand "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" within the scope of what Allah has set for Himself. As for what Allah has set for those who were wronged by the aggressor, punishment for the aggressor is necessary if his victims demand it.

﴿Except for those who repent before you have power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ The Qur'an makes the faith-based method one single dough, so it divides matters into sections, like man-made legislation that is arranged into chapters. Thus we find the Qur'an treats judicial rulings as opportunities for the soul to awaken, and so it leads the soul to a directive command to obedience.

We gave an example earlier, when the Qur'an spoke of family matters in Surat al-Baqara:

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already set for them an obligation, then half of what you have set, unless they forgive, or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgives. And that you forgive is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness among yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ (237) (Surat al-Baqara).

After that, it comes to the matter of the prayer:

﴿Maintain the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah devoutly obedient. And if you fear, then on foot or riding. And when you are secure, remember Allah as He has taught you that which you did not know.﴾ (238-239) (Surat al-Baqara).

Thus Allah placed the prayer between two matters of the family, saying after His command to maintain the prayer, even during fighting:

﴿And those who are taken in death among you and leave wives behind—a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without eviction. But if they leave, then there is no blame upon you...﴾ (part of verse 240, Surat al-Baqara).

He brought the command to maintain the prayer among the family problems, both so that religion becomes one single brick, and because a soul charged with hatred and crowded with matters of marriage, bequest and divorce, when it stands to pray to Allah, becomes calm. And for us in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there is an excellent example, for when a matter distressed him and weighed heavily upon him, he would stand to prayer.

Thus Allah, exalted is He, does not present the matters of religion as separate compartments, a chapter for prayer, another for fasting, and a third for zakat. Rather, He blends all of these into a single dough. Therefore, when He sent down the punishments of killing, crucifixion, cutting off (of hands and feet), and banishment upon those who spread corruption and wage war against Allah, that was to cultivate the awe of dread in the human soul. And when the dread awakens in the human soul, the Truth says:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means (wasilah) to Him and strive in His cause that you may succeed.﴾ (5:35)

He has brought us out of a stern atmosphere and talk of punishments into the fear of Allah (taqwa). And taqwa, as we know, is for a person to place between himself and what harms him a shield (wiqayah).

We have learned that the One, exalted is He, who says, "Fear Allah," is the very One who says, "Fear the Fire." We have learned how to understand the fear of Allah: that we place a shield between ourselves and Allah. If someone says: Allah, exalted is He, asks us to cling to His method (manhaj) and to always be in His company, then let us place a shield between ourselves and His punishment, and among His punishment is the Fire.

So His saying, "O you who have believed, fear Allah," means that we should guard against the attributes of His majesty (sifat al-jalal). The Fire is among the creation of Allah and among His soldiers. His saying, exalted is He, "and seek the means (wasilah) to Him," means that we search for the link that connects us to His obedience and His pleasure and to His love. Is there any means other than what Allah, exalted is He, has legislated? And does a person draw near to any being except by what he knows that being loves?

On the human level, we find someone asking: What does so-and-so like? It is said to him: So-and-so likes neckties, so he gifts him a number of neckties. It is also said: So-and-so likes a fine prayer beads, so he brings him a magnificent set of prayer beads. Thus every person draws near to any being by what that being loves. So what of drawing near to Allah? What He loves, He has clarified for us in His sacred hadith: "Whoever shows enmity to a friend of Mine, I have declared war upon him. My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give to him, and if he seeks refuge with Me, I will surely grant him refuge." (1)

So Allah, exalted is He, opens the way before the servant, and He says, exalted is He, in the sacred hadith: "My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts."

That is, the servant draws near to Allah through matters the Truth has not obligated upon him, but which are of the same kind as what He has made obligatory. There is therefore no innovation in worship. Thus, seeking the means to Allah is obedience to Him and standing upon the method in "do" and "do not do."

The means (wasilah), for us too, is a rank among the ranks of Paradise. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked us to ask Allah for him the wasilah, saying: "When you hear the muezzin, say the like of what he says, then send blessings upon me, for whoever sends blessings upon me, Allah sends blessings upon him tenfold. Then ask Allah for me the wasilah, for it is a rank in Paradise that is fitting only for one of the servants of Allah, and I hope I will be that one. Whoever asks Allah for me the wasilah, intercession becomes lawful for him." (2)

We do not wish to enter here into the field of seeking intercession (tawassul) through the Prophet or the saints, because it is a matter that should not be a subject of dispute by anyone. Yet some of them rule that these people are disbelievers.

To those who declare disbelievers those who seek intercession through the Prophet or a saint, we say: soften this statement somewhat. The emergence of such a statement is the result of a lack of understanding. The one who seeks intercession with Allah through the Prophet or a saint believes that he has a standing with Allah. Does anyone believe that the saint flatters Allah so that He gives what is not due to the supplicant? Of course not.

And there are those who say: seeking intercession through the living is permissible, but seeking it through the dead is forbidden. We say to them: you are constricting a matter that is broad, for the life of the living has no bearing on tawassul. If the tawassul is made in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) to Allah, then you have made the tawassul by your love for the one you know to be nearer to Allah than you. It is your love for him that intercedes, and beware of thinking that he will bring you what you do not deserve.

As for the group who say: it is not valid to seek intercession through the Prophet because the Prophet has passed on to the Highest Companion, we say to them: wait a moment, and pay attention to what our master ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said. He said: "In the time of the Messenger of Allah, when the rain was withheld, we would seek intercession through the Messenger of Allah and ask for rain through him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away, ʿUmar sought intercession through his uncle al-ʿAbbas." They said: If tawassul through the Messenger of Allah were permissible after his passing, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, would not have turned away from seeking intercession through the Prophet after his passing and gone instead to seeking intercession through the uncle of the Prophet. And we ask: Did ʿUmar say, "We used to seek intercession through your Prophet, and now we seek intercession to You through al-ʿAbbas"? Or did he say, "And now we seek intercession to You through the uncle of Your Prophet"?

Therefore, those who forbid this narrow the scope upon themselves, because tawassul is not only through the Prophet, but also through whoever is connected by kinship to the Prophet (ﷺ). When one person seeks intercession through another, it means he believes that the one through whom he seeks intercession cannot do anything by himself. I seek his intercession with someone else because I know that he cannot accomplish my request for me. So let us remove the matter of associating partners with Allah (shirk) from this field, and say: we seek intercession through him to another because we know that the one sought for intercession is the Capable, and the one through whom intercession is sought is powerless. This is the utmost certainty and the utmost faith.

However, the one through whom intercession is sought may benefit or may not benefit. When ʿUmar sought intercession through al-ʿAbbas, the uncle of the Prophet, he was doing so for the sake of rain, and the rain in this case would not benefit the Messenger of Allah. Therefore he brought one of the family of the House, as if he had said: "O Lord, the uncle of Your Prophet is thirsty, so for his sake we ask You for rain."

So ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab's seeking intercession through the uncle of the Prophet is evidence against those who forbid seeking intercession through the Prophet after his passing to the Highest Companion. And to get out of the disagreement, we say: righteous deeds embodied in "do such-and-such" and "do not do such-and-such" are the pure means, and by that we are freed from disagreement and do not enter into labyrinths.

"O you who have believed, fear Allah and seek the means to Him and strive in His cause that you may succeed." Let us look at the faithful altruism (al-iythar al-imani) which the Truth wishes to cultivate in the believing soul through the fear of Allah, which is manifested in keeping away from His prohibitions and seeking the means to Allah by following His commands.

Religion did not come for your own self alone. Your faith will not become complete unless you love for your brother what you love for yourself. If you have loved for yourself that you be upon the method, then take great care that this be so for your brothers as well. Your believing brothers are not only those who live with you, but also those destined to exist after that. Therefore, you must strive in the cause of Allah so that the word of Allah may be exalted. Thus the believing aspiration widens and is not confined to the self or to the contemporaries of the believer. And for this reason, the Truth sets out for us the straight path, clarifies it, and makes it plain to us.

The beginning of the path was that the believer in Allah, when he trusted that Allah has bliss and recompense in the Hereafter that is better than what he lives, offered his blood and became a martyr. For this, a noble Companion said: "Is there nothing between me and Paradise except that I enter this battle, so that either I kill them or they kill me?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes."

The Companion threw away the dates he was eating and entered the battle.

It is certain, then, that he knew the life awaiting him was better than the life he lived. Yet Allah did not make jihad a means at the very beginning; rather He kept commanding them to wait and be patient until those who carry the call were trained. He, exalted is He, did not make it a suicidal operation.

Then, during the journey of calling to Islam, we see a Companion grieving because, during the fighting, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs had slipped away from him, and Khalid ibn al-Walid had fled. The days confirm that people do not know that the knowledge of Allah had reserved Khalid and saved him from the sword of that Companion, so that through Khalid Islam would be victorious; and likewise, Allah reserved ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs for another victory for Islam.

Thus jihad in the cause of Allah is a guarantee for the believer that the method in which he believed will remain a means of reaching the Hour, and that cannot be achieved except by spreading the method throughout the whole world. When the believing soul dedicates itself to striving in the cause of Allah, it has within it some of the faithful altruism, and it knows that it has taken the best of faith and wishes to convey it to others. It does not accept to take the best of faith while depriving its contemporaries in lands other than the abodes of Islam, and it is eager that the whole world be believing. If we look at this matter, we find that it represents a deep understanding of the meaning of life. When people are good, a person benefits from all of their goodness; when they are evil, some of their evil reaches him.

Thus it is in the interest of goodness that its goodness spread among people, for if it spreads its goodness, it expects to benefit from the usefulness of that goodness and for its goodness to return to it, because people feel safe from the good man and no evil comes to them from him. He loves that all people be good and upon the balance of faith, for if they are upon the balance of faith, the good person benefits from their goodness. But if people remain upon their evil and the good person remains upon his goodness, then the goodness of the good person will continue to be extended to them and their evil will continue to be extended to the good person.

Thus it is among the wisdom of faith that a person "transmits" goodness to others. The call of the believer to the path of Allah, and for the spread of the method of Allah, requires preparation before the encounter. Before meeting the adversary on the battlefield, good preparation is necessary. When the believer prepares himself, he finds that the whole movement of life is with him, because the call to Allah requires good conduct, and good conduct spreads among people. Here the camp of faith is strengthened, rising in conduct and action. When the camp of faith is strong, it can extract the treasures of the earth and protect the land of faith through industrial, scientific and military advancement. The Truth says: {And We sent down iron, wherein is great might and benefits for mankind} (Qur'an 57:25).

He, exalted is He, sent down the Qur'an and sent down iron. And following that:

﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen﴾ (Qur'an 57:25).

And the meaning of might (ba's) came for this reason. And this is the second reason which the Truth enjoined upon us:

Beware lest you take the method of Allah only as what is confined to "do" and "do not do," but take the method of Allah in what protects the method of Allah, which is scientific progress through extracting the treasures of the earth and manufacturing them, such as iron for example.
