Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 51:

And after that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies (awliya'); they are allies of one another. And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them. Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (5:51)

We note that the address here is to those who believe, and the prohibited matter is taking the Jews and the Christians as allies. What is the meaning of al-Wali (the ally)? Al-Wali is the helper and the supporter. This word is derived from waliya–yali, meaning to stand at his side. We call the one who acts on behalf of the woman in the marriage contract "al-wali," and likewise "wali al-maqtul" (the guardian of the slain person, who has the right to demand retribution). The intended meaning is: O you who have believed, take careful note that you are people entrusted with a mission, which is to remove misguidance from mankind. This misguidance has taken the form of distorting religions whose origin was guidance, so that they became misguided. Beware lest you place your hands in theirs seeking aid and support.

So His saying, the Truth: "Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies" is a legal ruling (hukm taklifi), and its basis is faith in Allah. For as long as you have believed in Allah, anyone whose faith you find deficient through his opposition to the method of his Lord is not fit to be a trustworthy supporter of you, because he was not faithful to what he had. Would you expect him to help you with the trust you carry? No, because he was not faithful to what was revealed to him of the method. Walaya is support, and support is the supporter's eagerness to assist the one being supported. Do you find in them any eagerness toward you, supporting and aiding you, or do they feign support for you? Know well that they will do what the Truth has said:

﴿Had they gone out with you, they would not have increased you except in corruption.﴾ (9:47)

If they had entered your ranks, they would have acted toward you just as the hypocrites act. How much more so those who betrayed the trust of the Books revealed to them? Therefore, allegiance, support and assistance must come from one who is united with you in the supreme goal, and as long as there is someone who differs with Islam in the supreme goal, which is faith, it is not valid for a Muslim to trust him. And He, glory be to Him, says: "They are allies of one another." A person may ask: how does the Truth say about them:

﴿And the Jews said: The Christians are not upon anything﴾ (2:113)

and He, glory be to Him, also says:

﴿And the Christians said: The Jews are not upon anything﴾ (2:113)

and He, majestic is His affair, says:

﴿Thus said those who do not know, the like of their statement﴾ (2:113)

We are, then, before three categories: Jews, Christians and polytheists. The polytheists of Quraysh said the same as the People of the Book, both factions, although they are in fierce disagreement and each denies the other. And He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿So We have put enmity and hatred among them﴾ (5:14)

How, after this, does He, glory be to Him, say: "They are allies of one another"? This is a matter that requires a pause of faith, so that we may see the whole picture. We know that those who oppose the method of Truth may have disputes among them over temporal authorities, but when they face a giant capable of demolishing all the structures of their lies, they unite. This is what we see in real life: the Eastern bloc that was hostile to the Western bloc, yet as soon as something related to Islam appears, they agree with one another, despite the defeat of the Eastern bloc, because Islam with its method is a danger to these and those, and to their authorities. Yet in reality it is a mercy to them: it brings them out of darknesses into light. And they act in the light of what the Truth has said: "They are allies of one another."

And when each of them is alone with the other, the saying of the Truth applies to them:

﴿So We have put enmity and hatred among them﴾ (5:14)

Thus we understand the nature of the relations among the enemies of Islam.

The Truth says: "And whoever among you allies with them, then indeed he is one of them." That is, whoever takes them as supporters and helpers will inevitably fall into the snare of hypocrisy, because he will be with the Muslims with his tongue and with the enemies of Islam with his heart.

The Truth concludes the verse by saying: "Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people." We know that wrongdoing (zulm) is placing a right in other than its rightful owner, and the highest degree of wrongdoing is associating partners with Allah, which is the great wrongdoing. The Truth says:

﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrong﴾ (31:13)

For when a person wrongs another human being and takes something from him to give to someone else, is there a human who can take anything from Allah? No. A human cannot wrong Allah, but he incurs the punishment of association, and this is a futile wronging of the self. The one who associates partners with Allah gains nothing but loss, and that is the whole of frustration.

Because wrongdoing, when it achieves some benefit for the wrongdoer, is a light wrong; but the great wrong is that a person associates others with Allah and receives nothing but a severe punishment. If the polytheist refuses the method of Allah in matters, would he dare to refuse Allah's involuntary decrees concerning him, such as death, for example? And the Truth commands man to believe and to what belongs to faith: testimony to His oneness, belief in His messengers, His books and the Last Day, performing the prayer, paying zakat, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House for those able to undertake it. The polytheist refuses faith and its obligations; would he dare to refuse sickness or death? No. Therefore he wrongs himself with a futile wronging, and Allah, glory be to Him, does not guide him, because guidance means that a person finds one who shows him the path leading to the goal. So "He guided them" means He showed them the path that leads to the goal. He does not act unjustly toward His creatures by withholding guidance from them; rather, those who wronged themselves and did not believe are the ones who do not receive the care of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, by their own choice.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 52:

And the Exalted Lord says:

﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease hastening toward them, saying, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us." But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him, and they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful.﴾

The context here concerned the prohibition of taking the People of the Book as allies (awliya', pl. of wali, "protector" or "ally") instead of Allah. Whoever hears this prohibition while faith is in his heart accepts the advice, but the one whose heart is blinded by the disease, which is hypocrisy (nifaq), is the one who takes them as allies, and he hastens toward this alliance. We know that al-musara'a (hastening, racing) means reducing the time taken to cover the distance that leads to the goal. So if a journey requires fifteen minutes of walking, hastening obliges a person to cover it in less time than that.

There are two constructions: "yusari'u ila" (hastens toward) and "yusari'u fi" (hastens into), as in the saying of the Truth:

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ (Qur'an 3:133).

Here the goal is forgiveness from Allah, and the believer must hasten toward it. But when one says "yusari'u fi kadha" (he hastens into such-and-such), it means that he was originally immersed in this matter. When the Truth says "yusari'una fihim" ("they hasten into [friendship with] them"), it is as if they had been with these disbelievers from the beginning; hence their hastening is within their circumstances, and they rush headlong toward them. The general cause is that there is a disease in their hearts which led them to invent and fabricate excuses, and these excuses are "We fear that a misfortune may strike us."

The alliance here stems from fear that the circumstances may turn, and that we will need them because they have wealth and weapons. This is what the hypocrite 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said; he said: "I am a man who fears reversals," meaning he fears events and calamities, just as we say: "The days are turns (duwal)." But the word "duwal" is transitional and may not involve harm, whereas "dawa'ir" (misfortunes) is transitional and involves harm. The opposite of this is what 'Ubada ibn al-Samit said, may Allah be pleased with him:

"I will take the wilayah (guardianship/allegiance) of Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, and I will shake off from me the wilayah of the Jews and the Christians."

The Truth quoted the hypocrite's words: "We fear that a misfortune may strike us, but perhaps Allah will bring a conquest." When we hear the word "al-fath" (conquest), let us know its most apparent meaning: it is judgment (al-hukm).

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ (Qur'an 7:89).

That is, judge, O Lord, between us and them.

So His saying, "But perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him," means the judgment that puts an end to the matter of alliance with the People of the Book and those who do not know.

The command from Allah is also a judgment from Allah, addressed to the believers in Him. The believer in Allah has deeds that are performed as causes leading to effects, but sometimes things come to believers without any preliminaries on their part, and they are a bounty from Allah. So "perhaps Allah will bring a conquest" means through causes you yourselves produce: you prepare what you can of equipment and provision, and you harass them. Therefore He said in another verse:

﴿You did not spur upon it any horse or camel﴾ (Qur'an 59:6).

An example of this is what happened with the Banu al-Nadir: there was the expulsion, and the Muslims took possession of the land of the Banu Qurayza, and this was the conquest from Allah, the Glorified. Thus the Truth deals with the believers in two ways: the first is that the believers produce preliminaries that lead to results:

﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ (Qur'an 9:14).

Here the Truth made the believers' fighting a cause. The second is the command from Him, by way of support through His lordship.

When you hear "'asa" (perhaps) and "la'alla", the meaning is hope (raja'), and hope means that the speaker hopes that what follows "'asa" will occur. For example, when we say, "'Asa an tukrima Zaydan" (Perhaps you will honor Zayd), the one who says it hopes that the listener will honor Zayd, and this means the speaker does not have in his hand the honoring of Zayd. But if the speaker says, "'Asa Allahu an yukrima Zaydan" (Perhaps Allah will honor Zayd), has the hope been transferred from humans to Allah? The speaker here is human and the one hoped for is Allah, and the power of Allah is wider than every power. Here we enter into the widening of the circle of hope. How much more so when the speaker is Allah Himself? Thus this is an expectation from a Generous One that must certainly be realized.

Through this we recognize the degrees of hope: hope from a human toward a human; hope from a human toward God for a human; and hope from God toward God for a human. Since the last hope is from the Supreme Owner of His own essence, He is the one who gives, so "perhaps Allah will bring a conquest or a command from Him," and this has in fact been realized. When they said, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us," while they were maintaining their relationship with the People of the Book for the sake of alliance and support, then afterward the conquest came by Allah's command. So what was their stance?

The stance became "they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful," meaning that they came to regret. Thus their saying, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us," became a disclosure of the disease of hypocrisy in their hearts. They had dressed the disease and expressed it with these words as a veil over what was in their hearts. It is as if what they concealed in their souls was hatred of this religion and hatred of this methodology, and that they did not want this methodology to prevail over others.

So the Exalted Lord shows us that the statement that arose from them, "We fear that a misfortune may strike us," was not the direct cause; the cause was the disease in their hearts. The disease is that they do not love the methodology of Islam to triumph, because they live on the wealth of those who oppose the religion, and when Islam holds sway their prosperity ends. Likewise, the People of the Book in Medina before Islam came were possessors of knowledge, wealth and standing, and the Aws and Khazraj would take wealth from them through usury, buy weapons from them, and take knowledge from them. When Islam came, all of that was lost to the Jews, so the disease took hold of their hearts, because Islam stripped them of temporal authority, the authority that had enabled them to distort the books of Allah. If they had entered into distorting the books of Allah, will they not also enter into enmity with you, O Muslims, and deceive you by claiming to help while they betray?

"So they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful." When they hear this divine speech, the Qur'an, which is recited, worshipped through its recitation, read in the mosques and heard, and there had been no conquest and no command, Allah informs them of their fate: "they will become, over what they had concealed within themselves, regretful." This means that He, the Glorified, wrote down what was in their souls, just as He said earlier: "and they say within themselves" (Qur'an 5:8 context, cf. 58:8). That is, they said it within themselves and the Creator heard them. Had they not said it within themselves, they would have declared that they had not said that; but they were confounded when the Truth exposed them, disgraced them, recorded what was in their souls, and set down the content of the saying. They should have acknowledged the content of the saying, and it was necessary for them to turn to faith, but they did not do so, and so they came to regret, according to the text of the verse that was revealed before a conquest or command came from Allah.

And Allah says, after that:

﴿Those who believe will say, "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?" Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers.﴾ (5:53)

Here the believers see with their own eyes the regret of these people. Regret (nadam) is the heart's breaking in the present over an earlier action, just as a person commits a folly and its effects appear afterward, so he says, "Would that I had not done that." It is a breaking of the soul over a previous action, and this breaking of the soul shows on the surface of the face. When the victory comes, you find the hypocrites and the People of the Book suppressed with a forced suppression, the kind of suppression its owner would not dare to show, so he claims to be happy; it is forced, pressed by an intention, and the trace of this appears on their faces.

Here the believers take notice of this, and so they say: "Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?" Had these hypocrites been truthful, they would have rejoiced, their faces would have been radiant, and joy would have appeared on them. But they became the opposite of that: they became regretful and suppressed.

"And those who believe say, 'Are these the ones who swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that they were with you?'" meaning: their deeds and their saying "We are with you" have come to nothing (habita). Habt, as we have said, is the bloating that afflicts a beast that eats food unsuitable for it, so people think it has grown fat, but when they look closer they find it afflicted with a fatal bloating. "Their deeds have become worthless, and they have become losers." The clear meaning of loss (khasara) is that the capital diminishes. The hypocrites did this to conceal themselves behind the Muslims, but this matter did not succeed for them, and they were exposed.

The Almighty then says:

﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion - Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah, and not fearing the blame of a critic. That is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.﴾

The address here is to the believers, and every call of this kind may be followed by a ruling, a glad tidings, or a warning to the opponent. What may appear to be a difficulty, though it is not really one, is that this statement comes and what follows it is the matter of faith itself, as in the words of the Almighty: "O you who have believed, believe." He calls them as believers and asks them to have faith. An example of this is the saying of someone: "O standing one, stand up," although one would expect: "O standing one, sit down," or "O standing one, come here," or "O standing one, go to so-and-so." So how does the Almighty say, "O you who have believed, believe"? Here we say: what is faith? Faith is the settling of belief in the heart, so that it no longer floats in the mind to be debated afresh; we call that 'aqidah (creed), meaning a matter that is tied (ma'qud) in the heart.

Therefore, when the Almighty addresses them and demands that they believe, the meaning is that the Truth says: You had faith before I called you, and with the secret of faith I called you, so guard this faith always and renew your faith constantly, for I have called you by the description of faith which I knew in you.

The Truth makes clear: O you who have believed, persist in your faith, and let every moment of your coming life be in lofty, elevated faith. Before I speak to you by the description of faith, you first believed, so I called you; so guard that and remain steadfast in your faith.

The meaning of His words "whoever among you reverts from his religion" is: whoever among you turns back from Islam, Allah will bring in exchange for him, and He will bring a people who will not be like those apostates. So whoever apostatizes should understand that he will not diminish the army of Allah by one, because He who decreed that His law should descend upon a messenger and a final prophet will not leave this messenger and this method at the mercy of people's changing states. If some people depart from the method, Allah replaces them with others. In this verse there is a grammatical form that differs from the verse in al-Baqarah in its i'rab (grammatical aspect). The Almighty says in the verse of al-Baqarah:

﴿They ask you about the sacred month - about fighting therein. Say, "Fighting therein is grave, but averting from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and [preventing access to] al-Masjid al-Haram and expelling its people from it are greater with Allah; and fitnah is worse than killing. And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able. And whoever reverts from his religion [and] dies while he is a disbeliever - for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah)

Here we found the Truth saying: "wa-man yartadid minkum 'an dinihi" (and whoever among you reverts from his religion). But in the verse we are concerned with in Surah al-Ma'idah, He says: "man yartad minkum 'an dinihi" (whoever among you reverts from his religion). We find the two styles differ, and the supreme wisdom in the Almighty bringing verses in His Book with the same meaning but with differing grammatical aspects is to show us that the Qur'an was revealed to all people. Before the Qur'an was revealed, there were two dialects: the dialect of Tamim and the dialect of the Hijaz.

The difference between the two dialects was confined to the word that contains doubling (tadh'if), that is, it contains two letters of the same form, i.e., identical. The word "yartadd" contains two "dal"s, and its original form is "yartadidd," while "yartadd" contains two identical letters, and pronouncing them is difficult. Therefore in such a case people tried to assimilate one into the other (idgham). So it was necessary to make the first of the two identical letters sukun (unvocalized), while the second "dal" should be unvocalized as well, because "man" is a conditional particle that causes jazm (apocope). The first "dal" originally takes kasra, and idgham is necessary, and idgham requires the first letter to be unvocalized. So for the sake of idgham we do that.

We know that two unvocalized letters do not meet, and the first letter was made unvocalized because it is necessary for idgham, while the other unvocalized letter is the one that arises incidentally, so we deal with it. Therefore we make it vocalized with fatha in order to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and so we say: "man yartadd," with fatha.

Once a question came to me: how does the Qur'an use "yartadd" in the accusative, that is with fatha? I said: it is not a "fatha of accusative." The questioner understood that "man" is either a relative pronoun or the conditional "man." If it were a relative pronoun, the statement would be "man yartaddu" with damma; and if it were the conditional "man," it would come unvocalized. Since the letter before it came unvocalized for idgham, we escape the sukun with a fatha, which is the fatha of escaping two unvocalized letters, because, as we have said, two unvocalized letters do not meet.

What appears to us is that the verse of al-Baqarah in which the Truth says "wa-man yartadid" is evidence, since when He coordinated, He said "fayamut" with jazm, as a conjunction after "yartadid." As for the reason the answer of the condition is clear in the verse of al-Ma'idah, it is that no second verb or conjunction came; the answer of the condition is the words of the Truth: "fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu," and what shows this is the entry of the "fa'" on "sawfa." But if the Truth had said, "man yartadd minkum 'an dinihi ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu," it could be quickly understood that "man" is conditional, because the word "ya'ti" would come apocopated by deleting its last letter. From here it becomes clear that the fatha in "yartadd" is the fatha of escaping the meeting of two unvocalized letters.

And what is the reason that the Truth brings one verse in this pattern and another verse in that pattern? We know that the Qur'an was revealed in the dialect of Quraysh, and Quraysh held sovereignty, and there was no tribe able to confront Quraysh. We all know that no one would dare to attack the caravan journeys of Quraysh to Yemen, and likewise in their journeys to Syria, because Quraysh settled where the Sacred House of Allah is, to which every Arab makes pilgrimage. And on the day anyone attacks the caravans of Quraysh, he must await punishment for himself or his tribe. So the Sacred House is what created for them that awe, and therefore the Truth alerts them to that when He said in Surah al-Fil:

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plan into misguidance? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and He made them like eaten straw.﴾ (Surah al-Fil)

Allah's threat against the companions of the elephant was carried out because they intended to demolish the Sacred House of Allah. Then the Truth follows Surah al-Fil with His words in Surah Quraysh: "For the accustomed security of Quraysh - their accustomed security in the caravan of winter and summer." (Surah Quraysh)

To make clear that among the causes of the safeguarding of the Sacred House of Allah is that He preserved for Quraysh security during the caravans of winter and summer; and had the House that secured Quraysh's sovereignty been destroyed, people would have attacked the Quraysh from every side, because He is the One who said regarding those who aimed to demolish the Sacred House of Allah:

﴿So He made them like eaten straw.﴾ [Al-Fil 5] ﴿For the accustomed security of Quraysh.﴾ [Quraysh 1] (Al-Fil 5 and Quraysh 1)

And since that matter was arranged by Allah for Quraysh, they must worship the Lord of this House:

﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.﴾ (Surah Quraysh)

So Quraysh took sovereignty among the Arabs through the status of the House, and they also took sovereignty in language. All the markets of the Arabs were held there, the most famous being the market of 'Ukaz, and in Quraysh was gathered the refined essence of beautiful dialects from the various tribes, and thus they took the purified, selected language. Every poet would present the best of his poetry, and every orator would bring the best of his speeches, and thus Quraysh would hear the finest words. Therefore the language they had was the elevated language. Hence, when the time came to write down the Qur'an, the instruction was:

If anything disputed arises among you, write it in the dialect of Quraysh, for the dialect of Quraysh has taken the finest qualities of the dialects. Banu Tamim and the Hijaz differed in some things, and therefore when we learned i'rab we would hear the teacher asking us: is "ma" Hijazi or Tamimi? This shows us that there is a difference in pronunciation between the two tribes.

In the verse we are concerned with we assimilate and say "man yartadd," while in the verse of al-Baqarah we pronounce it without idgham, saying "wa-man yartadid."

It is as if the Truth brought a verse in the dialect of the Hijaz and a verse in the dialect of Tamim, and that is a new proof that the Qur'an did not come to establish sovereignty for Quraysh; rather it is for all people, therefore we find a word from every dialect, to make clear that the Qur'an is for all people in general.

When we read the words of the Truth: "man yartadd minkum 'an dinihi fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu" (from verse 54 of Surah al-Ma'idah), we know that He, glory be to Him, teaches us that He is able to bring people of faith other than those who reverted from Him, just as He told us earlier: "wa-man yartadid minkum 'an dinihi fayamut wahuwa kafir fa-ulaika habitat a'maluhum fi'd-dunya wal-akhirah wa-ulaika ashab an-nari hum fiha khalidun" (from verse 217 of Surah al-Baqarah).

The statement here is news about the destiny of the apostate to Hell after the Hour arises. But the saying "man yartadd minkum 'an dinihi fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu" indicates that an event will occur before the Resurrection. And who could imagine that a God would send down a Qur'an with which He challenges, then bring in the Qur'an a matter still in the unseen and gamble with it, if it were not going to happen? The Truth says: "fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu," and "sawfa" informs us of a coming situation that will arrive afterward. We say here: who can control people's choices regarding faith? No one can control people's choices regarding faith except Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. He is the One who controls and decides, and He informs us that He will bring people who believe in place of the apostates.

But if people apostatize and wait to see their replacement, and it does not come, what then becomes of the matter? People would necessarily turn away from religion, and the Truth would not gamble and let it pass upon the tongue of Muhammad that a people would apostatize while he did not know whether apostate people would come. Knowledge came in this verse as in all the Qur'an from Allah, may He be exalted; and the Truth stated it as a cosmic fact: "fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu." Is there a people whom Allah loves while they do not love Him? We say: this does not happen with Allah, though it does happen in human life, just as the Arab poet said:

You are the beloved, but I seek refuge in Him
from being a lover who is not loved in return.

The misery of lovers comes only from a lover loving someone, and that beloved does not reciprocate the love, so the lover remains weeping all his life. And we may notice that the love of Allah comes first in this noble saying: "fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu," because this is the attribute of disclosure of knowledge: the Truth knew that they would turn toward Him, so He loved them; and when they came, they did what made them beloved to Allah. Then what is love? It is the affection of the heart, and we have said much before about the matter of the heart's affection. We know that there is one kind of love governed by the intellect, and another kind of love not governed by the intellect but governed by emotion.

An example of this: when we go to a doctor and he prescribes for us a medicine of bitter, unpalatable taste, we find the person prescribed the medicine goes to the pharmacy to ask about the medicine; if he does not find it, he goes around and searches in all the pharmacies of the town, and if he does not find it, he asks a traveler abroad, perhaps he may bring him the medicine; and if a friend brings him this medicine, he is filled with gratitude and joy. Does the patient take the unpalatable medicine with his emotion or with his intellect? He takes the medicine of unpleasant taste and loves it, and he loves it with his intellect; so intellectual love is the preference of what is beneficial.

An example of this: a father of a foolish son loves another man's intelligent son.

The father here loves his foolish son with his emotion, but he loves his neighbor's son because he possesses a store of intelligence. So there is intellectual love and emotional love, and this is what happens in the human sphere, but as regards Allah, it is not so.

When the Truth says: "fa-sawfa ya'ti Allahu bi-qawmin yuhibbuhum wa-yuhibbunahu," that means they love Allah with their intellects, and their love may rise until it becomes with their emotions. This may be tested when Allah brings upon people things that are evil in appearance, yet they remain in devotion to Allah; and that means their love of Allah has moved from their intellects to their emotions. And Sayyidina 'Umar went through this with him...

Almighty Allah says next:

﴿Your only walī (ally, protector) is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe: those who establish the prayer and give the zakāh (obligatory charity) while bowing in prayer.﴾ (5:55)

When Allah forbade us to take the Jews and Christians as awliyā' (allies, protectors), it is incumbent upon us to apply analogical reasoning (qiyās) that the prohibition encompasses all opponents of our religion, so we do not take any enemy of the religion as an ally for ourselves. This is because He, glory be to Him and exalted, has not left us without a walāyah (guardianship), for He is our walī, and likewise the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and those who believe.

If we wish to compare the walāyah of Allah with the walāyah of the enemies of Allah, let us know that every enemy of Allah has limited power, because he is a human being. As for Allah's walāyah over us, it has absolute power. Any enemy of ours may feign walāyah toward us out of hypocrisy, but there is no hypocrisy in Allah's walāyah toward us, because there is no power higher than His. And if Allah has forbidden us to take His enemies as allies, that is to free us from limited guardianship, to give us the guardianship that does not change, which is His guardianship, glory be to Him and exalted: ﴿Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. Thus the compensation in guardianship is greater than any imagination. And whenever we see (innamā, "only"), let us know that there is what we call (al-qaṣr, restriction) or (al-ḥaṣr, exclusivity).

For example, we say: (innamā al-karīm Zayd, "only Zayd is generous"). It is as if the speaker has surveyed people's opinions and found no generous person except Zayd, and it is as if he is saying: "Zayd is generous, and other than Zayd is not generous," and he abbreviated the two sentences into one sentence by his saying: (innamā al-karīm Zayd), and by this statement he affirmed generosity for Zayd and negated it from others. But if the speaker says: (Zayd is generous), this statement does not prevent others from being generous too.

Indeed, Allah, glory be to Him, restricts the walāyah in His saying: ﴿Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾, and He had already forbidden us earlier from the walāyah of the People of the Book, and from the walāyah of everyone in whom there is no affection or love that helps the believer in his mission of faith. For if one of the People of the Book or the atheists had affection and love that helped the believer carry out his mission, that person would not have remained upon his distorted methodology or upon his atheism; rather, that would lead him to go to faith in the message of Islam.

We find that the unbeliever's remaining upon his disbelief, his atheism, or his non-belief in the message of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is evidence that he has not been able to reach guidance, or that he—if he is of the People of the Book—has not been able to be trustworthy regarding the Book revealed to his Prophet, which contains the glad tidings of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. So how, then, could such a person help a Muslim? He is unable to help, nor to be an ally, nor to be upon guidance, because he has not been able to guide himself. That is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: (Do not believe the People of the Book and do not disbelieve them, but say: "We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you").

For he who cannot guide himself will not be able to guide others.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, forbade us to ask the People of the Book, he knew that they were in doubt about themselves, and in error and confusion; either they mix truth with falsehood, or they are in rage at those who believe. Therefore the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, forbade us to ask them. This is the precaution for the religion: a believer may ask them a question, and they answer truthfully, so the Muslim disbelieves them; or they answer falsely, and the Muslim believes them. Therefore it is not right or proper for a Muslim ever to ask them about anything, because he is exposed to one of two matters: either he believes in falsehood, or he disbelieves in truth. And the People of the Book themselves have contradicted one another. Did not the Truth speak upon their tongues: ﴿And the Jews said: "The Christians are not upon anything"﴾ (part of 2:113), and likewise the Christians said: ﴿"The Jews are not upon anything"﴾ (part of 2:113).

So which of the two positions shall we believe? Shall we believe the Jews' opinion about the Christians? Or shall we believe the Christians' opinion about the Jews? We cannot deny the Jews' opinion about the Christians, nor can we deny the Christians' opinion about the Jews. Therefore, when Allah, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾, we must understand that, since He has forbidden you to take allies besides Allah, He will not leave you, O believers, without a walī. Rather, He has only prevented you from the guardianship of those who cannot be sincere in aiding you or supporting you.

He, glory be to Him, has willed by the absoluteness of His power to be your walī, and the Messenger of Allah is also your walī, and likewise those who believe. Some say: The Truth has here enumerated the walāyah in Allah, glory be to Him, and in His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and in the believers; why then did He not say: "Your allies are Allah, the Messenger, and those who believe"?

We say: Was the Messenger's walāyah separate from the walāyah of Allah and the believers? Was the believers' walāyah separate from the walāyah of Allah and His Messenger? No; because all walāyah is directed to Allah. The Truth did not isolate the Messenger from his Lord, nor did He isolate the believers from the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and He did not divide walāyah into parts; rather, it is all one walāyah and one matter. We note that the address in the (second-person pronoun "kum") is plural: ﴿Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾, and the (kāf of address, "kum") here includes the believers together with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. So Allah, glory be to Him, is the walī of the Messenger and the walī of the believers, and the Messenger is the walī of the believers. And concerning the believers the Truth said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are awliyā' of one another﴾ (part of 9:71).

How many degrees of walāyah are there here, then? Allah is the walī of the Messenger and the walī of the believers. That is because He, by His grace, willed not to isolate or divide walāyah, but made it one walāyah; the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is the walī of the believers; and the believers are awliyā' of one another. Therefore we find that every believer is required to aid and support his believing brother.

Man, as we know, is a son of changing states, and since man is a son of changing states, we must know that the believers will not all remain always in the state of giving counsel, nor all always in the state of receiving counsel. Each one of them is at one time an advisor and at another time one advised. When weakness afflicts a believer in some part of his methodology, he finds that his believing brother has hastened to advise him so that he may be set right. And when weakness afflicts the advisor in some part of his methodology, the one previously advised hastens to advise his brother so that he may be set right. He who created creation is the best knower of them, and knows how changing states affect creation, and how each person has his own thoughts, his own suspicions, and his own moments of weakness and moments of strength. He, glory be to Him, did not ask people merely to counsel one another to good, but He said: ﴿And they counselled one another to truth and counselled one another to patience﴾ (part of 103:3).

Why, then, counselling to truth? Because the paths of truth are arduous, and because the people of truth encounter hardships from the people of falsehood. Therefore the people of truth must support one another, so that a person of the truth says to his brother what helps him hold fast to what is dearer than comfort, health, and wealth. We must make the truth clear in our lives and conduct, and the people of truth must recall to one another what happened to others and how they endured patiently; thus is the mutual counselling among believers.

And that is the walāyah of the believers toward one another: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are awliyā' of one another﴾.

So His saying, the Truth: ﴿Your only walī is Allah﴾ is what they call in the language (the style of exclusivity, ḥaṣr), meaning you have no walī except Allah. When a person turns away from limited-power guardianship and takes his recompense in what is not of limited power, that is a great gain for the servant. For this reason the Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: (Whoever relieves a believer of a distress of the distresses of this world, Allah will relieve him of a distress of the distresses of the Hereafter; whoever conceals the faults of a Muslim, Allah will conceal him in this world and the Hereafter; and Allah is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his brother).(1)

How will you, O servant, be in the aid of your brother? This is realized for you by offering your believing brother aid, support, backing, and counselling. You offer your brother of your time, your strength, your ability, and your wealth what helps him. And beware of reckoning the matter as though you could have done such and such with the time you gave to your believing brother; rather, you must reckon that Allah is the One who gave you the time, the wealth, and the effort, and that you do nothing by your own power, and that your limited power, when you give a portion of it to your brother, joins your limited strength to the Possessor of unlimited strength, who is Allah. Thereby Allah is with you in aid, and you become the greatest gainer. Whoever has Allah beside him will always be with creation in aid; and by this conduct the believer rises to the highest degrees of intelligence.

﴿Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. Glory be to Him, He wishes to show us the distinguishing features of the people of faith, for when we recognize the branches of faith and its beautiful attributes, we distinguish believers from others by these qualities. Establishing the prayer is the predominant attribute in describing those who believe in Allah, because the prayer is the renewed connection that proclaims allegiance to Allah five times each day. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said:

(Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing the prayer, giving the zakāh, fasting Ramadan, and pilgrimage to the House.)(2)

These five pillars are the supports and foundations upon which the edifice of Islam is erected. But no house stands on foundations alone; there are many other things, dozens of virtues and requirements beyond the foundations. If each of us reviews his relationship with the foundations of Islam, he will find that he bears witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah once in his lifetime, and after that establishes the prayer. Then he gives zakāh, but if he is poor he is exempt from paying zakāh. And even the one who pays zakāh pays it at one time in the year. Then he fasts Ramadan. But the sick person, the traveller, or one with an excuse breaks the fast and makes up the fast, and offers a ransom for the fast: the sick person whose recovery is not hoped for, and the elderly person for whom fasting causes severe hardship. And whoever makes pilgrimage to the House does so once in his lifetime, if he is able to find a way to it.

These are the pillars of Islam, and they contain many exemptions for the Muslim. Except for the prayer: it is a foundation that recurs, and therefore the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: (The head of the matter is Islam, and its pillar is the prayer.)(3)

And he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: (Between a man and shirk and kufr is the abandoning of the prayer.)(4)

And he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: (The covenant between us and them is the prayer; whoever abandons it has disbelieved.)(5)

Therefore it never falls. We pray standing, we pray sitting, we pray lying on our sides; and we pray when we are unable to make any movement. We pray with faith. Whoever cannot move his head in the motions of prayer during severe illness prays with his eyes. And whoever is afflicted—God forbid—with paralysis that prevents him from moving his eyelids in the motions of prayer, prays with his thoughts and his consciousness; that is, he performs the pillars of the prayer upon his heart. As for one whose consciousness has departed, the prayer has fallen from him.

That is why the Truth says: ﴿And those who believe, those who establish the prayer﴾, and then says: ﴿and give zakāh﴾, because giving zakāh means strengthening the effect of your movement toward others and extending the effect of these movements to the weak who are unable to do so; when you give zakāh, you are giving wealth, and wealth is the product of the effect of your movement in existence, and your giving of your wealth in zakāh also indicates faith. Then the Truth concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿while bowing﴾. Is the bowing here in the sense of bowing in prayer? Or in the sense of submission to all the obligations of Allah's methodology? Or was it revealed here on a particular occasion concerning a particular situation?

There is a report that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salām came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and said: "Some people of Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr have deserted us and separated from us, and they have sworn not to sit with us, and we cannot sit with your companions because of the distance of our dwellings." ʿAbd Allah complained of what he met from the Jews, and that verse was revealed: {Your only walī is Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe, those who establish the prayer...}
