When a person looks at the end, he finds that each animal has a task with the others, and this task leads to the good in what is good for the human being. The Truth has forbidden some things as direct sustenance, because they are indirect sustenance. Direct sustenance is what a person eats directly and what he wears, and indirect sustenance is a means to direct sustenance; and what Allah has forbidden are creatures that serve as means to the health of others.

﴿O you who have believed, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress﴾ – that is, do not make the forbidden lawful, nor make the lawful forbidden. And "do not transgress" means: eat of the good things without exceeding the limit, and this is the meaning of His saying, the Truth: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾ (part of verse 31, surah al-A'raf).

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.
.
2 Narrated by Muslim; al-Bukhari narrated it with the wording: (One of them said: As for me, I will pray at night forever. Another said: I will fast the whole year and not break my fast. Another said: I will abstain from women and never marry...)..

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ (88)

First, we ask: what is *al-rizq* (provision)? *Al-rizq* is that from which one benefits. What you eat is provision, what you drink is provision, what you wear is provision, what you learn is provision, and moral qualities such as forbearance, courage and others are provision. Everything from which one benefits is called provision.

However, when the Truth says ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾, it refers to what a person eats. And when He, glorified, says this, what is meant is that a person should eat from lawful and good provision. Thus, there is forbidden provision. An example of this is the thief who steals something from which he benefits. This is provision that came by a forbidden means, and if he had been patient, the morsel would have come running to his mouth because it was his provision. Or, provision is what Allah has made lawful. Here the scholars differed. Some asked: is provision only the lawful, and is the rest not provision? Others asked: is provision that from which one benefits, some of which is lawful and some of which is forbidden? The Truth says: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾ (part of verse 88, Surat al-Ma'idah).

"Eat what He has provided for you" is one style. "﴿Of what Allah has provided for you﴾" is another style. If it meant "what Allah has provided for you" in the sense that we eat all of it, this is not valid, because we obviously do not eat all of it. Rather, we will eat some of it, because what is eaten and consumed either is suitable for producing its like, or is not suitable for producing its like. When a person keeps flour, for example, it does not produce an ear of wheat. Therefore we must eat some and retain some that is suitable to produce its like. When we keep wheat, it is suitable to produce ears of wheat. Therefore the command came that we should eat some of what Allah has provided us, so that we retain some of the provision and do not eat it. This means that we preserve the continuation of provision. If a person ate all the wheat he had, how would it happen if he wanted to plant? Thus, preserving provision requires that we keep some of the provision in order to create a continuing provision in life.

Lawful provision here is of two kinds: that which is suitable for its continuation, so it is necessary to set aside some of it so that a person may use it to obtain another provision; and that which is not suitable for its continuation, such as flour for example. We eat some of it and keep some of it for those who cannot move about.

For this reason we find that the Truth, in Surat Yusuf, speaks of the king's dream: ﴿And the king said, "Indeed, I see seven fat cows being eaten by seven emaciated ones, and seven green spikes and others dry. O eminent men, explain to me my dream, if you should interpret dreams."﴾ (43) (Surat Yusuf)

Here the people who interpret dreams said: ﴿"They are confused dreams, and we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams."﴾ (44) (Surat Yusuf)

This is confusion in the answer, because saying they are "confused dreams" means they have no meaning, while their statement afterward, ﴿"And we are not learned in the interpretation of dreams,"﴾ means that they have an interpretation. And indeed they had an interpretation. Then who saw the dream? It was the king. And the Truth brings Yusuf to explain the dream. Thus it is not necessary that the one who sees the dream be a believer or righteous. Someone may say: how does Allah inform him of such matters? We say: a dream may be an honour for the one who sees it, and a dream may be an honour for the interpreter who knows the interpretation, and here it is an honour for the interpreter, who is our master Yusuf. Our master Yusuf knew how to decode ("cipher") the dream. What is remarkable about the dream is that the lean cows eat the fat cows. Here Yusuf said: ﴿"You will sow for seven years consecutively, and what you harvest, leave in its spike, except a little of what you eat."﴾ (47) (part of verse 47, Surat Yusuf)

That is: eat part of it, and let it be little by little. Do not be wasteful with it, so that you may benefit in the seven hard years, which are years of drought, eating in them what you gathered in the years of abundance. Leave the other part for the continuation of the species. It became clear that the best way to preserve wheat grains in our age is to leave them in their spikes, and likewise to leave maize in its husk. The interpretation of the dream was precise, because it intends to preserve for the people their lives in the time of drought, and likewise to preserve the animal fodder, so that people eat the grain and livestock eat the remaining straw. Likewise, the Truth guaranteed the foundations of life for everything necessary for life. We notice that what is eaten in this verse is little, while what remains in its spikes is much. This is in days of plenty. So what about days of drought?

﴿Then after that will come seven hard years, which will consume what you have stored for them, except a little of what you have guarded.﴾ (48) (Surat Yusuf)

That is, in years of drought people will eat much of the grain that is in the storehouses, and they must keep a little of what they guard in these storehouses, in order to preserve part of the wheat for sowing.

Therefore, "min" (from) in the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted: ﴿Eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾ is partitive, meaning: eat some of what Allah has provided for you. If things are such that their survival is a cause for the continuation of their kind, then the kind remains continuous. An example of this is a man who has watermelon seeds, plants them, and after the fruit comes, eats both the fruit and the seeds. From where will he plant in the coming year? He should have kept some of them to be seeds, and he should have kept part of the watermelon to give to his neighbour or to the needy.

Thus the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted: ﴿of what Allah has provided for you﴾ is suitable both for preserving the species and for directing the surplus to those who are unable (to provide for themselves). ﴿And fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾ means: when you fear Him whom you believe in as a God, there is no disgrace in that, because you believe that He is a God and a power. Disgrace lies in being commanded by an equal to you. As for submission and obedience to one above you, this is not a cause of disgrace; rather it is an honour and a dignity for you.

The Truth legislates this for us in the story of our master Musa with the magicians. Musa, peace be upon him, threw his staff, and the magicians saw it as a living serpent. The sorcerer looks at the thing he has bewitched and sees it in its true reality and original form, whereas those who are bewitched in sight are the ones who see the form that is intended for them to see. The magicians saw their ropes as mere ropes, and it was Musa's staff that became a serpent.

Here they realised that this was a different matter, so what did they say? ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ (47–48) (Surat al-Shu'ara')

They knew that this was a matter outside the scope of humanity. Thus, what the magicians did before Pharaoh's people was only an illusion to the sight: ﴿It appears to him, from their magic, that they are moving.﴾ (66) (part of verse 66, Surat Ta-Ha)

And the Truth said: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people.﴾ (116) (part of verse 116, Surat al-A'raf)

As for Musa, peace be upon him, when he threw the staff the first time and found it alive, he was afraid, because he saw in it a reversal of reality. But with the magicians, their ropes were not really serpents; they were magic upon the eyes of the people, that is, an illusion to the observer. Another example is our master Sulayman when he sent (a message) to Balqis, the Queen of Sheba. His messenger came to her saying: ﴿"Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission."﴾ (31) (Surat al-Naml)

So what did she say to her counsellors, the men of war? ﴿"I have never decided a matter until you witness it."﴾ (32) (part of verse 32, Surat al-Naml)

Here the counsellors understood that the matter required a political opinion, so they said: ﴿"We are people of strength and of great might, but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ (33) (Surat al-Naml)

Opinion, then, is the right of the politician who weighs matters by the scales of reason, the scales of probable outcomes, and the scales of reaction. Balqis wanted to deal with the matter politically, so she sent a gift befitting a queen. If the gift pleased him, then he was seeking worldly things and wanted their good. When her envoys arrived with the gift, what did Sulayman say?

﴿So when he came to Sulayman, he said, "Would you give me wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, you rejoice in your gift. Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from there in humiliation, and they will be debased."﴾ (36–37) (Surat al-Naml)

Here Balqis knew that Islam was a necessity. Behold the precision: that a command from an equal gives honour to the one who commands and humiliation to the one commanded, whereas if the command comes from one who is not an equal, and from the Highest, glorified is He, there is no humiliation in it for anyone. And Balqis's faith was a kingly faith.

So she said: ﴿"And I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ (44) (Surat al-Naml)

She did not say "I submitted to Sulayman," but said: ﴿"I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah."﴾ Thus there is no disgrace in her faith. This is so that her people would not think that she had brought them down to the depths of humiliation by being ruled by another human being. Rather, she and Sulayman are both subject to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and there is no disgrace in that. Now we return to His saying, majestic is His glory:

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers.﴾ (88) (part of verse 88, Surat al-Ma'idah)

That is: make for faith a rationale. As long as you have believed, you are obeying the command of the One in whom you believe. You believe only in one whom you trust to deserve belief. His saying first in the previous verse: ﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾ (88) (Surat al-Ma'idah)

and His saying as a conclusion to this verse: ﴿and fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾ (88) (part of verse 88, Surat al-Ma'idah)

is an encircling and enclosing of obedience by two faiths: a faith by which they were addressed, and a faith which they acknowledged.

The following is a passage from al-Sha'rawi's commentary (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 89:

And after that, the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately bound. Its expiation is feeding ten needy people with the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may be grateful.﴾

When we consider the words of the Truth, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths﴾, we know that (yu'akhidh) comes from (akhadha), and (ya'khudh) comes from (akhadha). If you say (akhadhtu fulanan bi-kadhā), this is evidence that you have inflicted punishment upon him, because he did not enter into a mutual covenant of goodness with you. But if you say (ākhadhtuhu), it is as though a mutual engagement has occurred, in that he has entered with you into a covenant of faith. For this reason the Truth seizes the disbelievers with the seizing of the Mighty, the Powerful. But He holds the believers accountable (yu'ākhidhu). Why? Because the believers are a party to the covenant, whereas the disbelievers are not a party to the covenant; therefore He seizes them with the seizing of the Mighty, the Powerful.

Thus, accountability (mu'ākhadhah) is other than seizing (akhdh). Accountability is the infliction of punishment upon one who has a covenant with you and who violates it by committing a transgression that has been stipulated; so one is never held accountable for a transgression that has not been stipulated, and no punishment is imposed on anyone without prior warning. For this reason, in civil law they say: there is no punishment except for a crime, and no crime except by a text (la 'uqūbata illā bi-jarīmah wa-lā jarīmata illā bi-naṣṣ).

Thus there must first be a text establishing the punishment for the crime, because a text declaring a given act to be a crime causes a person to reflect upon himself before undertaking such an act. As for the absence of a text stating that such an act is a crime, it leaves the person free to do it or not to do it, because it is a permitted act.

We must also observe the covenant in His words, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths﴾. When we consider the meaning of (al-laghw), we find it to be that which runs over the tongue without intention of the heart, such as a person's saying in colloquial speech: "No, by Allah," or "By Allah, you will come to lunch with us." This is al-laghw; that is, speech without the heart having any resolve in it. Allah, glorified and exalted, created us and He knows us best, glorified is He, that there are words that run over our tongues which we do not mean. The evidence for this is that a mother who loves her only son may invoke a curse upon him, but that is with her tongue, whereas her heart refuses that. For this reason the popular proverb says: "She curses her son, yet she hates whoever says 'Amen.'"

Thus the Truth, glorified and exalted, knows our human nature, and knows that the tongue may produce utterances that have not passed through the heart. Hence He says, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths﴾, and the Truth follows that with, ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately bound﴾. When we see the word (but, lākin), we know that there is a corrective exception (istidrāk), and istidrāk is the affirmation of what is supposed to be negated, or the negation of what is supposed to be affirmed. And when we see the word (you have bound, 'aqadtum), it is evidence that it is an act of firm resolve of the heart, and that before a person utters the oath he has considered the matter in his mind and his thoughts and has arrived at this decision.

Thus al-laghw is a word passing over the tongue without passing over the heart, and we have given an example of this, namely a mother's invocation against her only son. We see that there are many words that pass over tongues and may lead to disbelief, but the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, the conveyor from Allah, sets for us the sincerity of intention, saying: "He erred out of excessive joy." The Messenger of Allah said this in reference to a man who said: "O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your lord." (1)

This is al-laghw, and it is by Allah's mercy toward us that He pardons with His deep and vast mercy, saying to us: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately bound﴾. The word (you have bound, 'aqadtum) is evidence that the tongue did not merely bind something, but bound it with strong firmness. When you exaggerate an event, you bring for it the word that denotes the meaning precisely, with establishment and confirmation. Accordingly, the word ('aqd) differs from ('aqd) [in intensity]; thus the word ('aqd) means that a person has made a firm knot. As an example of emphasis, the Truth, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And the doors were bolted (23)﴾ [Surah Yusuf, verse 23]

Someone may say: Would it not have sufficed for the Truth, glorified and exalted, to say (ghullaqat al-abwāb, "the doors were closed")? We say: No; the Truth has used the verb that confirms the firmness of the closing. The closing of doors differs in degree from one to another: there is closing of a door by its latch-tongue (ṭablah), and there is closing by a bolt (mizlāj). His saying, ﴿And the doors were bolted﴾, means that the woman of the ruler exaggerated in bolting the doors. Likewise His saying, ﴿you have bound the oaths﴾, means that it has circulated in your hearts in a circuit that confirms the sincerity of your intention in swearing. There is another expressive image that meets this one in meaning, when the Truth, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing (225)﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah].

Here we observe that the hearts have "earned" (kasabat). What do hearts gain in such a case? We know that earning (al-kasb) is the existence of a yield above the capital. The additional earning in an oath is that a person confirms this oath with his heart; that is, the oath is concluded by tongue and heart together. The occasion of revelation of the verse in Surah al-Ma'idah, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for what is unintended in your oaths﴾, was that the Companions who had forbidden upon themselves the good foods, clothing and marriage, and swore to that, then when the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not prohibit the good things that Allah has made lawful for you, and do not transgress; indeed, Allah does not love transgressors (87). And eat of what Allah has provided for you [as] lawful and good, and fear Allah, in whom you are believers (88)﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah),

they said: "How shall we deal with our oaths?" Then this verse was revealed; that is, prohibiting what is lawful is unintended speech for which there is no expiation. We know that a person may not properly swear to something that has no bearing on him, such as a person's saying: "By Allah, I will not pray." Such an oath is not binding, and therefore it has no expiation. But if he says: "By Allah, I will drink wine," we say to him: follow what came in the hadith of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else better than it, let him do what is better and let him expiate for his oath." (2)

And the Truth, glorified and exalted, says, ﴿but He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have deliberately bound﴾. Thus there is a corrective exception concerning the emphatic oath, and it calls for accountability. How can there be accountability when it is a punishment, even though there is no punishment except by text? Allah, glorified and exalted, has concealed the punishment and prevented it through expiation: ﴿Its expiation is feeding ten needy people with the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. But whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days﴾. Expiation is a concealment of the punishment. Does this mean that a person is obliged to expiate as long as he has bound the oaths? No; expiation applies only when you break the oath and do not fulfil it. Thus in this domain the expiation is as follows: feeding ten needy people with the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave, or fasting three days for one who cannot find [the means].

What is appropriate in expiation differs in the view of jurists according to the one who breaks the oath. An example: a caliph in al-Andalus swore an oath and wished to discharge expiation for the oath. He came to the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id and asked him about the expiation for this oath. He said: "You must fast three days." Another person was sitting there, who gestured to the judge, but Judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id paid no attention to that gesture. When the judge left, the other person accompanied him and asked: "O Abu Sa'id, there is something in my mind about your fatwa; why did you not tell the caliph that the expiation for an oath is freeing a slave or feeding ten needy people?" Judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id replied: "Should the Commander of the Faithful be rebuked with the freeing of a slave or the feeding of ten needy people?"

This shows us that Judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id exerted himself to choose the expiation that would deter. It teaches us that expiation is, on one side, a deterrent to the self and, on another side, a remedy for the sin. Judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id preferred the deterrent aspect over the remedial aspect of the sin, because a caliph would not be burdened by feeding ten needy people, clothing them, or freeing more than one slave. (3)

As for feeding ten needy people with the average of what we feed our families, someone may ask: is the "average" here with respect to quantity or quality? We say: both quantity and quality are taken into account. If a person's meal consists of one loaf of bread, let him know that among his family there are those who eat three loaves at one meal, so the average in such a case is two loaves together with whatever relish is customary, such as meat and fat. Likewise with clothing: a person who expiates an oath by clothing ten needy people should clothe them with what covers the nakedness and with which prayer is valid, such as a wrapper and a cloak, or a shirt and a turban, or any garments that cover them. Now we find that the expiation of freeing a slave comes in the rank before last, and after it comes the Truth's saying, ﴿but whoever cannot find [the means], then fasting three days﴾. Thus the Truth did not arrange the expiations in order; rather, we must choose from among them the expiation that suits.

Then the Truth proceeds with the words, ﴿And guard your oaths﴾, and guarding is non-neglect. As for how we guard our oaths, we say: a person should not let oaths run on his tongue; this is the first. The second: a person should try not to break an oath. This requires that a person not swear to something he says with his tongue and subjects to his heart unless he is certain that he will mobilise all his limbs to carry out this deed that he has sworn to do; and this is the meaning of the Truth's saying, ﴿And guard your oaths﴾.

The Truth concludes the noble verse: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may be grateful﴾. Gratitude is the praise of the one who is favoured to the Benefactor for the favour. It is as though these legislations deserve our gratitude, because they have made unintended speech something for which there is no accountability, and because they have made an oath that you have bound subject to expiation; and in each of the two matters there is an ease that deserves gratitude to Allah.

(1) A hadith narrated by Imam Muslim.
(2) Narrated by Ahmad, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi from Abu Hurayrah.
(3) The majority hold that one does not expiate by fasting unless one lacks these three things: feeding, clothing, and freeing a slave.

Al-Sha'rawi continues: "Surely wine (khamr), gambling (maysir), idols (ansab), and divining arrows (azlam) are an abomination (rijs) of Satan's handiwork, so avoid it that you may prosper" (5:90). ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan; so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾

Whenever you hear the word "innama" ("indeed/only"), know that the grammarians call it an exclusive particle (adat qasr, a particle of restriction). For example, when we say "innama Zayd mujtahid" ("Zayd is only diligent"), we have restricted Zayd to diligence. But if we say "innama al-mujtahid Zayd" ("the diligent one is only Zayd"), then in this case we have restricted diligence to Zayd. When you restrict a person to a quality, this is called qasr mawsuf 'ala sifa (restriction of the qualified to a quality). When we say "innama Zayd sha'ir" ("Zayd is only a poet"), this means that Zayd is only a poet and is not a writer or an orator. But if you say "innama al-sha'ir Zayd" ("the poet is only Zayd"), this means that there is no poet except Zayd; it is as if you have denied to others that they are poets, and that Zayd alone is the poet, though he may also be a writer, an orator, and a scholar while being a poet. So, whenever you see "innama," know that it is one of the particles of restriction.

The Almighty says here: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan; so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah)

That is, wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are all an abomination from the work of Satan. Rijs is the bad, filthy, impure thing. Filth and impurity may be physical, like wine, or spiritual, like idols and divining arrows; the Almighty combined both in this verse. He did not say that wine is grape juice or apple juice; rather, He spoke of khamr, which includes everything that covers and veils the intellect. Some scholars were astonished that this verse was revealed in lands where there was no grape juice at all, because they assumed that only grape juice veils the intellect; but the Truth came with a comprehensive prohibition of everything that veils the intellect. Why, then, are wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows an abomination from the work of Satan?

The Almighty created man, made him a vicegerent (khalifah) on earth, subjected everything in existence to him, and asked him to worship Him alone and to cultivate this earth. The Truth willed to guarantee for man the safety of several things: the safety of his self, so that he is not attacked by killing or otherwise; the safety of his intellect, so that nothing is imposed upon it that veils the mechanism of choosing between alternatives; the safety of his honor, so that no one slanders it, and so that the offspring who populate the universe are pure lineages; and the safety of his wealth, so that the trace of his effort in life is preserved for him and others do not take the fruit of his effort. This is so that the worker does not lose interest in work, and that the faculties do not become accustomed to taking what is not theirs, becoming lazy and dependent. When a person gets used to taking without working, work becomes difficult for him. Thus the protection of wealth means that no energy is squandered, no right is wasted, and no one is given a right that belongs to another. In this way, artificial incapacity does not spread in the universe. Therefore the Truth, who is the giver of all wealth, said:

﴿Who is it that will loan Allah a goodly loan?﴾ (from verse 245 of Surah al-Baqarah)

That is, He, the Giver, the Exalted, has respected human activity, so that no one becomes comfortable with idleness. When unemployment spreads, Islam addresses the matter with profound wisdom: it asks the ruler to provide them with the means to work, so that they do not become accustomed to taking without working, lest it become a calamity for society. With the tolerant (samhah) Shari'ah, He willed to protect man from everything that destroys him. Thus, when He prohibited wine, He prevented man from veiling his intellect, because man's distinction over the animal is the intellect.

Man differs from the animal in that he preserves his life by his intellect, while the animal preserves its life by instinct. Therefore the animal has only one response when it is attacked: the dog bites the aggressor and the cat scratches the aggressor. But man, when someone attacks him, chooses between alternatives for responding to the aggression: he may strike, or kill, or forgive.

An example of this we see in the countryside: when a rider tries to force a donkey to jump over a small water canal, the donkey completely refuses, and no matter how much its rider beats it, it refuses to jump, because its instinct prevents it. But man may be seized by vanity, thinking he is able to leap over the canal, so he jumps but may fall into the water. Recklessness exists in man, but it does not exist in the animal, which is governed by instinct.

Another example from the animal world: we see the male buffalo approach the female to smell her, and if he finds her pregnant he does not mount her; such is the animal. But man is not like that. The donkey eats from clover, for example, only what satisfies it, and never increases its food no matter how much its owner beats it, because it is governed by instinct; but man may eat beyond his capacity.

Thus we find that instinct is what protects the animal, and the intellect is what protects man. Therefore the animal does not possess the capacity for choice, but the balance of its instincts never falters. As for the balance of instincts in man, it may falter.

God distinguished man from the animal by choosing between alternatives through intellect. Therefore it is not right or proper for man to obliterate this capacity with wine. If he obliterates the capacity to choose, his instincts in that case do not benefit him, because they are not equipped to protect him. Therefore, whoever obliterates his intellect places himself in a rank lower than the animal, because the animal is protected by instinct, while man is preserved by his intellect; and in this state he has obliterated and covered it. God prohibited wine because it veils the intellect. Everything that veils the intellect is khamr, even if its origin is permissible, because the intellect is the basis of responsibility (taklif). Likewise God prohibited gambling.

Consider the precision of the name God chose for gambling: it is "al-maysir" (ease/gain), and He did not name it "al-mu'sir" (hardship). No one engages in gambling while thinking he will lose; everyone who plays gambling does so in hope of winning. Therefore He used the name that expresses the state of the gambler: he plays under the illusion of winning; and if he wins, the gain tempts him to more play.

Losing also tempts one to play more, in the hope that some gain will compensate for the loss he has suffered. The gambler may sell everything he owns in order to make up his loss, and yet the gain from gambling is light upon the soul, which squanders it and spends it on what does not benefit, and may even spend it on what harms. The gain is not truly his, while the loss is charged to him. Those who gamble with one another are not bound by friendship or affection; each is eager to take what is in the other's pocket. This kind of play paralyzes the capacity for lawful earning, because lawful earning requires movement in the universe. Gambling paralyzes the winner's movement, because it makes him indifferent to work; and losing paralyzes the loser's movement, because however much he strives on earth, he may not be able to pay his debts.

Thus the Almighty wills to guarantee for people that no one benefits from anything except as a result of his own toil and work. The Truth wills that the body of every person be made from the fruit of his sweat in lawful work, and likewise the bodies of those he supports. He also informed us that idols (ansab) are an abomination from the work of Satan. The ansab were three arrows that were kept with the soothsayer (kahin): one arrow was inscribed "My Lord commanded me," the second was inscribed "My Lord forbade me," and the third was blank, free of writing, bearing no sign. If a person intended to travel, or to marry, or to trade, he would go to the soothsayer to cast these arrows for him. If the arrow inscribed "My Lord commanded me" came out, he would do it. If the one inscribed "My Lord forbade me" came out, he would not do it. But if the blank arrow came out, he would recast the arrows until one of the two came out: either the one bearing the command or the one bearing the prohibition. No one asked why, when the blank arrow came out, it was not considered as falling outside the scope of prohibition, and was treated as permission, a matter of choice whether to act or not. God made them forget this, so that He would show us that this is a false matter the soothsayers brought from themselves. If a questioner asked them: "Which god ordered the prohibition?" one of them would answer: "God is the One who commanded and the One who forbade." ﴿And Allah knows that they are liars.﴾

When the Almighty forbids us these things, He wants man to develop the faculty of choosing between alternatives. Man must deduce, analyze, and understand the premises, study them, and analyze the steps to reach conclusions; not disable the perceiving faculty that chooses between alternatives. Wine veils the intellect; likewise gambling places man between the jaws of illusion; and likewise idols paralyze the capacity to strive and cause submission to soothsayers. When you ask a drinker: "Why do you drink it?" he answers: "I want to cover up my worries." But covering worries does not end them; rather, facing worries is what ends them, through the means available to man. If your means are not strong, then turn to the Causer, in accordance with the saying of the Truth:

﴿Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ (from verse 62 of Surah al-Naml)

When you exhaust your means and turn to Allah, He helps you with the difficult matter that causes worry. For us, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is the model. When a matter distressed him, he would stand to pray. The word "hazabahu" (distressed him) means that it went beyond the scope of his means. Therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to turn to the Lord of causes. Some may say: "I call upon God much, but He does not answer me."

We say to him: either you prayed without real distress (idtirar), or you did not pay attention to the causes. And when you neglect the causes, you reject the hand of God extended to you through causes. I challenge anyone to find a person who has truly exhausted all means and yet no relief came to him. When you pray for a need and it is delayed for you, we say to you: you prayed without genuine distress. I often give this example, and to God belongs the highest example, free of all imperfection: suppose a major wholesale merchant sits in front of the warehouses he owns, and trucks arrive with crates of his goods, and workers are carrying the goods to put them in the warehouses. Suddenly he sees one of his workers about to fall with a crate he is carrying. Here you find the merchant rushing without thinking to rescue the worker. How much more, then, is the Truth who created the causes for us? If you exhaust the means, God helps you, in confirmation of His saying:

﴿Or who responds to the distressed one when he calls upon Him and removes the evil?﴾ (from verse 62 of Surah al-Naml)

Therefore wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan. Divining arrows are a kind of gambling. They used to bring a she-camel or a slaughtered camel, butcher it, and divide it into twenty-eight portions. They allotted one portion to one person, two portions to the second, three portions to the third, four to the fourth, five to the fifth, six to the sixth, and seven portions to the seventh. They would bring seven arrows: one arrow named "al-fadhdh," and the winner by it takes one portion; the second arrow named "al-tawam," which takes two portions; the third arrow named "al-raqib," which takes three; the fourth arrow named "al-halis," which takes four; the fifth named "al-nafir," which takes five; the sixth named "al-musbil," which takes six; and the seventh named "al-mu'alla," which takes seven portions. There were three other arrows: "al-munih," "al-safih," and "al-waghd," and these three receive nothing but pay the price of the slaughtered animal. That is an abomination from the work of Satan.

A sound soul does not incline to such actions; rather, some greed must stir it. Violations arise from two sources: either from the self, or from Satan. The violation that comes from the self is one that fulfills a particular desire, so that if the self is turned away from it, it still wants it. The violation that comes from Satan's suggestion is different: Satan may suggest theft to a person, and he refuses; then Satan knows that this person has immunity against

[The text breaks off here in the source; the remaining characters are garbled and cannot be rendered meaningfully: "ااا لالاتاااااا ااااببلللاااممممككططكممنخهقهخعثقعؤثقهعقثهخعقثاقلعانيب"]

So then enmity has already been established between Adam and Satan. How, then, can we, the children of Adam, accept his whispering? How can we accept his incitement? How can we accept his enticements? It is necessary, then, that we avoid all of that, because it is an abomination from the work of Satan, so that we may be saved from every evil, and all success may come to us.

The Truth says:

﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling, and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ (5:91)

Here the Truth did not mention the stone idols (al-ansab) or the divining arrows (al-azlam), because the believers do not hold any belief in them and have already abandoned them, and the address here is directed to the believers.

So why did the Truth, in the earlier prohibition, join intoxicants and gambling with the stone idols and the divining arrows? He, glorified is He, said that so as to make the matter appear abhorrent to us. He placed intoxicants and gambling together with the stone idols and the divining arrows, so that we would understand that the ruling prohibiting intoxicants and gambling came to link them with the stone idols and the divining arrows. And since they are believers, they must have already given up the stone idols and the divining arrows.

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you﴾. Will (irada) is the specifying of what is possible by some of what it may take. Will is connected to one who wills, so is he able to carry out what he wills or not? If he is able to carry out what he wills, then power comes after will.

When the Glorified and Exalted wills, power brings the willed thing into being; His power is never defeated and His will is never thwarted, because everything is subject to Him, glorified and exalted is He. The matter differs with man and with Satan. Man wills, but does he have the power to carry that out? Sometimes he has some measure of power to carry out what he wills, and sometimes not.

Satan wills, but can he carry out what he wills? He is able to do so when a human obeys him. This is the nature of Satan's will: he loves that disobedience should occur from a person, he wishes for it, and he plans for it. But the act does not come into existence unless the human agrees to obey Satan.

So if a will is from one who is able to compel and to bring about, it makes the action appear immediately, and the Absolute Capable is Allah, and He judges what He wills. That is why His saying, the Truth, comes:

﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ (36:82)

But the creatures' will is not such that things are subject to them in the way they are subject to their Creator, because the will of created beings requires that a person carry out according to his capacity, and however much it increases, it remains limited. Satan's will works by stratagem upon the human until he does what he desires, and Satan cannot force a person by compulsion to do something, but he adorns the deed for him. Satan has no authority of coercion to overpower a person into an action, and Satan has no ability of persuasion or of bringing proofs that make a person do Satan's purpose while he is content with his deed. That is why Satan says in the Hereafter to the wrongdoers: the sin is their own.

﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I called you and you responded to me.﴾ (part of 14:22)

Thus Satan declares that he has power over mankind, not by compulsion nor by argument; he only adorned the matter for them. Whoever has a desire, Satan adorns it for him, and he commits the sin. And Satan declares:

﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me.﴾ (part of 14:22)

Satan acknowledges that however much he cries out for help on the Day of Resurrection, no one will come to his aid; likewise the people of sins who followed him will cry out and will not find from Satan any help that rescues them from punishment. And "asrakha fulan fulanan" means he went to remove his cry and to come to his aid. So the Truth's saying: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you﴾ explains to us that Satan's will is a will of adornment, not a will of power to compel or to persuade. And when you hear the word (yuqi'), understand that there are two things whose original state is joining, and there is someone who wants to place between them something that separates that joining. That is why it is said: "So-and-so walked with al-wiqa'a," meaning he wanted to make a breach and a crack between two people whose original state is joining.

The phrase (baynakum, "among you") indicates separation. And this separation is where the discord is placed. Why? Because the believers are brothers, and the believer to the believer is like a solid structure, each part strengthening the others, and Satan works through intoxicants and gambling to walk with discord among the believers. And we find that in gatherings of drinking this occurs: those drinking together often end up in fights and exchange insults. And gamblers take one another's wealth, and thus they turn from a unity like a building into division, and enmity and hatred arise between them.

What is the difference between 'adawa (enmity) and baghda' (hatred)? 'Adawa is the separation of two who were joined, between whom enmity and hatred have arisen. Baghda' is the agitation of the heart by something disliked. It is as though hatred exists in the breasts after aggression has occurred, so that enmity becomes the middle ground that has pushed these two persons apart after they had yielded to Satan's incitement, whereas these two had previously been joined by purity, affection, love, and faith-based brotherhood.

Enmity in this case draws from the feelings of each side, because if enmity is from one side its life is short, but it lasts if it is between two parties. That is why the battle is fierce between two enemies each of whom feels enmity toward the other. And it becomes a kindled and blazing enmity if no third party intervenes to decide between the two with truth, so that the one who is upon falsehood is disgraced and the truth is taken from him and given to its owner, and here the one with the truth feels that there is someone supporting him. By this, enmity is settled and ends. But if the two parties find neither one who restrains nor one who deters, enmity remains aglow. That is why, when the Truth presented the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, and the matter of Pharaoh, He said about Musa:

﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ (28:8)

And why did they pick up Musa? ﴿So that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (28:8)

Did they know from the beginning that he was an enemy? No. They picked him up so that he would be a delight for their eyes, but Allah defeated their purpose. The lam in His saying (liyakuna, "so that he might become") is the lam of ultimate purpose and consequence, not the lam of effective cause, and by this He, glorified is He, established that Pharaoh is not a god, and that his followers were a foolish people without discernment. For if Pharaoh had been a god, he would have known that this infant whom he was raising would become his enemy.

And is this enmity only from Musa's side toward Pharaoh? No. It is enmity between Allah and Musa as one party, and Pharaoh as the other. Therefore He said:

﴿Cast him into the river, and let the river throw him onto the bank, and there an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his shall take him﴾ (20:39)

And this enmity did not end except with the drowning of Pharaoh. The Truth warns us: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through intoxicants and gambling﴾, and the (fi, "through") here is causal, like the saying of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she tied up; she neither fed it nor let it eat from the creatures of the earth until it died."(1)

In our daily lives we say: So-and-so was taken to prison for years over a quantity of narcotics. That is, he brought himself into something disliked because of a certain thing. And the Truth's saying ﴿through intoxicants and gambling﴾ indicates that enmity and hatred are contained within intoxicants and gambling. He then says: ﴿and to hinder you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾

The mention of any matter means that this matter should always be in the focal point of consciousness. Every piece of information a person recalls is in the focal point of his awareness, and afterward another piece of information moves to take its place. When a person's mind is occupied with something, that thing does not shift from the focal point of awareness to its periphery until another matter comes that occupies the mind.

So we say: beware of believing that the mind understands any matter from one time, or two, or three. No, the mind understands from one time, like a camera, and what matters is that at the moment of capturing the information it be free of other things. That is why we knew that our blind brethren who studied with us were more capable of retentive comprehension than we, the sighted; for the sighted person, when he is engaged in a problem, his eyes may be occupied with something, so the focal point of his awareness is scattered. As for the blind, the focal point of his awareness records only what he hears.

Thus we know what (dhikr, "remembrance") is. Intoxicants obliterate the intellect and veil it, so how can one remember Allah? Likewise prayer, which is the best of remembrance, is veiled from us by intoxicants. And likewise gambling, in which the illusion of gain gleams like a mirage, so the player pants after the game hoping he will win, and loses the capacity to remember Allah and to pray.

And because enmity has already been established between man and Satan, we find that Satan, as the Truth relates of him, said:

﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ (38:82)

Satan knew how to swear: he swore by the might of Allah that he would lead His creation astray. So if Allah had willed His servants, Satan would not have seized them. The Truth concludes the matter of intoxicants and gambling with His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ This is an interrogative, and an interrogative is a request for understanding a thing; this is what we know when the interrogative comes from humans. But when such an interrogative comes from Allah to us, it is the command of the Commander, glorified and exalted is He. How? There is a command from the Commander that is a binding ruling, and there is a command that Allah wills from the one commanded so that he commands himself by it.

This is a expression of trust from the highest Commander in the believing human who receives such a command. An example of this—and to Allah belongs the highest similitude—is that a father says to one of his sons: your neglect of your lessons will make you incur my anger and your classmates' contempt for you, and you will fall behind others; will you therefore stop playing and idling first? He did not say: "Stop playing," because the father wanted to set out the grounds so that the son would judge for himself, and so that he would manage the matter by its counterpart, and find nothing but to say: "I have stopped playing."

Here the matter also came in this form: instead of being a ruling from Allah, it became a ruling from the commanded servant. This is the most eloquent form of ruling, because the speaker casts the command in the form of a question, so that the one questioned manages every answer and finds only the answer the questioner wants. An example of this is when revelation paused from the presence of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the people of Quraysh said: "The Lord of Muhammad has forsaken him and hates him and abhors him." Then revelation came down to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with the words of the Exalted:

﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He hated you﴾ (93:3)

Revelation continues: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ (93:6)

And when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reflects on this matter, he answers: "Yes, my Lord, You found me an orphan and gave me shelter." This is called the commanded one sharing in the reason of the Commander, and this is the most eloquent form of command.

When the Truth says: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾, those addressed know what Allah desires, and they say: "Yes, our Lord, we have desisted." And they went to great lengths in this desisting. Imam 'Ali—may Allah ennoble his face—said: "If a single drop of it fell into a sea, the sea would dry up, and grass would grow in it, and my tongue would hang out from hunger, I would not draw near to it." This was not an obligation imposed, but exaggeration in desisting to the utmost degree.

And here is our master 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "If a single drop of it fell upon my hand, I would forbid it to myself." Thus was the response to the Truth's saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ And with that the matter of intoxicants was settled. We know that the legislation prohibiting intoxicants came gradually, and the religious obligations come through the tongue of a messenger, and a messenger does not come unless corruption has spread through society and in human beings simultaneously. So we do not find anyone who blames himself or intervenes to turn another from his corruption; here heaven intervenes by sending a messenger, and heaven does not pour all its rulings out at the very beginning, but calls, through the messenger, to faith in the one God, so that they may receive the ruling from him. Faith in the Oneness of Allah is the summit of creed, on which there is no leniency.

But in matters that relate to rulings, the rulings change customary conditions and social conditions current among people. So if Allah wills to change a custom by a ruling, He brings this matter ...

1 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Majah from Abu Hurayra.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 5, verse 92:

He, glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear notification.﴾ (92)

Having finished this particular ruling, Allah moved on to a general ruling, which is obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger. When you survey the command to obey Allah, you find it in several forms. Once He says:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ (Qur'an 5:92)

Here He repeats the command to obey Allah and to obey the Messenger. Obedience to Allah is in the general ruling, and obedience to the Messenger is in its detail.

Another time He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Say, obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ (Qur'an 3:32).

Here He does not repeat the command to obey. There is one command to obey, one who is obeyed, and one who obeys, and those addressed are the ones who obey. So here He unifies the command to obey; the one obeyed is Allah, and the Messenger is mentioned coordinated with the divine name.

Another time the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And obey the Messenger﴾ (Qur'an 24:56).

So we are before cases of obedience: the first, "And obey Allah and obey the Messenger"; the second, "Say, obey Allah and the Messenger"; and the third, "And obey the Messenger." Only once is "those in authority" (ulu al-amr) coordinated with these, when He, exalted is He, says:

﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ (Qur'an 4:59).

When the Truth says: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ (Qur'an 5:92),

He repeats the command to obey in relation to Allah and in relation to the Messenger; but in relation to those in authority, He, glory be to Him, did not bring the word ﴿obey﴾. This is because obedience to those in authority comes from within the two obediences: obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger. There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator. When the Truth says ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾, obedience to Allah is in the general ruling, and obedience to the Messenger is in the detail of the ruling. The example is His saying: ﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ (Qur'an 3:97).

Here we obey Allah in the general ruling, and we obey the Messenger in the detail of the pilgrimage, because the detail did not come in the Qur'an, and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ﴿Take from me your rites﴾. When the two commands are unified, ﴿Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾, this means that there is one command issued by Allah, and the Messenger's performing and carrying out of the act is for exemplary conduct and as an example, and as confirmation of the ruling.

If Allah has a command in summary and the Messenger has a command in detail, He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾. And if the command is only from the Messenger and nothing of it has come from Allah, it is a command issued by delegation from Allah, based on His saying:

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (Qur'an 59:7).

Thus we find that no obedience is confused with another obedience, and no obedience contradicts another obedience. The Truth here says: ﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware.﴾ Why this warning? This warning comes to teach us that Satan will not let us enter the domain of obedience to Allah and obedience to the Messenger, and he will strive hard to confuse the matter for us. When Satan notices an inclination in a person's soul toward some kind of desire, he enters through the gate of sins. If a person has closed some paths before Satan, so that he cannot tempt him, for example, with theft or drinking wine, he does not leave him; rather he enters through the gate of obedience. Satan comes to a person at the moment of ablution and makes him forget whether he washed this hand or that, whether he perfected the ablution or not. Or Satan comes to the believer at the moment of prayer and makes him forget the number of rak'as or the number of prostrations. In this way Satan enters the believer through the aspect of obedience.

The meaning of His saying ﴿and beware﴾ is: beware that Satan should trick you, because he will try to enter to you from every entrance. He enters upon the one who wastes himself in sin, and the most severe works of Satan against the believers is that he enters upon them through the gate of obedience. Therefore the Truth said ﴿beware﴾. Often we find one of us forgetting some matter, and when he comes to prayer he remembers that matter. Satan does not leave a person in such a state. Satan swore an oath, saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ (Qur'an 38:82).

And the Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ (Qur'an 7:16).

He swore that he would stand on the straight path, not on the crooked path. An example of this is when a person gives charity and announces it, saying: "I have given more than so-and-so." Thus his reward is lost. Satan thus tries to enter upon us through a door we do not notice, which is the door of obedience. I will narrate to you this story so that you know how far Satan's intrusion reaches. It happened to the Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him: a man came to him asking for a fatwa on a strange matter. The questioner said: "My money was lost. I had buried it in a place in the ground, and a flood came and obliterated the place of the money and removed the stone I had placed as a marker of its location." Imam Abu Hanifa said: "Go tonight after the 'isha prayer, stand before your Lord until dawn breaks, and tell me what will happen." When the dawn prayer came, the man came to Abu Hanifa joyfully and said: "I have found my money."

Abu Hanifa asked him: "How?" The man said: "While I was standing for prayer, I imagined the place where I had put the money, and when the flood came, and how it flowed, and so I measured the distance and estimated it until I knew the location of the money." The Imam laughed and said: "By Allah, I knew that Satan would not let you complete your night with your Lord." Thus you see how Satan enters through the door of obedience. Therefore the Truth said:

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger and beware. But if you turn away, then know that upon Our Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ (Qur'an 5:92).

That is: if you turn away from what you have been charged with, know that by your turning away and aversion you will not harm the Messenger, because the Messenger was only charged to deliver the clear notification; rather you have harmed yourselves when you turned away from what you were charged with. The Truth knows from eternity that some of His servants may say: "This ruling has not come in the Qur'an." Therefore He brought the command to obey the Messenger. Thus obedience to the Messenger became an independent obedience, which Allah willed, so as to forestall those who ask for a text that contains every detail, whereas these details are found in the noble Sunna of the Prophet. An example is the number of rak'as of each prayer: it did not come in the Qur'an, but we know it in detail from the Messenger, and the Truth delegated legislation to His Messenger:

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (Qur'an 59:7).

He, glory be to Him, knew from eternity that there would be someone who claims he will obey only the Qur'an. Therefore the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Soon a man among you will sit on his couch, speaking of my hadith, and say: 'Between us and you is the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Whatever we find in it as lawful, we deem lawful, and whatever we find in it as unlawful, we deem unlawful.' Indeed, what the Messenger of Allah has made unlawful is like what Allah has made unlawful."(1) That is, the Messenger is the one who conveys from his Lord, and we must beware of Satan when he wants to enter upon us through the gate of obedience. But why did the Truth say ﴿But if you turn away﴾? And from what does the turning away occur?

The Truth said that to make clear to us that a person has the choice to go to obedience, and has the choice to go to disobedience. If a person turns away from obedience to disobedience, and from the faith that the Messenger brought, who conveyed from Allah, to remaining in disbelief, then that person should know that the Messenger has fulfilled his mission and discharged it. What is required of the Messenger is that he convey the method, and he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has conveyed a clear, comprehensive, evident notification that encompasses all the matters of life.

The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has informed us of what Allah requires of us: to believe in one God, capable, wise, possessing all the attributes of perfection. That is the first command in creed. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed us that we should keep away from what the Arabs were upon: the idols (ansab), the images (awthan), and the statues (asnam). The Messenger's notification requires of us faith and action, and action divides into two kinds: positive action and negative action. Positive action is concentrated in "do such-and-such," if you are not doing it; negative action is that you refrain from what Allah has forbidden you and the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has forbidden you.

So the first requirement is faith in the one God, and that we refrain from worshipping idols and statues. And a demand, as we know, is that you produce speech by which you ask your addressee to do something that was not being done at the time of the demand. So when the Truth makes clear "do not worship idols," this is a demand for an act, namely that we refrain from worshipping idols. When the Truth commands us to pray, to fast, to pay zakat and to perform the pilgrimage to the House, these are demands for acts. The demand for an act is called (amr, command), and the demand to refrain from an act is called (nahy, prohibition).

If you look at all the obligations in Islam, you will find they did not come all at once, but came over the course of twenty-three years. When Islam came, people believed in it, and none of the rulings that were revealed over the years of the mission had yet been enjoined upon them to implement; rather, only a small part of them was required, and they performed it. Some of them were only informed of the necessity of believing in the one God, believed in that, and then their end came, and they had Paradise. Others had their lives prolonged, so new rulings were added to them, and they implemented them, and their Islam was thereby complete Islam.

Therefore, completeness in Islam is the implementation of every work that came in the rulings the Muslim attained. If a Muslim attained only one ruling and implemented it, he has all that the Truth promised. An example is (Mukhayriq the Jew), who embraced Islam and bequeathed his property to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When the day of Uhud came, he stood among his people saying: "O assembly of Jews, by Allah, you know that the victory of Muhammad over you is a truth." They did not answer him, so he took his sword and his equipment and said: "If I am killed, my property is for Muhammad to do with as he wishes." Then he went out to fight and fought until he was martyred. He had not implemented any ruling of Islam, but he fought and attained the honour of martyrdom, and the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of him: "Mukhayriq is the best of the Jews."(2)

We must always distinguish between (the pillars of Islam) and what is required of the Muslim. We all know that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, the establishment of prayer, the giving of zakat, the pilgrimage, and the fasting of Ramadan."(3)

These are the pillars of Islam. As for the Muslim, what is required of him may differ. What is required of the Muslim is that he bear witness once in his life that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. And it is always required of him to establish prayer, whatever his condition. But the obligation of zakat may fall from him if he has no property. The fast may fall from him if he is ill with an illness from which recovery is not hoped, or if he is elderly and unable to fast, in which case he owes the expiation of feeding a poor person; as for the sick person whose recovery is hoped for, and likewise the traveller, they make up the fast after the excuse has passed, and likewise the menstruating woman and the woman in postpartum bleeding. The pilgrimage may also fall from him because he does not have sufficient wealth. Thus the pillars of Islam differ from one Muslim to another, and thus we know that whoever lived at the beginning of Islam and implemented the few rulings that were revealed until he died or was martyred, has fulfilled what Islam requires of him.

1 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Darimi, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.
2 Narrated by Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Abu Nu'aym in Dala'il al-Nubuwwa, Ibn Kathir in al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya, and Ibn 'Asakir in Tahdhib Tarikh Dimashq.
3 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i from Ibn 'Umar.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 5, verse 93:

When the prohibition of wine (khamr) and gambling (maysir) was revealed, some people went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to ask him about the fate of their companions and brothers in faith who had died or been martyred before the prohibition of wine and gambling was revealed. The very act of asking is a sign of faithful vigilance, for a person is not a believer until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Here, the Truth, glory be to Him, revealed the noble words:

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good, and Allah loves the good-doers.(93)﴾

The Truth revealed this verse to reassure the believers who asked about the ruling concerning their brothers who died or were martyred while they used to drink wine before the ruling of its prohibition was revealed. ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾, and "ṭaʿimū" (what they have eaten) does not refer to food only, but also includes and encompasses drink. Thus the Truth says:

﴿Indeed, Allah will test you with a river; whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me﴾ (part of verse 249, Surat al-Baqarah)

Accordingly, water is food, meaning that its tasting is in the mouth. Thus the Muslims who had asked about their brothers who died or were martyred learned that their Islam had been limited to the rulings revealed during their lifetimes, for they had carried out what was required of them by abandoning the worship of idols. Some of them may have died before prayer was prescribed, or before the rulings on zakat or fasting were revealed, and therefore they did not perform them. Accordingly, their righteous deed is the implementation of the teachings that were revealed to them. They feared Allah and carried out the requirement of faith to the extent of what the Truth demanded of them; they believed in the God who imposes obligations, and they placed between themselves and Allah a shield by carrying out His requirements, in command and prohibition, glory be to Him.

Faith has a summit, which is that a person believes in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, and after that in the rulings that descend from heaven. The scholars differed among themselves on the question of the increase and decrease of faith. Some scholars said: faith neither increases nor decreases. Other scholars said: faith increases and decreases. Those who said faith neither increases nor decreases looked at faith in its doctrinal summit, which is belief in Allah. Those who said faith increases and decreases looked at faith in terms of the rulings that Allah sends down, and they derived this from His saying, the Truth:

﴿And when a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice.(124)﴾ (Surat al-Tawbah)

So every verse that descends with new rulings increases faith. When the ruling on zakat was revealed, the Muslims believed in it and implemented it. Some of them did not possess wealth, so they did not implement the ruling, although they believed in it.

The Muslim believes in the ruling, and if he is able, he carries it out, and if he is unable, he does not carry it out. For this reason they used to rejoice at the rulings that the verses brought down. Accordingly, the disagreement of the scholars is a disagreement from separate aspects. We observe that the Truth says:

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten, if they fear Allah and believe and do righteous deeds, then fear Allah and believe, then fear Allah and do good, and Allah loves the good-doers.(93)﴾ (Surat al-Ma'idah)

So here there are three stages. There is one who lived to see a ruling, feared Allah, believed and did righteous deeds, and then passed on to his Lord, so there is no blame upon him. There is one who lived to witness other rulings, believed in them and acted upon them. And there is one who lived to witness rulings that had increased, and he acted upon them also. The first faith was linked to righteous deeds, and likewise the second faith mentioned in the verse. Then the third faith comes linked to ihsan (excellence).

Ihsan, as we know, has two aspects. The first is that the believer worships Allah as if he sees Him, and whenever an obligation comes, the believer performs it excellently, as if he sees Allah; and if he does not see Him, he senses that He, glory be to Him, sees him. When the Muslim comprehends all of Allah's rulings, which in turn encompass all the affairs of life, he performs these rulings excellently. The second aspect of ihsan is that the believer increases in performing these obligations beyond what Allah has prescribed, which are the voluntary acts (nawafil). Thus the believer does not suffice with affirming the rulings that were revealed, but increases in their kind. The Truth says:

﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs (15), taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that good-doers (16)﴾ (Surat al-Dhariyat)

The Truth gives the reason, which is: ﴿Indeed, they were before that good-doers﴾ (part of verse 16, Surat al-Dhariyat).

The manner of their ihsan is that one of them does not stop at what Allah has obligated him with, but adds to what Allah has obligated of the same kind. The Truth has obligated five obligations upon Muslims, and the good-doer is the one who adds and draws near to Allah through voluntary acts. Allah has obligated upon the Muslim the fasting of Ramadan, and the good-doer is one who performs the fast of Ramadan completely and adds the fasting of other days of the year. Allah has obligated upon the Muslim zakat on wealth at two and a half percent, which is one-fortieth, and the good-doer may increase zakat beyond that. Allah has obligated upon the Muslim the Hajj to the House for whoever is able to find a way to it, and the good-doer is the one who increases the number of pilgrimages.

Thus, the good-doer is one who loves the obligation from Allah and knows the station of nearness to Allah, so he finds that Allah has obligated him less than he deserves from Us, glory be to Him, and so he increases the deeds that bring him nearer to Allah. The Truth adds in describing the good-doers: ﴿They used to sleep little of the night (17)﴾ (Surat al-Dhariyat).

Allah did not obligate us to sleep only a little of the night. He obligated us only to pray the 'isha' prayer, and after that we may sleep so that we wake up to pray the dawn prayer. But the good-doer, who has known the sweetness of solitude with Allah, sleeps only a little of the night. The Truth, glory be to Him, adds in describing the good-doers: ﴿And in the hours before dawn they seek forgiveness (17)﴾ (Surat al-Dhariyat).

Allah did not obligate the Muslim to seek forgiveness at dawn, but the good-doer does so. The Truth, glory be to Him, adds:

﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived (19)﴾ (Surat al-Dhariyat).

He, glory be to Him, did not say "a known right," because the known right is zakat. These three stages are what bring the believer into the rank of ihsan. Therefore, in the last stage of the verse we are concerned with, the Truth speaks of ihsan: ﴿then fear Allah and do good﴾, meaning that the believing person increases in the kind of what Allah has obligated. At the time when the obligations were in the phase of completion, each ruling that came was received by the believer with faith and action. As for those who witnessed all the obligations during the twenty-three years — the period that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) remained and lived as a messenger, then passed on to the Highest Companion — the obligations became equal for them, and if they wished to do ihsan, they must increase in the kind of obligation.

The Almighty then says: "O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of the game that your hands and your spears can reach, so that Allah may know who fears Him unseen. Whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment" (5:94).

This is a transition to a new ruling. After Allah spoke about what He made lawful for us, saying: "Lawful for you are the grazing animals of the livestock" (part of 5:1),

and after He spoke about what He forbade us, namely carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, that over which other than Allah has been invoked, the strangled, the beaten, the fallen, the gored, what the beast of prey has eaten except what you slaughter, and what is sacrificed on stone altars (ansab), and divining by arrows (istiqsam bil-azlam), as well as intoxicants and gambling, He wished to give us prohibitions of a special kind. In order to know these prohibitions, we must know that there are things forbidden in every time and every place, such as intoxicants, gambling, fornication and other constant prohibitions, whether they are idol worship, divining arrows, or eating carrion, blood and the flesh of swine. There are also prohibitions bound to particular times or particular places. Every act, whatever it is, must have a time and must have a place.

We are commanded to pray at its time in any clean place suitable for prayer. Likewise, fasting is governed by time. As for the Hajj, what governs it is both time and place. As for the 'umrah, what governs it is place, because a person can perform 'umrah at almost any time. Here, the Almighty speaks of a prohibition in a specific place and at a specific time: game is not forbidden except when a person is in a state of ihram (ḥaram).

We know that the word "ḥurum" is the plural of "ḥaram" (sacred state of pilgrim consecration). A person is in the state of ḥaram either at the place where the prohibition begins. For example, the area of Rabigh, where ihram begins for the people of Egypt. If you arrive at this place and begin any act of Hajj or 'umrah, the first act is ihram. From the moment of ihram, even if you put on ihram from your own country or house, hunting is not permitted to you. Al-Ḥaram is also a description of a place, even if the person is not a pilgrim; hunting is forbidden in the Haram, and the Haram has boundaries that the Shari'ah has defined. Hunting in it is forbidden to both the one in ihram and the one not in ihram. We know that the Umma of Muhammad (ﷺ) has been granted by Allah the entire earth as a place of prostration and a means of purification.

Accordingly, any place can be a place of prayer, a place where knowledge may be studied, a place where a factory may be built, or a place where crops may be sown. Thus any land is suitable to be a masjid in the sense of a place of prostration. But masjid in the technical sense is the place specifically designated for prayer. As for al-Masjid al-Haram, its center is the Ka'bah, around it is the ṭawāf, and around that are the boundaries of the Haram. Al-Masjid al-Haram lies within the circle of the Haram, which begins at al-Tan'im, al-Ji'ranah, al-Hudaybiyah, al-Juhfah and others; these are the boundaries of the Haram. So when a person comes to the miqat of Hajj at Rabigh, for example, he does not hunt, because he has entered the circle of the Haram, and hunting is forbidden to him even if he is not performing Hajj or 'umrah.

Hajj, as we know, is a journey that Allah has enjoined once in a lifetime, to which the Muslim sets out, living in every place by the blessing of the Benefactor. When the Muslim sets out for Hajj, he sheds all the blessings that create distinction for him, so that he stands equal with all of Allah's creation. The first distinguishing mark of a human being is clothing, therefore Muslims take off their garments and put on a uniform garment in which they are all equal. When a Muslim leaves all blessings, it is because he is going to the Benefactor.

After that, Allah wishes to train us in a faith-based discipline with all existence. In Hajj, Allah clarifies this entire matter: all are equal in clothing, nearly identical, all with dishevelled hair and dusty, all saying: "Here I am, O Allah, here I am." Thus distinction among people is cleared away through ihram.

Then we look at the lower kind, which is animals. Allah teaches us courtesy toward this kind, so He prescribes the prohibition of hunting them. He also teaches us courtesy toward the plants beneath the animals, so He prevents the Muslim from cutting the trees of the Haram. In this way the entire matter is purified, and servitude becomes a path for all.

In Hajj all titles and differing ranks disappear from the moment they turn toward Hajj. Around the Ka'bah one sees the guard and the minister, and he weeps, and everyone feels that all are equal. Allah says: "Whoever enters it is safe" (part of 3:97).

So animals are safe, and likewise plants. This is what Allah commanded within the circle of the Haram, because it is a training for the human being to come out of the blessing toward the Benefactor. After that he enters the masjid and circumambulates the Ka'bah. We find the human being, the master of existence, taking a different stance toward everything in existence that serves him: animals take their dignity, and likewise plants, and likewise inanimate things take their dignity too. Thus, from the Black Stone the ṭawāf begins, seven circuits.

In Hajj a person shakes off any arrogance from himself and stands equal with all people. He shakes off his arrogance before the lower kind, which is animals, so He forbids hunting them, and we know that animals nourish humans. He also shakes off his arrogance toward plants, which nourish humans, so He forbids cutting them.
